«Ne cédons pas à l’esprit de défaite, à la fatalité», a lancé Emmanuel Macron à la tribune des Nations unies. Dans son dernier discours en tant que président à la tribune des Nations unies, le président français a appelé à la défense de l’organisation et de la diplomatie multilatérale. Sur la justice internationale, sur l’intelligence artificielle, sur la question palestinienne, il a aussi pris l’exact contre-pied de Donald Trump. «Nous devons nous mobiliser, encore et encore, pour défendre le droit international et le droit international humanitaire», a dit le président français. «En temps de guerre, il ne peut y avoir de paix sans justice. C’est pourquoi la France soutient, politiquement et opérationnellement, les mécanismes internationaux…. Et nous continuerons de soutenir la Cour internationale de Justice et le rôle central qu’elle joue. Nous ne pouvons pas accepter ce nouvel ordre d’impunité que certains tentent d’ériger», a affirmé Macron.

items.title: Une bijouterie cambriolée en pleine nuit à Lyon, les auteurs du vol en fuite et une enquête a été ouverte
items.summary: Un braquage a eu lieu à Lyon, dans la nuit de mardi à ce mercredi 23 septembre, dans la bijouterie Edenly. Quatre personnes ont cassé la vitrine à coups de marteau afin de voler les bijoux. Une enquête a été ouverte. Les auteurs sont toujours en fuite et activement recherchés.
items.body_text:
BFM LyonRomain Ethuin, Pauline Revenaz avec Elisa Lanzarone
Un braquage a eu lieu à Lyon, dans la nuit de mardi à ce mercredi 23 septembre, dans la bijouterie Edenly. Quatre personnes ont cassé la vitrine à coups de marteau afin de voler les bijoux. Une enquête a été ouverte. Les auteurs sont toujours en fuite et activement recherchés.
Un cambriolage bruyant et spectaculaire en pleine nuit. Une bijouterie de la rue des Archers, dans le 2e arrondissement de Lyon, a été victime d'un vol par effraction, dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi, vers 3h30, ont appris BFMTV et BFM Lyon.
Les auteurs ont pris la fuite en voiture après que l'alarme a été déclenchée. Pour l'heure, aucune interpellation n'a eu lieu.
Le préjudice est en cours d'évaluation et une enquête a été ouverte par le parquet de Lyon des chefs "de vol en bande organisée et participation à une association de malfaiteurs", a indiqué le parquet de Lyon ce mercredi 23 septembre. En ajoutant que les investigations confiées à la DIPN du Rhône "se poursuivent pour identifier et interpeller les auteurs de ces faits".

Des images circulant sur les réseaux sociaux montrent quatre personnes vêtues de noir casser la vitrine à coups de marteau et rentrer dans la boutique avec un sac de courses afin de voler les bijoux.

items.summary: Les candidats à la primaire socialiste vont débattre pour la première fois entre eux à cinq. La justice a rejeté ce mercredi la demande de réintégration de Philippe Brun.
items.body_text:
DIRECT. Primaire socialiste: le PS "prend acte" de la décision de justice conernant Philippe Brun et de ses déclarations
L'ESSENTIEL
- Au lendemain de l'audience en référé contre le PS concernant l'exclusion de Philippe Brun du parti, mais aussi de la primaire pour la présidentielle, la justice a décidé de rejeter la demande de réintégration du député. Lire l'article
- Le député écarté Philippe Brun dénonce "un coup monté" et une "affaire Olivier Faure" après son "exécution politique". Lire l'article
- Les candidats à cette primaire débattront pour la première fois tous ensemble ce mercredi soir. Lire la brève
- Le ministre du Commerce Serge Papin a annoncé sur BFMTV-RMC que la nouvelle aide grands rouleurs du gouvernement sera "versée en octobre". Lire la brève
- Concernant le budget 2027, le Premier ministre propose de rencontrer les socialistes afin de "poursuivre" la démarche de "compromis" engagée en 2025. Lire la brève
La députée LFI Aurélie Trouvé dénonce un "trou noir" dans les marges de Total
Au micro de BFMTV, la députée LFI Aurélie Trouvé dénonce "un trou noir" dans les marges de Total, alors qu'elle participe à une mission parlementaire sur les prix du carburant. "On se demande où est passé l'argent des Français", explique la députée, qui explique ensuite que "la marge n'a pas augmenté du côté des distributeurs".
"En audition, on se rend compte que tous les hauts chefs de l'administration n'ont pas de données. La seule donnée qu'ils ont, c'est que les marges des raffineurs, globalement, ont été multipliées par huit en six mois, c'est délirant", fustige-t-elle.
Elle rappelle que La France insoumise demande le blocage des prix du carburant et ajoute que cela n'engendrerait pas de pénuries. "Les stocks privés sont au même niveau qu'avant la crise" et les stocks stratégiques "quasiment à 100%", ajoute-t-elle en se basant sur la mission parlementaire.
L'argent ne serait pas "du côté de l'État", assure-t-elle. "C'est vraiment Total qui, a mon sens, s'en met plein les poches".
"Je crois qu'il se moque un peu de nous": le député PS Arthur Delaporte déplore le manque de "preuves" de Sébastien Lecornu dans sa demande de compromis
Questionné sur la proposition de "compromis" de Sébastien Lecornu avec le PS, le député socialiste Arthur Delaporte assure sur BFMTV qu'un "compromis, ce n'est pas simplement des promesses, des mots en l'air, [...] c'est des preuves".
"Aujourd'hui, les preuves que nous donne le Premier ministre, c'est-à-dire les annonces budgétaires, c'est exactement l'inverse de ce qu'on porte", soit "rien sur le pouvoir d'achat, la transition écologique, la justice fiscale", fustige-t-il.
"Je crois qu'il se moque un peu de nous, pour faire un compromis, il faut être deux", continue le député.
Il dit attendre les propositions du chef du gouvernement sur le budget, notamment sur "où est-ce qu'il va chercher de l'argent".
Le Parti socialiste "prend acte" de la décision de justice sur Philippe Brun et des déclarations de ce dernier
Dans un communiqué, le Parti socialiste déclare "prendre acte" de la décision de justice rendue ce matin sur Philippe Brun, mais aussi des déclarations de ce dernier et de son intention de faire appel.
"Le Parti socialiste réaffirme qu’il ne se substitue pas aux instances et juridictions compétentes qui se prononceront par la suite dans le respect de l’État de droit et de la présomption d’innocence", conclut le parti à la rose.

L'initiative doit permettre de saluer le début de sa visite de quatre jours dans l’Hexagone, prévue jusqu’à lundi prochain.
items.body_text:
Visite du pape: les cloches des toutes les églises de France vont sonner à l'unisson ce vendredi
Les cloches des églises de France sonneront à l’unisson pendant 7 minutes, vendredi 25 septembre à 10 heures. Une initiative symbolique, prévue à l'horaire auquel le pape Léon XIV est attendu à l'aéroport de Paris Orly pour le début de sa première visite dans l'Hexagone depuis son élection.
"Les cloches sonneront pendant 7 minutes: un geste simple et symbolique pour marquer le début de ce voyage apostolique et permettre à chacun de s’y associer, où qu’il soit", développe le site internet pape-france.fr, géré par la Conférence des évêques de France (CEF).
Toutes les églises de France, des Bouches-du-Rhône au Nord et du Doubs au Finistère, s'accorderont donc pour célébrer ensemble la visite du souverain pontife.
À Paris, les cloches sonneront aussi à 17 heures
Après la cérémonie de bienvenue prévue à son arrivée à Paris Orly, Léon XIV sera conduit à l’Élysée où il rencontrera Emmanuel Macron à 11 heures. Lors de sa première journée de visite, Léon XIV visitera ensuite dans l'après-midi le siège de l’Unesco, avant de célébrer les vêpres à Notre-Dame de Paris.
Dans la capitale, les cloches des églises sonneront à nouveau simultanément à 17 heures, au passage du souverain pontife dans les rues de Paris.
Ce voyage apostolique sera aussi marqué par une étape à Saint-Denis, où le pape assistera à une veillée au Stade de France avec 80.000 jeunes âgés de 17 à 35 ans. À Paris, près de 600.000 personnes se sont déjà inscrites pour assister à la messe qu’il célébrera ce samedi sur la place de la Concorde.
Léon XIV restera en France jusqu’au lundi 28 septembre, après avoir fait escale à Lourdes et Metz.

items.title: Comment bénéficier de l'aide aux grands rouleurs, étendue à plus de 5 millions de Français face à la hausse des prix des carburants ?
items.summary: Le gouvernement a annoncé mardi un paquet de mesures s'élevant à 450 millions d'euros pour soutenir les Français touchés par la flambée des prix des carburants.
items.body_text:
Comment bénéficier de l'aide aux grands rouleurs, étendue à plus de 5 millions de Français face à la hausse des prix des carburants ?
Le gouvernement a annoncé mardi un paquet de mesures s'élevant à 450 millions d'euros pour soutenir les Français touchés par la flambée des prix des carburants.
Une aide pour mettre un peu plus d'essence dans son réservoir. Le gouvernement a annoncé, mardi 22 septembre, la prolongation et l'élargissement de l'aide aux grands rouleurs, mise en place en avril et qui permettait à certaines personnes utilisant un véhicule à des fins professionnelles, sous certaines conditions, de recevoir 100 euros pour se déplacer.
Ce coup de pouce, déjà perçu par 1,5 million de Français depuis le mois d'avril sur 3 millions de personnes concernées, pourra désormais être versé à 5,5 millions de personnes éligibles, si elles en font la demande. Franceinfo vous explique comment en bénéficier.
1 Vérifiez que vous êtes éligible
Si vous faites partie des 1,5 million de Français qui ont déjà bénéficié de cette aide depuis le mois d'avril, bonne nouvelle : elle sera automatiquement prolongée jusqu'à la fin de l'année. Elle "représentera l'équivalent de 40 centimes par litre de carburant" pour les mois d'octobre à décembre, contre 20 centimes par litre jusque-là, a détaillé mardi soir la porte-parole du gouvernement, Maud Bregeon. Une adaptation aux territoires ultramarins est également en discussion.
Jusqu'à présent, il fallait gagner, pour une personne seule, "en dessous de 17 000 euros par an", ou "pour un couple avec deux enfants, (...) 50 000 euros par an", avait précisé en avril le ministre de l'Economie, Roland Lescure. Désormais, les travailleurs modestes touchant jusqu'à 2 050 euros pour une personne seule, 4 070 euros pour un couple et 6 100 euros pour un couple avec deux enfants pourront en bénéficier.
Pour être éligible, il faut aussi utiliser un véhicule thermique ou hybride non rechargeable à des fins professionnelles, pour se rendre à son travail (pour au moins 15 km par trajet domicile-travail) ou lors de déplacements liés à son activité professionnelle (si vous effectuez au moins 8 000 km par an). "C'est par principe déclaratif, car l'Etat ne sait pas combien de kilomètres vous parcourez pour vous rendre au travail", a souligné mercredi matin sur franceinfo la porte-parole du gouvernement. Les véhicules 100% électriques, eux, ne sont pas concernés par cette mesure.
Ces critères seront élargis pour les infirmières libérales et les aides à domicile. Un "bonus territoires et ruralité" de 80 euros va être créé pour les infirmières libérales qui parcourent plus de 100 km par jour en moyenne, "sans condition de ressources", a précisé le cabinet de la ministre de la Santé, Stéphanie Rist. Cette même source a par ailleurs ajouté que les aides à domicile bénéficieraient d'un "accès spécifique à l'aide grands rouleurs", pour "toutes celles qui utilisent leur véhicule personnel, qui travaillent à mi-temps ou plus et qui font 30 km par jour".
2 Connectez-vous sur le site des impôts
Si vous remplissez les critères cités, rendez-vous sur le simulateur disponible sur le site des impôts. Munissez-vous de votre dernier avis d'impôt, sur lequel vous trouverez votre revenu fiscal de référence et le nombre de parts fiscales de votre foyer. Gardez auprès de vous le numéro d'immatriculation de votre véhicule utilisé à des fins professionnelles et son numéro de carte grise. Ils vous seront demandés pour remplir le formulaire.
3 Remplissez votre demande

items.summary: Stéphane Hardouin, magistrat et directeur de la "police des polices" était l'invité de franceinfo, quelques heures après la publication du rapport annuel de l’Inspection générale.
items.body_text:
La loi sur la présomption de légitime défense pour les forces de l'ordre "ne dispensera pas de faire des enquêtes", assure le directeur de l'IGPN
Stéphane Hardouin, magistrat et directeur de la "police des polices" était l'invité de franceinfo, quelques heures après la publication du rapport annuel de l’Inspection générale.
La "police de la police", l'Inspection générale de la police nationale (IGPN) a dévoilé, mercredi 23 septembre, son rapport annuel. Parmi les principaux points : une baisse des tirs mortels par les policiers et une augmentation de 45% des "atteintes à la probité" dans la police en 2025.
Les tirs mortels de policiers sont ainsi en baisse en 2025 par rapport à 2024. L'IGPN a enregistré une baisse du nombre de morts liés à des tirs par arme à feu de la part de policiers, avec 12 morts en 2025 contre 16 morts en 2024. Parmi ces douze décès, aucun n'est en lien avec des refus d'obtempérer comme c'était déjà le cas en 2024, après trois morts en 2023, dont Nahel. En revanche, il y a eu 19% de plus de blessés graves l'année dernière par rapport à 2024.
"Ce qui est notable cette année, c'est l'évolution non pas du nombre total d'enquêtes, mais l'évolution de la structure du portefeuille puisque le nombre d'affaires pour usage de la force, et en particulier les usages d'armes, sont finalement assez minoritaires. Il s'agit de 30% à peu près des affaires de l'IGPN, quand c'était 50% l'année dernière, observe mercredi sur franceinfo Stéphane Hardouin, magistrat et directeur de l’IGPN. Et quand on remonte aux affaires 2019-2020, il y avait les 'gilets jaune', on était vraiment sur une part très majoritaire".
"Pour les affaires de tirs mortels ou ayant entraîné des blessés graves, nous avons des cas qui ensuite ont été dans les deux-tiers, voire les trois quarts, judiciairement justifiés."
Stéphane Hardouin, directeur de l’IGPN
à franceinfo
La proposition de loi votée en juillet, qualifiée de "permis de tuer" pour les policiers par ses opposants, est accusée d'organiser une impunité policière. "Ce n'est pas une présomption de légitime défense mais d'usage d'armes, assure Stéphane Hardouin. Je rappelle que les policiers, comme les gendarmes, ont le monopole de la force légitime. Ça ne dispensera pas de faire des enquêtes. Nous serons dans une approche où il faudra, le plus et le plus vite possible, rassembler les éléments, vidéo et analyse des tirs. Au moment de l'audition du policier, cela permettra de savoir s'il y a des éléments qui justifient une audition sous un régime de mise en cause, et peut-être le régime de la garde à vue".
Stéphane Hardouin indique que "c'est sur ce plan-là qu'il pourrait y avoir une incidence sur un plan technique, mais certainement pas sur la nécessité de conduire une enquête et de rassembler tous les éléments à charge et à décharge pour savoir ce qu'il en est. Nous sommes dans des affaires qui, évidemment, justifient que l'IGPN s'y penche".
Algorithmes et repérages des "signaux faibles"
L'IGPN a "diligenté 235 enquêtes judiciaires pour des atteintes à la probité" et constaté une hausse de plus de 45% des atteintes à la probité, dont un tiers relève de faits de corruption. Le patron de l'IGPN fait un lien avec la lutte contre le narcobanditisme. "Incontestablement, les groupes criminels ont intégré et utilisent des vulnérabilités humaines qui se traduisent par de la corruption", reconnaît Stéphane Hardouin.
Si le nombre d'enquêtes est en hausse, il rappelle toutefois qu'il y a "153 000 policiers". Mais le risque n'est pas sous-estimé, assure-t-il. "c'est pour ça que nous nous sommes équipés d'algorithmes et nous utilisons des techniques spéciales d'enquêtes" inédites.
Pour détecter un policier plus fragile qu'un autre, "l'agence française anti-corruption nous a fait travailler sur la détection de ce qu'on appelle les signaux faibles, explique directeur de l’IGPN. items.title: L'écrivain Thélyson Orélien accusé d'avoir utilisé une IA : "Il faut quand même être très prudent", déclare Philippe Claudel, président de l'Académie Goncourt
items.summary: L'écrivain Thélyson Orélien, l'une des stars de la rentrée littéraire française, est la cible d'attaques sur X l'accusant d'avoir eu recours à l'intelligence artificielle pour écrire son roman "C'était ça ou mourir", ce qu'il a fermement démenti.
items.body_text:
L'écrivain Thélyson Orélien accusé d'avoir utilisé une IA : "Il faut quand même être très prudent", déclare Philippe Claudel, président de l'Académie Goncourt
        
        
      
    
    
  
  
  L'écrivain Thélyson Orélien, l'une des stars de la rentrée littéraire française, est la cible d'attaques sur X l'accusant d'avoir eu recours à l'intelligence artificielle pour écrire son roman "C'était ça ou mourir", ce qu'il a fermement démenti.
"Il faut quand même être très prudent", déclare sur franceinfo mercredi 23 septembre Philippe Claudel, écrivain et président de l'académie Goncourt à propos de la polémique concernant le livre de Thélyson Orélien C'était ça ou mourir. L'auteur canado-haïtien est accusé notamment par un collectif, par le biais d'un compte X, d'avoir écrit son roman en ayant recours à une intelligence artificielle. Des accusations que l'auteur rejette. "Je laisse toujours bénéficier du doute à ceux qu'on jette en pâture comme ça à l'opinion", ajoute Philippe Claudel.
Les accusations sont parties d'un compte anonyme sur X, qui affirme que plusieurs extraits du roman auraient été rédigés à l'aide d'une intelligence artificielle. Des passages testés par franceinfo avec un logiciel de détection ont également été considérés comme générés par une IA. Mais ces résultats ne constituent pas une preuve irréfutable, rappelle Philippe Claudel. Thélyson Orélien "a dit lui-même qu'il a écrit complètement son texte", rappelle le président de l'Académie. "Pourquoi remettre sa parole en doute ? Il dit qu'il est en train de rassembler des preuves avec ses éditeurs pour monter un dossier, pour convaincre l'opinion. Je crois que ça doit être très, très difficile pour lui en ce moment."
"Ni les moyens techniques ou humains" pour vérifier
Au-delà du cas de C'était ça ou mourir, l'affaire pose selon lui une question beaucoup plus large : celle de la relation entre l'écrivain et son lecteur. "Quand j'achète un livre, je vois un nom sur une couverture. J'achète un livre qui a été écrit par cet être humain qui porte ce nom et je lui fais confiance", explique Philippe Claudel. Pour le président de l'Académie Goncourt, l'utilisation de l'intelligence artificielle dans l'édition est désormais inévitable. Il souligne que l'Académie "n'a ni les moyens techniques ou humains, ni les compétences d'intelligence ou scientifiques" pour vérifier qu'un auteur a utilisé l'IA.
Pour Philippe Claudel, c'est finalement la définition même de la littérature qui est en jeu, et qui repose, selon lui, sur "le partage d'émotions". "À partir du moment où l'art, quel qu'il soit, serait généré par des machines, on perdrait une dimension essentielle", explique-t-il. 
"La littérature, c'est avant tout l'humain, c'est le partage d'émotions, c'est le partage d'un moi, c'est le partage d'une intimité."
Philippe Claudel, président de l'Académie Goncourt
à franceinfo
Quant au roman aujourd'hui soupçonné, Philippe Claudel assure n'avoir rien détecté lors de sa lecture. Il dit avoir apprécié sa langue "qui était par moments chantante et musicale", ainsi que son traitement de la question migratoire. La présence de ce livre dans la deuxième sélection du Goncourt n'est toutefois pas garantie. "On a toujours un fonctionnement démocratique avec un système de vote qui nous fait passer de seize titres à huit titres, explique le président de l'Académie. Il n'est pas évident que le livre, quelle que soit la polémique, soit sur la deuxième liste. Ça je n'en sais rien." Cette liste sera publiée le 6 octobre.

items.body_text:
Michigan won the game on a Hail Mary and got dropped out of the AP Top 25 anyway. Why?
Michigan won the game against Western Michigan but lost most of its support in The Associated Press Top 25 college football poll.
Just like many viewers Saturday night, Top 25 voters were confused when one second was put back on the clock after it appeared time had run out at Michigan Stadium. And they were dazed when JJ Buchanan came down with Bryce Underwood’s second Hail Mary pass to turn the four-touchdown-underdog Broncos’ 12-7 upset into a 13-12 loss.
The Mid-American Conference submitted appeals to the NCAA and the College Football Playoff administration asking for the result to be overturned to let the record show the Broncos actually won the game for purposes of rankings, evaluations and selection deliberations. The NCAA said its rules don’t allow a move like that and the CFP won’t release its first rankings until November.
Top 25 voters have weighed in, though.
The Wolverines dropped from No. 16 in the preseason poll to out of the Top 25 altogether in the first regular-season poll. It was the biggest fall from ranked to unranked after a win since at least 2008.
Michigan had appeared on all 69 preseason ballots and was listed as high as No. 10 on one. The Wolverines were on just 22 ballots Tuesday.
Bob Asmussen of the Champaign (Illinois) News-Gazette, in his 16th year as a voter, put Michigan No. 12 on his preseason ballot and said he knew that was a mistake as he watched Michigan’s offense sputter after scoring on its first possession. Voters sometimes hesitate to penalize a team that wins, but Michigan was going to drop off Asmussen’s ballot regardless. Forty-six other voters agreed with him.
“I saw them lose in my mind, but they didn’t technically lose,” Asmussen said. “It was so easy to drop them because of how horrible they were.”
Kirk Bohls of the Houston Chronicle, in his fourth decade as a voter, had Michigan No. 20 on his preseason ballot but said the Wolverines looked nothing like a Top 25 team. Bohls said he was disturbed by the way the end of the game played out, and the Big Ten’s statement about why 1 second was put on the clock after it showed zeroes didn’t convince him.
“We were all watching and the Big Ten told us don’t believe what you just saw with your eyes, and it’s kind of hard to unsee that,” Bohls said.
Bohls said he’ll be curious as to how the CFP selection committee will look at the game if Michigan ends up under consideration for an at-large playoff bid.
“Some people probably on the selection committee might view it as a loss or at the very least a tainted victory,” he said. “It could ultimately be a tie-breaker that goes against Michigan.”
Lots of choices for No. 1
Ohio State is No. 1 by a wide margin going into its showdown at No. 4 Texas this weekend but there is far from universal agreement on which team is best in the land.
Seven teams received first-place votes, the most since the same number got first-place votes in the 2016 preseason poll. It’s the most in a regular-season poll since seven teams got first-place votes Sept. 2, 2014.
No. 8 LSU’s five first-place votes made the Tigers the lowest-ranked team to get at least one since ninth-ranked Texas A&M on Oct. 11, 2015. LSU hammered Clemson 51-10 in Lane Kiffin’s first game as coach.
SEC flex
The Southeastern Conference occupies seven of the top 12 spots in the poll with No. 2 Georgia, No. 4 Texas, No. 8 LSU, No. 9 Mississippi, No. 10 Texas A&M, No. 11 Oklahoma and No. 12 Alabama. The SEC has a total of nine ranked teams with No. 18 Tennessee and No. 23 Missouri.
The SEC is the only conference to ever have seven teams in the top 12. The SEC also had that many in the top 12 the week of Oct. 5, 2025.
The Big Ten’s 1-2 punch was short-lived: Ohio State and Oregon had given the Big Ten the top two teams in the preseason rankings for the first time in 65 years. The Buckeyes did their part to stay No. 1 with their rout of Ball State. The Ducks, tied with

items.body_text:
In North Carolina, a race is on to restore critical peatland before it dries up or is destroyed
Scientists and investors are restoring a 23-square-mile (60-square-kilometer) tract of peatland in North Carolina to help curb climate-warming emissions and restore native habitat. (AP Video: Joshua A. Bickel)
BELHAVEN, N.C. (AP) — The birds are up with the sunrise — warblers, flycatchers, sparrows and towhees calling across the treetops. Deer browse on tender buds emerging from dense shrubs. Black bears scrounge for roots, insects and other edibles.
It’s an idyllic setting in North Carolina’s Inner Banks, where fields of cotton, soybeans and corn stretch for miles, country roads wend through stands of pines and thousands of bird watchers converge to witness the spring migration.
But it’s what’s underground that has drawn scientists and investors to this 23-square-mile (60-square-kilometer) tract: spongy, dense peat up to 15 feet (5 meters) deep.
They’re here to save it.
Fifty miles (80 kilometers) of ditches dug decades ago for an abandoned farming venture drained much of the water from thousands of years of accumulated peat, leaving the site vulnerable to drought and wildfires, altering its native habitats — and allowing it to emit 130,000 tons of climate-warming carbon dioxide a year.
“Our goal is for perpetuity to conserve these lands so they can’t become oil and gas fields, so they’re not mined for phosphorus or turned into parking lots and shopping centers,” said Tripp Wall, CEO of Colorado-based company Pantheon Regeneration. “They’re just these incredible systems that I feel are underappreciated here in the U.S. (that) for 10,000 to 15,000 years have been climatologically resilient until we screwed them up.”
Peatlands are a climate paradox. Though they account for just 3% of global land surface, they store one-third of the Earth’s carbon dioxide, more than all forests combined. But when degraded — primarily when farmers lower the water table to grow crops — destroyed or burned, they become part of the problem, releasing huge volumes of greenhouse gases, now about 6% of the annual global total from all sources.
And the type of peatlands found in North Carolina, and for hundreds of miles along the Eastern Seaboard, are among the most threatened in the world.
Pantheon plans to reverse the damage by blocking off ditches to control the water table and significantly reduce carbon dioxide emissions. Then it will cull invasive species and replant native grasses, flowers and other plants.
The restoration is modeled after other projects by nonprofits and government agencies, including at the adjacent 175-square-mile (453-square-kilometer) Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge — one of the largest peatland restoration projects in the U.S. — which provides habitat for threatened and endangered species such as red wolves, yellow pitcher plants and Atlantic white cedar, and has become an important stopover for migrating birds such as Tundra swans.
But what sets apart Pantheon’s project is a plan to sell carbon credits to tech companies and other corporations that want to compensate for their own greenhouse gas emissions, then use the money to restore and preserve a million acres (1,562 square miles, or 4,047 square kilometers) of peatland from Virginia to northern Florida over the next decade.
Each property will be permanently conserved and rewilded — “big corridors, big birding habitats, big biodiversity hotspots that have an outsized impact on climate,” said Wall.
Ancient ecosystems under threat
Neal Flanagan pushes a metal tube through roots and around buried logs until it sinks about a meter (3 feet). When he pulls it out, it’s packed with black soil.
Near the surface, it’s dry and full of dead fibers from plants like wood fern, blueberry and Lyonia. The middle is crumbly, moist and odorless, with bits of charcoal from long-ago fires. But the saturated bottom, 50% carbon, is the consistency of axle grease.

items.title: Markets digest bank earnings after recent turmoil
items.body_text:
Stocks slid Friday after a slate of earnings beats from big banks fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next two meetings.
    
    
            Still, the major indices gained for the week. The Dow rose 400 points, or 1.2%. The S&P 500 gained 0.8% and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 0.3%.
    
    
            JPMorgan Chase on Friday reported first-quarter profit and revenue that crushed expectations, boosted by the Fed’s interest rate hiking campaign. Citigroup, Wells Fargo and PNC Financial also reported strong results.
    
    
            CEO Jamie Dimon warned investors in the company’s post-earnings conference call that they should prepare for interest rates to be higher for longer than expected.
    
    
            Wall Street seems to have taken note. Analysts increased their bets on a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed’s meeting in May and another in June.
    
    
            Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Friday that the central bank needs to continue tightening monetary policy, further weighing down markets.
    
    
            Austan Goolsbee, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said that it’s “definitely” possible the United States enters a mild recession after the tumult in banking last month.
    
    
            Meanwhile, retail sales data declined more than expected, suggesting that Americans’ spending power and the US economy are weakening.
    
    
            Consumer sentiment held fairly steady in April, even as concerns about a recession linger, according to the University of Michigan’s latest monthly survey.
    
    
            “There was too much news to digest this morning, but the key takeaway is that the Fed has room to do more harm,” Edward Moya, senior market analyst at OANDA, said in a note.
    
    
            The Dow slipped 144 points, or 0.4%.
    
    
            The S&P 500 tumbled 0.2%.
    
    
            The Nasdaq Composite sank 0.4%.
    
    
            As stocks settle after the trading day, levels might still change slightly.

items.title: Still haven't filed your taxes? Here's what you need to know
items.summary: So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 90 million income tax returns for 2022.
items.body_text:
So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 100 million income tax returns for 2022.
That means tens of millions of households have yet to file their returns. If yours is among them, here are some last-minute tax-filing tips to keep in mind as the Tuesday, April 18 deadline approaches.
Not everyone has to file on April 18: If you live in a federally declared disaster area, have a business there — or have relevant tax documents stored by businesses in that area — it’s likely the IRS has already extended the filing and payment deadlines for you. Here is where you can find the specific extension dates for each disaster area.
Thanks to many rounds of extreme weather in recent months, for instance, tax filers in most of California — which accounts for 10% to 15% of all federal filers — have already been granted an extension until Oct. 16 to file and to pay, according to an IRS spokesperson.
If you’re in the armed forces and are currently or were recently stationed in a combat zone, the filing and payment deadlines for your 2022 taxes are most likely extended by 180 days. But your specific extended filing and payment deadlines will depend on the day you leave (or left) the combat zone. This IRS publication offers more detail.
Lastly, if you made little to no money last year (typically less than $12,950 for single filers and $25,900 for married couples), you may not be required to file a return. But you may want to anyway if you think you are eligible for a refund thanks to, for instance, refundable tax credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit. (Use this IRS tool to gauge whether you are required to file this year.) You also are likely eligible to use IRS Free File (intended for those with adjusted gross income of $73,000 or less) so it won’t cost you to submit a return.
Your paycheck may not be your only source of income: If you had one full-time job you may think that is the only income you made and have to report. But that’s not necessarily so.
Other potentially taxable and reportable income sources include:
- Interest on your savings
- Investment income (e.g., dividends and capital gains)
- Pay for part-time or seasonal work, or a side hustle
- Unemployment income
- Social Security benefits or distribution from a retirement account
- Tips
- Gambling winnings
- Income from a rental property you own
Organize your tax documents: By now you should have received every tax document that third parties are required to send you (your employer, bank, brokerage, etc.).
If you don’t recall receiving a hard copy of a tax form in the mail, check your email and your online accounts — a document may have been sent to you electronically.
Here are some of the tax forms you may have received:
- W-2 from your wage or salaried jobs
- 1099-B for capital gains and losses on your investments
- 1099-DIV from your brokerage or company where you own stock for dividends or other distributions from their investments
- 1099-INT for interest over $10 on your savings at a financial institution
- 1099-NEC from your clients, if you worked as a contractor
- 1099-K for payments for goods and services through third-party platforms like Venmo, CashApp or Etsy. The 1099-K is required if you made more than $20,000 in over 200 transactions during the year. (Next year the reporting threshold drops to $600.) But even if you didn’t get a 1099-K you still must report all the income that you made over third-party platforms in 2022.
- 1099-Rs for distributions over $10 that you received for a pension, annuity, retirement account, profit-sharing plan or insurance contract
- SSA-1099 or SSA-1042S for Social Security benefits received.
“Be aware that there’s no form for some taxable income, like proceeds from renting out your vacation property, meaning you’re responsible for reporting it on your own,” according to the Illinois CPA Society.

items.title: Retail spending fell in March as consumers pull back
items.summary: Spending at US retailers fell in March as consumers pulled back amid recessionary fears fueled by the banking crisis.
items.body_text:
Spending at US retailers fell in March as consumers pulled back after the banking crisis fueled recession fears.
Retail sales, which are adjusted for seasonality but not for inflation, fell by 1% in March from the prior month, the Commerce Department reported on Friday. That was steeper than an expected 0.4% decline, according to Refinitiv, and above the revised 0.2% decline in the prior month.
Investors chalk up some of the weakness to a lack of tax returns and concerns about a slowing labor market. The IRS issued $84 billion in tax refunds this March, about $25 billion less than they issued in March of 2022, according to BofA analysts.
That led consumers to pull back in spending at department stores and on durable goods, such as appliances and furniture. Spending at general merchandise stores fell 3% in March from the prior month and spending at gas stations declined 5.5% during the same period. Excluding gas station sales, retail spending retreated 0.6% in March from February.
However, retail spending rose 2.9% year-over-year.
The effect of smaller tax returns
Smaller tax returns likely played a role in last month’s decline in retail sales, along with the expiration of enhanced food assistance benefits, economists say.
“March is a really important month for refunds. Some folks might have been expecting something similar to last year,” Aditya Bhave, senior US economist at BofA Global Research, told CNN.
Credit and debit card spending per household tracked by Bank of America researchers moderated in March to its slowest pace in more than two years, which was likely the result of smaller returns and expired benefits, coupled with slowing wage growth.
Enhanced pandemic-era benefits provided through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program expired in February, which might have also held back spending in March, according to a Bank of America Institute report.
A slowing labor market
Average hourly earnings grew 4.2% in March from a year earlier, down from the prior month’s annualized 4.6% increase and the smallest annual rise since June 2021, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The Employment Cost Index, a more comprehensive measure of wages, has also shown that worker pay gains have moderated this past year. ECI data for the first quarter of this year will be released later this month.
Still, the US labor market remains solid, even though it has lost momentum recently. That could hold up consumer spending in the coming months, said Michelle Meyer, North America chief economist at Mastercard Economics Institute.
“The big picture is still favorable for the consumer when you think about their income growth, their balance sheet and the health of the labor market,” Meyer said.
Employers added 236,000 jobs in March, a robust gain by historical standards but smaller than the average monthly pace of job growth in the prior six months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The latest monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, or JOLTS report, showed that the number of available jobs remained elevated in February — but was down more than 17% from its peak of 12 million in March 2022, and revised data showed that weekly claims for US unemployment benefits were higher than previously reported.
The job market could cool further in the coming months. Economists at the Federal Reserve expect the US economy to head into a recession later in the year as the lagged effects of higher interest rates take a deeper hold. Fed economists had forecast subdued growth, with risks of a recession, prior to the collapses of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.
For consumers, the effects of last month’s turbulence in the banking industry have been limited so far. Consumer sentiment tracked by the University of Michigan worsened slightly in March during the bank failures, but it had already shown signs of deteriorating before then.

items.title: Lukashenko reveals bizarre argument he and Putin have over who is the ‘bigger dictator’
items.summary: Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko told a youth forum that he and Vladimir Putin regularly argue over who is the bigger dictator.
items.body_text:
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko revealed during a speech to youth leaders in Minsk that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin regularly joke and argue over which of them qualifies as the ultimate dictator.
The Belarusian leader's comments at "Youth. Belarus. Future." Sept. 17 also underlines the close alignment between Moscow and Minsk with Lukashenko enjoying his position as Europe’s longest-serving head of state.
Lukashenko has ruled over Belarus unhindered since 1994, with Putin leading Russia since 2012, also serving as president between 2000 and 2008.
"You know what they say about me?" Lukashenko asked the audience during his Sept. 17 address, according to Novaya Gazeta.
TRUMP SAYS US HELPED SECURE RELEASE OF 5 PRISONERS IN BELARUS DEAL, THANKS LUKASHENKO
"[I am] the last dictator, the second-to-last dictator in Europe. Dictator, dictator. Vladimir Putin and I often joke and argue over which of us is more of a dictator.
"They say I’m the last dictator, the last dictator in Europe. Dictator — so be it. Well, Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin and I often argue, jokingly, about which of us is the bigger dictator."
Lukashenko, 72, a former Soviet collective farm manager, is also known to be Putin’s closest international partner and ally.
While Minsk has not committed ground troops to the war in Ukraine, it serves as a strategic staging ground for Moscow, with Russia relying on Belarus for military and strategic support in its ongoing war against Ukraine.
According to the Kyiv Post, Belarus specifically provides Russia with key weapons components and allows its forces to launch military strikes from Belarusian territory.
An August report by Ukrainska Pravda also highlighted a new railway construction capable of handling military trains in Belarus' Gomel Oblast near the Ukraine border.
RUSSIA’S STRIKES NEAR MOLDOVA RAISE ALARM OVER PUTIN’S PLANS FOR EUROPE’S EASTERN FLANK
The strength of the relationship between the two countries comes as Western officials increase pressure on Moscow and its allies and with the two leaders reported to be in frequent contact.
After meeting in Moscow Aug. 27, Lukashenko officially congratulated Putin Sept. 21 after the Russian election results.
He praised the "unprecedented turnout of millions of voters" and the majority secured by the United Russia party, calling it a proper response to "cynical attempts from the outside to discredit the campaign and sow discord."
Addressing the youth forum in Minsk on political succession in Belarus, Lukashenko insisted no one is prepared to take over power.
"Never believe those who say that Lukashenko is ‘clinging to power with blue-knuckled hands’," he told the audience.
"Good Lord, let them say it. I have had my fill of this power to the point where I could not possibly want any more of it.
"The only question is whether you are capable today of taking over the country and holding on to it," he added. "If you are, start tomorrow. To be frank, I cannot yet answer that question positively. Do not take offense.
"I became a dictator then because I stood up against the entire ‘civilized world.'"
Western nations maintain strict economic pressure on Minsk. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys recently reiterated the Baltic nation's firm stance.
"We do not see any reasons why our position on Belarus should soften as Belarus is not changing its behavior," Budrys said.
"On our side, we have to be very exact and continue what works, and that is the pressure on the regime."
Despite international sanctions, Lukashenko announced Sept. 11 that Belarus has begun selling potash, a primary export used in fertilizer, to the United States.

While Western nations maintain economic restrictions over human rights abuses, U.S. sanctions on Belarusian potash were lifted after recent political prisoner releases, though European Union sanctions remain active.

items.title: Battle-tested Zelenskyy sounds chilling alarm on where Putin’s war could head next
items.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns the risk of Russian drone, missile or land attacks against countries bordering Russia is "very high."
items.body_text:
UNITED NATIONS - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Tuesday that Russia could launch attacks against other European countries, telling Fox News Digital that the risk of a new offensive is "very high" as Moscow seeks to undermine European unity and weaken support for Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters following his meeting with President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future.
"That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin, unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv.
"How to divide unanimity in Europe? ... To attack somebody else. To attack and say, look, I will go further if you will not stop this," Zelenskyy said.
He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response.
Zelenskyy said Putin's inability to secure a decisive victory in Ukraine could push him toward additional confrontations, as he faces pressure to justify the war to the Russian public.
FINNISH FOREIGN MINISTRY OFFICIAL DETAILS HOW RUSSIA'S 'HYBRID WARFARE' RESHAPED BORDER SECURITY
Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer.
"Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said.
The warning comes amid heightened concerns about Russian activity in Europe. Zelenskyy's warning comes amid heightened tensions across Europe following a series of Russian drone incursions and warnings from European leaders about the possibility of further attacks.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned on Sept. 14 that peace in Europe was under threat, urging European countries to take the danger seriously. Speaking at an EU-Arctic Summit in Finland, Merz said Russia's presence in the region and its hybrid attacks elsewhere in Europe were increasing, calling for a united response from European countries and NATO.
RUSSIA’S STRIKES NEAR MOLDOVA RAISE ALARM OVER PUTIN’S PLANS FOR EUROPE’S EASTERN FLANK
The German leader's warning followed an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4, which German authorities publicly attributed to Russia on Sept. 1.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk issued a separate warning on Sept. 17 that Russia was planning drone or missile attacks against NATO countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, while potentially portraying the incidents as accidental to weaken the alliance's response.
The concerns are not limited to hypothetical threats. On Sept. 8, a drone entered Romanian airspace before returning to Moldova and crashing, according to Romania's Defense Ministry. A week later, Italian fighter jets operating under NATO's air defense mission shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus. items.title: Chinese Coast Guard rams Philippine boat in South China Sea, sparking diplomatic clash
items.summary: A Chinese Coast Guard vessel collided with a Philippine government ship in the South China Sea Friday, sparking a diplomatic dispute between Beijing, Manila and the U.S.
items.body_text:
Tensions in the South China Sea escalated again Friday after a Chinese Coast Guard vessel collided with a Philippine government ship, an encounter captured on video that prompted competing accounts from Manila and Beijing.
The Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat was distributing fuel to Filipino fishermen when the collision occurred at 11:13 a.m., roughly 54 nautical miles off the coast of Palawan province — an area Manila says is well within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone.
Footage released by the Philippine Coast Guard showed crew members shouting, "Brace for impact!" moments before the collision. Photographs taken afterward showed bent and detached railings, damaged metal supports and debris scattered across the Philippine ship's deck. No injuries were reported.
Philippine officials accused Beijing of deliberately ramming a civilian government vessel on what they described as a humanitarian and livelihood mission.
Jay Tarriela, the Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for West Philippine Sea concerns, said the Chinese vessel first cut across the Philippine ship's stern at a distance of about 33 feet before repeating the maneuver minutes later and colliding with it.
Beijing disputed Manila's account. Chinese Coast Guard spokesperson Jiang Lue said the Philippine vessel "intentionally adjusted its course and suddenly accelerated to cut across the bow" of the Chinese ship after disregarding repeated warnings. China said its vessel had been conducting lawful operations near Sabina Shoal and blamed the Philippine side for the collision.
The incident also drew Washington into the dispute. U.S. Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said the United States "strongly condemn[s] the China Coast Guard's deliberate ramming."
The Chinese Embassy in Manila responded by accusing the United States of backing Philippine "infringement and provocations" in the disputed waters.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Friday's collision was the latest in a series of maritime confrontations between China and the Philippines. In July, Manila accused Chinese forces of firing water cannons at government vessels near Scarborough Shoal and striking a Philippine Navy staff member in the head with a wooden baton during an encounter at Second Thomas Shoal.
Reuters contributed to this report.

items.title: Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
items.summary: Building dams and hydropower plants in the Himalayas holds great promise for providing electricity. In the wake of the Nepal disaster, experts are asking about the risks of such construction.
items.body_text:
Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
KATHMANDU, Nepal — On a recent September day, Sumana Shrestha Amatya stood alongside other protesters in the Nepali capital, urging the government to work faster to find their loved ones, trapped inside hydropower plants since flash floods devastated miles of a river valley in late August.
Amatya says she hasn't heard from officials about her husband, Sunil, a geologist. Still, she acknowledged the scale of the disaster that the government was grappling with: "It was like a Himalayan tsunami."
It's a description other Nepalis have used for the events of Aug. 26, when a glacier and its bedrock spanning more than 3,800 feet in width collapsed into a river valley, some 4,000 feet below.
That triggered 30-foot-high waves of boulders, water and ice that surged for miles downstream. It swept away a multistory border building and some 70 bridges and miles of highway, and buried 12 hydropower plants under mud and boulders along the Trishuli River, which was badly impacted by the floods.
Some 1,400 bodies have been recovered in Nepal, and more than 5,000 remain unaccounted for.
The dead and missing include 121 people who were trapped in hydropower plants, according to Brig. Gen. Subas Jung Thapa of the Nepali army, which is leading rescue efforts. He spoke in early September.
It took days just to find the power plants under the mud. It was like "a bomb's gone off," said Arnold Dix, a tunneling expert helping with rescue efforts. "It's removed the power stations from the surface, like they're just not there." Only three men were found alive in the plants since rescue efforts began.
Did hydropower projects add to the risk?
It is those hydropower plants that have received the most scrutiny in regional media since the floods, with experts reviving questions about whether developers had properly assessed the risks of building them in the Himalayas.
"We need to understand what is happening now in Nepal can happen in other parts of the Himalayas," says C.P. Rajendran, an Indian geoscientist who has been critical of big construction works in the Himalayas. (Rajendran, like many Indians, uses initials for his first name.)
Critics have also focused on the role of international institutions like the World Bank, which has long supported some of these hydropower projects and their associated dams.
They include one of the biggest hydropower projects in the river basin, known as the Upper Trishuli-1, which cost Nepal over half a billion dollars. It was backed by about $300 million in loans and equity by two arms of the World Bank.
The Upper-Trishuli-1 was under construction. Now it's under the mud. Thapa of the Nepali army said in his press briefing that he estimated some 50 people were trapped inside. On Wednesday, the Kathmandu Post reported the bodies of five men were recovered from the plant.
"Why did it have to happen in the first place?" asked Parineeta Dandekar, an expert on rivers who has written critically about these projects for the advocacy group South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People.
Dandekar accuses the World Bank of producing a flawed risk assessment report for the project from the get-go. Its many omissions, Dandekar says, included ignoring "the cumulative disaster risk that can happen after having so many projects across the same river."
Experts say the Trishuli river basin has 36 hydro power projects — including the dozen now under the mud.
Dandekar says the constant blasting of mountains to build these projects, including for miles-long tunnels, has its own impact.
It's a region where earthquakes and landslides are common, and where climate change is causing its glaciers to melt more rapidly, making them — and their slopes — more unstable. Initial analysis suggests global warming exacerbated the melting of the glacier that snapped off in August, triggering flash floods.

items.title: Karoline Leavitt Says Reporters Apologized To Her Off-Air
items.summary: Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ripped the performative nature of the press corps, calling out D.C. journalists as camera-hungry phonies who secretly apologize off-air for the nasty hit pieces their bosses force them to churn out. Leavitt’s comments come right on the heels of President Donald Trump targeting three top mainstream outlets, barring ...
items.body_text:
Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ripped the performative nature of the press corps, calling out D.C. journalists as camera-hungry phonies who secretly apologize off-air for the nasty hit pieces their bosses force them to churn out.
Leavitt’s comments come right on the heels of President Donald Trump targeting three top mainstream outlets, barring them from the Brady Briefing Room in his battle against “fake news.”
Appearing on Fox News with Sean Hannity on Tuesday, Leavitt — who stepped down from her post as press secretary last month — pulled back the curtain on the West Wing press pool, admitting there is a huge “performative aspect” to the daily briefing room circus. While reporters ham it up for their nightly news soundbites, Leavitt revealed that many privately admit they are just puppets on a string pulled by corporate bosses.
“They have to do that because their bosses are demanding it,” Leavitt said. “There’s been times reporters have even said to me, ‘I’m sorry I had to ask that today. You know, my bosses really wanted me to ask that.’ They know it’s an unfair question, but they’re not in control of their own livelihood. They are dictated by the editors and the execs at some of these companies.”
Over the weekend, the Trump administration officially yanked the press passes for journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico.
The lockout began Saturday morning at the White House gates, where guards turned away MS NOW correspondent Akayla Gardner and a photographer, confiscating Gardner’s hard pass and informing her the order came straight from “above.” CNN correspondent Betsy Klein met the same fate just an hour later.
The dramatic crackdown followed a fiery Truth Social manifesto posted last Friday by President Trump, who declared that the three outlets were officially banned for constantly churning out “FICTION and LIES.” Trump didn’t mince words: “I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here.” He also hinted that leftist outlets like The New York Times and The Washington Post could be next.
Trump took aim at Politico, railing against an “illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription” scheme funded by taxpayers under the Biden administration. Leavitt had previously targeted those massive USAID-funded subscriptions back in early 2025 alongside Elon Musk’s DOGE team.
CNN and MS NOW immediately labeled the action an unconstitutional assault on press freedom. The ban sets up a First Amendment showdown, echoing a 1977 federal appeals decision and a 2018 court battle over CNN reporter Jim Acosta that barred the White House from stripping credentials based on coverage. The administration is also at odds with the Associated Press, which was kicked off Air Force One after refusing to adopt the administration’s new “Gulf of America” instructions.
Trump’s move also sparked a response from Fox News, which joined four other networks in agreeing to suspend the presidential television pool in response to the media ban.

items.title: Patrick Clancy’s Radical Forgiveness
items.summary: For an innocent man whose ex-wife killed their children, Patrick Clancy gets an inordinate amount of scrutiny. From the nuts who claim he’s the actual killer to those who think he moved on too quickly after divorce, he’s found himself under the microscope of public opinion almost as much as Lindsay. Now, though, he finds ...
items.body_text:
For an innocent man whose ex-wife killed their children, Patrick Clancy gets an inordinate amount of scrutiny. From the nuts who claim he’s the actual killer to those who think he moved on too quickly after divorce, he’s found himself under the microscope of public opinion almost as much as Lindsay. Now, though, he finds himself facing criticism not for anything negative he’s done, but because he chose to forgive Lindsay for killing Cora, Dawson, and Callan.
In an interview with Ross Douthat on “60 Minutes,” Patrick told Douthat, “And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn’t get there, I would be eaten up inside, forever.” More shocking, though, was the revelation that Lindsay herself never asked to be forgiven. There are a variety of opinions on this, with some saying he made the right choice, some pointing out he has an ongoing civil case against her health providers and must guard what he says because of that, and others referring to him as a sniveling wimp. The reality is that his forgiveness isn’t a sign of weakness, but instead a sign of strength.
There are biblical reasons for Patrick to forgive his ex-wife. In the Book of Matthew, Jesus tells Peter, when Peter asks how many times he must forgive a brother or sister who has sinned against him, “I tell you not seven times, but seventy-seven times.” To illustrate this point, he tells the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant. In the parable, a servant owes the king a large debt, one he cannot repay, and begs the king for mercy. The king releases the servant from his debt, but when the servant faces a similar situation, he does not offer the same treatment. This enrages the king, who reinstitutes the servant’s debt and has him thrown in prison. The parable closes with, “This is how my heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother or sister from your heart.”
Granted, Lindsay is not Patrick’s sister, but there is still the command to forgive. As Patrick grew up in a large Catholic family, such teachings were part of his upbringing, as were ones from Ephesians that command believers to avoid unwholesome talk, bitterness, rage, and anger. The fourth chapter of the book concludes with “be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.”
Beyond the biblical reasons for forgiveness are the practical ones. As Patrick himself said, he didn’t want this to weigh on him for the rest of his existence. Trump disclosed the talks while meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York, saying U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were involved and that another meeting had already been set for the “very near future.”
“It was a very good meeting,” Trump said. “It was a meeting that lasted for three hours.”
The president said he could not imagine why Tehran would reject an agreement given the alternative now facing the Islamic Republic.
“It’s greatness, potential greatness, or obliteration,” Trump said. “In one case it’s obliteration, and the other alternative is potential greatness. It could be a great country.”
Witkoff, who was alongside Trump as he discussed the talks, initially offered little detail but struck an upbeat tone when pressed by reporters.
“I feel very good right now,” Witkoff said. Asked how he expected to feel Wednesday, he responded: “I think very good.”
Witkoff later clarified how the broader negotiating round had unfolded, saying the talks were conducted through mediators who moved between the U.S. and Iranian delegations throughout the day.
“Today, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, we engaged in lengthy talks with the Iranian delegation through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day,” Witkoff wrote on X.
“They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising,” he added. “The mediators will continue their work.”
Iranian state media separately confirmed contact between the two sides, reporting that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Witkoff and used the encounter to convey Tehran’s terms for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the Iranian account, those demands included lifting the U.S. naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and ending the war across what Tehran calls the “resistance fronts.” Iranian state television said Tehran’s “firm positions” were conveyed during the meeting.
The demand to lift the blockade goes directly at one of Washington’s principal sources of pressure on Tehran — and emerged as one of the clearest points of contention in the renewed talks.
The terms reported by Iranian state media were also broader than a proposal described earlier Tuesday by a senior Iranian official, who told Reuters that Tehran could reopen Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
The official said Iran had delivered that proposal through mediators the previous week, described the General Assembly as a “golden opportunity” to revive diplomacy and said the delegation in New York had full authority to negotiate.
Trump later described the renewed diplomatic channel in increasingly optimistic terms.
Meeting British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Trump predicted that Washington and Tehran would ultimately reach an agreement and said communication between the two sides was already developing.
“I think that a settlement is going to be reached,” Trump said. “They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us, even today they’ve been talking to us. And the relationship is developing.”
Trump carried that optimism into a later meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council members and other regional leaders.

items.summary: The Trump administration plans to cap next year's refugee inflow at 17,500 people, down from the 125,000 target set under President Joe Biden. The post Trump Cuts Refugee Inflow to 17,500, Down from Biden’s 125,000 appeared first on Breitbart.
items.body_text:
The Trump administration plans to cap next year’s refugee inflow at 17,500 people, down from the 125,000 target set under President Joe Biden.
The State Department laid out the plan in a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday, a week before the 2027 fiscal year opens in October. Admissions will “primarily be Afrikaners from South Africa,” the notice says, naming the Afrikaans-speaking white minority descended from Dutch and French settlers.
Biden’s agencies set the 125,000 target in his last year in office. Resettlement contractors put the long-run average at roughly 92,000 a year since the program started in 1980. Trump’s first term bottomed out at 15,000.
The administration set last year’s ceiling at 7,500, then lifted it to 17,500 after declaring that unforeseen developments in South Africa had created an emergency. Next year’s number holds at that level.
The notice argues Afrikaners face land seizures without compensation, policies that push them out of jobs and classrooms, and rhetoric that fuels violence against them. It also tells Congress the arrivals will assimilate in a way that “preserves taxpayer resources for U.S. citizens.”
Resettlement is projected to cost $500 million.
The refugee program transports invited migrants from favored countries and hands them special federal aid for several years. Once here, they are eligible for nearly all welfare programs, which deliver steady rent payments and consumer spending to nearby landlords and employers.
Applicants from Afghanistan, Sudan, the Republic of Congo, and Myanmar have been shut out since Trump reopened the program for Afrikaners.
Pro-migration groups that are paid to place refugees in American communities attacked the decision. Naomi Steinberg of HIAS claimed the administration is “diminishing and distorting” a four-decade legacy in service of political whims.
Marco Rubio’s State Department announced visa restrictions on South African officials last week over uncompensated land seizures and race-based discrimination. Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola argued the move echoed a mischaracterization pushed by fringe groups. Ramaphosa’s office asserted a sovereign right to address centuries of racial injustice.
U.S. Ambassador Brent Bozell said the visa policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures.

items.summary: Tehran Dangles Peace Deal Hours Before Trump Threatens To ‘Annihilate’ Iran

Iran offered Tuesday to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, hours before President Donald Trump threatened to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if the two countries fail to reach a deal.
Tehran’s offer targets one of the war’s most consequential pressure points for the United States, where disrupted energy flows through Hormuz have helped push American fuel costs sharply higher. The proposal also lands just weeks before the November midterm elections as polling shows broad public dissatisfaction with the war and Trump faces mounting political pressure over the cost of living.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said, including whether he would “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly,” according to the United Nations. (RELATED: Here’s What Doves And Hawks Think About The UN’s Iran War Crime Report)
Tehran told Washington it could reopen the critical waterway within seven days if the United States eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official. Iran delivered the proposal through mediators on Sept. 16 and said its delegation in New York has authority to revive diplomacy, according to the outlet.
“Iran is a perfect example of military hubris,” defense policy analyst and retired Marine Dan Grazier told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “This whole situation is a really good example of why it’s important for everyone involved in this process to remember that war is a human endeavor … prosecuted to serve human purposes.”
“Iran is clearly seeking relief from mounting military and economic pressure, but that does not mean the diplomatic opening is insincere,” Dania Thafer, the executive director of the Gulf International Forum, told the DCNF. “In fact, pressure is precisely what often produces diplomacy. The more important question is whether Tehran is prepared to translate its offer into reciprocal, verifiable concessions.”
Trump said at the U.N. that the alternative would be an agreement allowing Iran to rebuild and become a “far greater country,” and predicted Washington and Tehran would eventually strike a deal after the November elections.
“He’s doing a kind of a carrot and stick routine here … he’s wielding a very big stick while also dangling a fat juicy carrot,” Grazier told the DCNF. “Saying, on one hand, that he can annihilate the country very quickly. That’s the stick. And then saying that he can like rebuild Iran. That’s the carrot.”
The Pentagon referred to U.S. Central Command, which declined to comment, citing operational security. The White House also did not respond to a request for comment.
The president also used the speech to defend the U.S. campaign against Tehran and reiterate his demand that Iran never acquire a nuclear weapon.
“I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said, according to the United Nations. Trump also credited Operation Midnight Hammer with destroying Iran’s nuclear program and Operation Epic Fury with eliminating the Iranian navy. items.title: Let Them Eat Chicken: Rollins Tells Americans To Find Protein Alternatives As Beef Prices Soar
items.summary: ‘If it is too expensive, unlike fuel, Benny, you can eat chicken’
items.body_text:
Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins is telling Americans to find protein alternatives as beef prices soar.
Rollins, head of President Donald Trump’s U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), appeared on The Benny Show Monday, where host Benny Johnson asked her about the steep beef prices Americans are seeing at the grocery store and what the Trump administration is doing about it. (RELATED: Trump’s Beef Plan Gives A Little To Everyone But Enough To No One)
Johnson, referencing an earlier phone call Rollins received from Trump before going on air, said he believed he knew why the president called her.
“I know that Trump called you about the price of a Big Mac,” Johnson said, “as well as about the price of American beef.”
Johnson continued, saying he believed Trump was “very concerned” about the issue and appreciated the president’s “sensitivity,” before pressing Rollins on what the administration planned to do about the cost of beef.
“What are we going to do about American beef? Nobody likes it. Nobody likes these expensive steaks that cost $20 a pound. So, like gas prices and steak prices, no good,” Johnson said.
Rollins pushed back on Johnson’s characterization of her conversation with Trump, saying the call was not about beef prices.
“Well, it’s interesting. For the first time in, I think, six months, that’s not what he called me about,” Rollins said.
Rollins said Trump had called her about an issue involving another country and efforts to get “more fertilizer in,” while acknowledging that the two do discuss beef prices.
Returning to Johnson’s question, Rollins pointed to several factors affecting the price of beef. First, she said, “Beef is lower by 5 percent, so we are trending in the right direction.” (RELATED: Ranchers, Feds And Conservationists Battle Over The Fate Of 900 Bison)
Rollins then argued that beef prices had risen nearly 30 percent under former President Joe Biden.
Brooke Rollins: If beef is too expensive, you can eat chicken, eggs, other great sources of protein. pic.twitter.com/QpmH1fH6uK
— FactPost (@factpostnews) September 21, 2026
She also explained that rebuilding the nation’s cattle herd takes time because of the time required for reproduction, raising stock, and eventually bringing them to slaughter. Rollins pointed to additional obstacles, including the spread of New World screwworm along the southern border with Mexico, while noting that demand for beef has remained high.
Rollins then offered Americans an alternative if beef remains too expensive. (RELATED: Ranchers Say Beef Market Has ‘Been Hell’ As Trump Announces Plan To Try And Help)
“But if it is too expensive, unlike fuel, Benny, you can eat chicken, pork, salmon, eggs; there are other sources of really good protein, and all of those prices are going down,” Rollins said.
“It isn’t necessarily breaking out there, and listen, I’m a mom of four; I’m still feeding a bunch of hungry kids,” she continued. “We realize the price of groceries are too high, we are doing everything we can to bring them down after the Biden years of crazy, crazy inflation and we are making progress.”
“And I’m really, really proud of that,” Rollins said. “Coming to you soon, cheaper beef, even better beef.”
“America does it better than anywhere in the world,” she continued. “And saving these American ranchers and incentivizing that, we are on their side and they should keep building their herds going forward.”

items.title: Trump-Appointed Judge Smacks Down EPA’s Termination of Clean Energy Grants
items.summary: This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. A federal judge has declared that the Trump administration unlawfully terminated $7 billion in grant funding for clean energy programs in disadvantaged communities. The Solar for All (SFA) program, established during the Biden administration as part of the […]
items.body_text:
This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
A federal judge has declared that the Trump administration unlawfully terminated $7 billion in grant funding for clean energy programs in disadvantaged communities.
The Solar for All (SFA) program, established during the Biden administration as part of the Inflation Reduction Act, provided dozens of grants for states, municipalities, tribes and nonprofits designed to reduce electric bills, create jobs, and address the greenhouse gas emissions warming the global climate.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) canceled the program after President Donald Trump’s inauguration in 2025. The Conservation Law Foundation, Southern Environmental Law Center, Lawyers for Good Government, and Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island sued in the US District Court for the District of Rhode Island on behalf of workers, businesses, nonprofits, and individuals harmed by the withdrawal of funding.
“Congress’s clear intent was that EPA continue to administer the already obligated SFA grants,” Judge Mary S. McElroy, a Trump appointee, wrote in her ruling, issued Friday. “Defendants acted contrary to this intent, and with no other statutory authority, when they terminated the SFA program.”
The ruling means the EPA will have to release the funding, said Nick Torrey, senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center.
“We have seen this administration try to resist and appeal and fight,” Torrey said. “They don’t have any excuse for sitting on this money anymore. They have to get this money out.”
The EPA argued the court lacked jurisdiction over the plaintiffs’ claims and that the claims were meritless. The federal agency told Inside Climate News it is “reviewing the decision and considering options for appeal.”
The EPA awarded the grants in 2024 and said at the time the program would save families $350 million a year on electricity bills and support 200,000 jobs and workforce training opportunities. Among the recipients was a coalition of nonprofits in Florida, which received $156.1 million to create new and expand existing solar programs for low-income communities in the state.
The program was canceled before much of the funding could reach communities, according to the groups involved in the litigation. In 2025 Congress approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which repealed unobligated funding aimed at greenhouse gas emissions. The groups argued the program’s termination was unlawful because the funding was already obligated.
The lawsuit was filed on behalf not of grant recipients but what the litigation described as “downstream beneficiaries.” Among them were solar companies that invested in personnel and equipment based on funding awarded to the states of Georgia and Pennsylvania, a labor union that helped develop an implementation plan in Rhode Island, and a nonprofit that received a sub-award from a grant to the state of Indiana.
Grant recipients filed two subsequent lawsuits against the EPA. State grant recipients also filed challenges in the Court of Federal Claims.

When Louisiana authorities tried to extradite a California doctor last winter for sending abortion pills to women in their state, Gov. Gavin Newsom pushed back—hard. “We will not allow extremist politicians from other states to reach into California and try to punish doctors based on allegations that they provided reproductive health care services,” Newsom declared. “Not today. Not ever.”
Yet nine months after that ringing defense of abortion providers and reproductive freedom, Newsom has blocked Democratic efforts to enshrine the same anti-extradition policy into state law.
The soon-to-be-ex-governor has vetoed a bill that would have prohibited future governors from handing over abortion providers, helpers, and patients to red states for criminal prosecution. The bill also barred extraditions involving transgender care. Newsom’s decision was “incredibly disappointing” and “certainly not what we were expecting,” says Pavitra Abraham, director of state campaigns for Reproductive Freedom for All.
The veto of AB 2164—also known as the Care Without Fear Act—has alarmed reproductive rights advocates around the country because of California’s critical role in preserving abortion access since the Dobbs decision overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. The state is home to telemedicine providers, mail-order pharmacies, research organizations, and other groups that have helped keep abortion pills flowing even to the most conservative parts of the US.
Much of that abortion infrastructure is built on so-called shield laws that protect reproductive care across state lines. California has some of the most robust shield laws in the US, protecting providers, helpers and patients from out-of-state legal action over abortion and gender-affirming care.
Newsom signed California’s first shield laws in 2022 and has consistently backed legislation to strengthen those safeguards. But he has resisted efforts to codify one key protection: a ban on extraditions in criminal cases, like the one Louisiana authorities sought earlier this year. Instead, Newsom argues that decisions on extradition should remain an “executive function”—a prerogative of the governor rather than the legislature, preferably addressed by executive order rather than written into state law.
That distinction doesn’t matter much as long as California has a chief executive who supports reproductive rights. But it could be disastrous if a Republican won the governorship.
“Legislatively enacted laws are just on firmer footing when there are political changes at the executive level,” says Amanda Barrow, senior staff attorney at the UCLA Law Center on Reproductive Health, Law, and Policy. An executive order of the type Newsom has used to fight extraditions “could be revoked by a governor who is anti-abortion or anti–gender-affirming care.”
So, with Newsom winding up his second term as governor and widely expected to run for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, California reproductive advocates made a ban on extradition one of their top legislative priorities for 2026. Eighteen other Democratic-run states have enacted laws prohibiting extradition of abortion providers and patients.
AB 2164 would have gone even further than most of those statutes, extending California’s shield-law protections to providers and helpers based in other blue states where abortion and gender-affirming care are legal.
Supporters seemed confident that Newsom would sign the bill into law. After all, this is the same governor who, when faced with President Donald Trump’s extraordinary effort to gerrymander red-state congressional seats to rig the midterm elections, responded with his own redistricting plan, in the form of last year’s Proposition 50. Four years ago, he signed a law making California the first sanctuary state for trans minors seeking medical care.
