items.title: ONU
items.summary: La líder bolivariana posa sonriente con su antiguo enemigo y le agradece "su respaldo al proceso de reinserción de nuestro país en los espacios multilaterales"
items.body_text:
- Asamblea General Delcy cruzó ante 31 países en 75 pasos para comprometer a Sánchez a "seguir hablando de Venezuela"
La venezolana Delcy Rodríguez ha protagonizado una de las metamorfosis más increíbles y rápidas en la historia reciente de las relaciones internacionales. No tiene el talento y el carisma de Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, el camaleónico diplomático francés capaz de servir a reyes, revolucionarios y en la Restauración, pero sí su habilidad para la supervivencia y la sumisión, pasando en cuestión de meses de ser una de las figuras centrales del chavismo (sancionada por Washington) a convertirse en interlocutora privilegiada del Gobierno de Donald Trump y presidenta legitimada, que no legítima, de su país.
Su evolución la ha llevado a pasar de calificar las sanciones estadounidenses de "terrorismo de Estado" y de denunciar el "imperialismo" ante Naciones Unidas a quedar impasible escuchando al presidente norteamericano, en esa misma sala, llamar "dictador y criminal" a su ex jefe y decir que "el botín pertenece a los vencedores", en referencia al petróleo de su país. Y a posar sonriente y mostrando los dos dedos de la victoria en una foto con su hasta poco enemigo mortal, mientras casi de forma simultánea la líder de la oposición, María Corina Machado, intentaba reiteradamente, pero en vano, volver a Venezuela, atrapada en Panamá entre problemas administrativos, documentación caducada y las maniobras de Washington.
Para ella, lo ocurrido este martes en Nueva York es la mejor noticia posible. Al mismo tiempo, la administración ha tendido una mano a su régimen y dado un nuevo portazo a su principal rival. Rodríguez habla del "respaldo al proceso de reinserción de nuestro país en los espacios multilaterales" y tiene toda la razón. El de hoy ha sido el paso más importante en esa senda, pero seguramente no sea el último.
"Sostuvimos una histórica reunión con el presidente de los Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, con quien conversamos sobre el fortalecimiento de la relación bilateral", escribió Rodríguez en su cuenta oficial de X.
Figura clave junto a su hermano en los años de Nicolás Maduro, Estados Unidos incluyó a Delcy Rodríguez en septiembre de 2018, durante el primer mandato de Trump, en su lista de sancionados por violaciones de derechos humanos. Sin embargo, tras la captura de Maduro en enero de 2026 y el establecimiento de un Gobierno 'interino', Washington pasó progresivamente de la política de máxima presión a una relación de cooperación con Caracas. Ya no se habla de transición, elecciones ni democracia ni hay ruta para Machado.
El 1 de abril el Departamento del Tesoro eliminó formalmente a Rodríguez de la lista de sancionados. En julio, la Administración pidió al Departamento de Justicia que reconociera su inmunidad frente a una demanda civil en Florida, argumentando que ahora era la jefa de Estado de Venezuela. Y a final del verano el acercamiento ha llegado a una dimensión adicional, después de que Washington y Caracas llegaron a un acuerdo increíble sobre petróleo, deuda y reconstrucción de la industria venezolana.
Félix Plasencia y Oliver Blanco, los dos poderosos escoltas de Delcy en su golpe de efecto en la ONU
Sánchez planta a Trump y besa a su encargada
Por su parte, el Gobierno español, que hasta hace poco llamaba a la mandataria "presidenta temporal", y que acogió a Edumundo González y otros exiliados políticos de primer nivel, la ha invitado a la Cumbre Iberoamericana que se celebra en Madrid a principios de noviembre, a pesar de las sanciones comunitarias que en teoría le impiden pisar suelo europeo y que fueron clave en la polémica y nunca del todo aclarada parada en aeropuerto de Bajaras en 2020, con encuentros con el ministro José Luis Ábalos y sus colaboradores.
El paso final de su reconversión, y de su blanqueamiento diplomático, ha llegado este martes en Nueva York, durante la semana grande de la Asamblea General de la ONU. Por la mañana, Rodríguez logró acaparar titulares con una imagen llama

items.title: América
items.summary: Las tres tentativas de las últimas horas se suman a cuatro previas para volver a su país
items.body_text:
Ni en barco ni en avión. La líder democrática María Corina Machado ha intentado regresar a Venezuela en las últimas horas, sin éxito. "No la dejan regresar a su propio país. Suman siete intentos en las últimas semanas", corroboró Pedro Urruchurtu, director de Relaciones Internacionales del equipo de la Premio Nobel de la Paz.
Según adelantaron el diario ABC y la cadena televisiva NTN24, Machado había planificado un regreso en barco desde Panamá atravesando el Caribe hasta Venezuela y coincidiendo con el encuentro en Nueva York entre Donald Trump y Delcy Rodríguez. Cuando todo parecía ya preparado para iniciar la travesía marítima, una avería sospechosa lo impidió, por lo que el viaje fue cancelado.
Tras el primer fracaso, Machado intentó volar a Aruba (isla administrada por Países Bajos a solo 25 kilómetros de Venezuela), desde donde navegaría a Venezuela, lo que fue impedido por las autoridades holandesas.
Posteriormente, el objetivo se trasladó a Curaçao, otra isla holandesa, precisamente la que le sirvió de puente en su salida en diciembre pasado camino de Oslo, donde recogió el premio Nobel. El despegue también fue negado por las autoridades.
"Prohibirle la entrada a María Corina Machado es inaceptable. Ningún poder ni autoridad, interna o foránea, tiene la legitimidad para prohibirle la entrada a un ciudadano venezolano a su país. Déjenla entrar y pongan la fecha de las elecciones. No jueguen con el pueblo venezolano", criticó sin ambages Juan Pablo Guanipa, dirigente de Primero Justicia muy próximo a Machado.
Los cuatro intentos previos
Las tres tentativas de las últimas horas se suman a cuatro previas. El primer bloqueo a la líder democrática sucedió horas después del doble terremoto del día de San Juan, en junio, cuando Machado contrató un avión privado desde Virginia a Curaçao. En pleno vuelo, funcionarios de Washington ordenaron al piloto que regresara al punto de partida, confirmaron a EL MUNDO fuentes del entorno de Machado.
Horas después, Machado intentó subirse a un avión de la aerolínea panameña COPA para volar desde Ciudad de Panamá hasta Caracas, pero en esta ocasión fue el gobierno de Delcy Rodríguez el que impidió su viaje.
Desde finales de junio, Machado ha permanecido en Ciudad de Panamá bajo el amparo de su presidente, José Raúl Mulino, aliado de Estados Unidos. En la anterior etapa, desde su regreso al continente americano, había permanecido en Washington.
En la actualidad, Machado cuenta con un documento, concedido por Panamá, que le permite viajar como medida humanitaria, al carecer de pasaporte venezolano.
En las últimas semanas, este periódico ha conocido, de forma extraoficial, que Machado se había planteado volver a su país por tierra desde Colombia. El plan tampoco prosperó.

items.body_text:
El parking de Triana en Monte Pirolo ya tiene fecha y precios: así se asignarán las plazas y los abonos
Del total de plazas disponibles, habrá 70 que estarán destinadas solo a residentes
El parking de la plaza Monte Pirolo en Triana está pensado para paliar el déficit de plazas de aparcamiento en el barrio. Tendrá en total 100 plazas para vehículos y 10 para motocicletas. Del total de espacios para vehículos, 70 se destinarán a residentes, y los otros 30 a uso rotatorio. En cambio, las 10 plazas de motos serán para uso residencial.
Para acceder a estas plazas para residentes, hay que esperar a que se abra el plazo de solicitudes que se estima sea durante el último trimestre de 2026.
Será imprescindible que los solicitantes estén empadronados en el distrito Triana y que sean titulares del vehículo o que figuren como conductores habituales en la póliza del seguro obligatorio.
Asignación de plazas
Una vez se abra el proceso de solicitud, habrá dos fases. En primer lugar, podrán acceder a estas plazas los residentes de las calles más próximas al aparcamiento, la denominada 'Zona A'. Esta zona estará delimitada por el perímetro interior de las calles por ambas aceras: San Jacinto, Pagés del Corro, San Vicente de Paul y Avenida Santa Cecilia. Las calles interiores a este perímetro son: Maestro Jiménez, Vicente Flores Navarro, plaza Alcalde José Hernández Díaz, Antonio García Corona, plaza Monte Pirolo, Rafael Salas González, Aceituneras, José Cruz Auñón, Sor Manuela Ramos, plaza del Zurraque, jardines Hermanos Garduño, Maestro Guerrero, Maestro Bretón, Sor Milagros, jardín Francisco Gaitán Sánchez, Maestro Guridi, Miguel Ángel Olalla, Doctor Jerónimo Pou e Ignacio Gómez Millán.
En caso de que la demanda supere la oferta, los espacios del aparcamiento se asignarán por sorteo.
Una vez concluida esta primera fase, en el caso de que quedaran plazas libres, podrán presentar su solicitud resto de personas empadronadas en el distrito Triana.
Cada domicilio podrá disponer de un solo abono a no ser que sobren plazas. En cualquier caso, se creará una lista de espera permanente y ordenada en función de la fecha de presentación de la solicitud.
Precio de los aparcamientos y abonos
- 
Turismos de residentes: 110 €/mes
- 
Motos de residentes: 25 €/mes
- 
Uso rotatorio: 0,03 €/minuto
-

items.body_text:
Rueda señala a Galicia como la comunidad «más perjudicada» por Sánchez
El presidente de la Xunta denuncia los privilegios que el Gobierno concede a otras autonomías, mientras la oposición le reprocha carencias en sanidad, educación y vivienda
Santiago
Pedro Sánchez es un presidente «chantajeado», no solo por otros países, sino también por comunidades autónomas. Así lo definió Alfonso Rueda, en una alusión implícita a Marruecos y a Cataluña durante sus respuestas a la oposición este miércoles en la sesión de control en el ... Parlamento autonómico. Y Galicia, para el presidente de la Xunta, «por lo menos últimamente», es la comunidad más «perjudicada» por los privilegios que Sánchez concede a otras.
Lo sostuvo en sus intervenciones para contestar a Ana Pontón (BNG), aunque se explayó sobre todo en su respuesta al socialista José Ramón Gómez Besteiro, cuando este le reprochó sus políticas públicas en materia sanitaria y educativa. «¿Le parece normal que las infraestructuras del Gobierno central que están en Galicia estén como están, mientras vemos cómo se compromete con otras comunidades? Las de siempre, las de siempre», respondió a Besteiro el jefe del Ejecutivo autonómico.
Rueda puso varios ejemplos de esa discriminación de Sánchez hacia Galicia en comparación, sobre todo, con Cataluña, a la que no citó expresamente. Y lanzó a Besteiro otra pregunta de la que tampoco esperaba respuesta: Sánchez «da asignaciones directas siempre a las mismas comunidades autónomas, que son las que chantajean. ¿Le parece normal que les den todas las facilidades en los procesos de transferencia y a nosotros, cada vez que se pide una competencia, cueste sangre, sudor y lágrimas?».
Mencionó también la financiación autonómica, con una reforma que, según lamentó Rueda, el líder del PSdeG «aplaude con las orejas» pese a que con ella «Galicia pasa a ser la tercera comunidad autónoma peor financiada de todas». En este sentido, el presidente de la Xunta recordó, ante las críticas de Besteiro por no negociar con el Gobierno central, que el Ejecutivo autonómico envió 17 alegaciones «bastante extensas» sobre la propuesta del nuevo plan de financiación autonómica, pero todas fueron «ignoradas» y ni siquiera recibieron contestación.
«Galicia pasa a ser la tercera comunidad peor financiada de todas»
Alfonso Rueda
Presidente de la Xunta
Rueda también aludió a la gestión del Gobierno en Ceuta y al reparto de menores migrantes entre las diferentes comunidades autónomas. En este punto, el presidente de la Xunta volvió a dirigirse al líder del PSOE gallego con otra pregunta. Le planteó si «le parece normal» que, ante la situación por la que están pasando los ceutíes, Sánchez diga «que lo arregle» el presidente de la ciudad autónoma. «¿Usted cree que diría eso si fuera otra comunidad autónoma que todos tenemos en la cabeza?», le preguntó Rueda, otra vez en alusión implícita a Cataluña.
El presidente de la Xunta continuó, en la misma línea retórica: «¿Le parece normal que haya comunidades que digan que no están dispuestas a acoger a más menores y que se diga que sí, que no pasa nada, porque ya se nos intentará meter a todas las demás sin planificación, sin diálogo y sin financiación?».
Todas estas respuestas -en forma de preguntas retóricas- llegaron después de una intervención de Besteiro en la que había criticado que «el 40 % de los gallegos viven en núcleos donde no hay equipamientos ni sanitarios ni docentes». El líder socialista concluyó, a partir de ese dato, que «en Galicia, el código postal no solamente dice dónde vives, sino qué derechos tienes». A esta afirmación concreta, Rueda respondió que no hay que olvidar que la mitad de los núcleos de población de toda España están en Galicia.
«En Galicia, el código postal no solamente dice dónde vives, sino qué derechos tienes»
José Ramón G. Besteiro
Secretario general del PSdeG

items.body_text:
Los Juegos Deportivos de Escuelas Católicas de Madrid buscan nuevos árbitros para la temporada 2026-2027
Desde el Departamento de Deportes ya han convocado los cursos de formación arbitral para la XXXVIII edición de una competición que arranca el día 14 de noviembre
Madrid
La XXXVIII edición de los Juegos Deportivos de Escuelas Católicas de Madrid ya está aquí y desde el Departamento deDeporte Escolar y Valores se encuentran inmersos en la preparación de la temporada 2026-2027 que arrancará el sábado 14 de noviembre con ... la disputa de la primera jornada. Pero para que la competición pueda comenzar, es necesario que los árbitros den el pitido inicial. Por este motivo, desde la organización ya han abierto el plazo de inscripción para los cursos de formación arbitral, totalmente gratuitos y con prácticas en situaciones reales, para conformar al colectivo que dirigirá los encuentros de esta temporada.
El fin de semana del 2, 3 y 4 de octubre, Noelia Gutiérrez, árbitra Internacional FIFA y de Segunda división de fútbol sala, será la encargada de impartir el curso de este deporte y contará con la asistencia de Javier Esteban, director del Departamento y ex árbitro de Primera División. Por otro lado, los días 16, 17 y 18 de octubre tendrá lugar el curso de voleibol, cuyo profesor será Javier Rivero, responsable de competición. Para terminar la formación teórica, el curso para los noveles de baloncesto será impartido el mismo fin de semana por Carlos Gómez, coordinador de árbitros.
Además, el viernes 23 de octubre tendrá lugar la formación administrativa de todos los deportes y el sábado 24 se celebrarán los partidos correspondientes a la formación práctica, cuya asistencia es obligatoria para aquellas personas que aprueben la parte teórica. Las instalaciones del colegio Sagrado Corazón de Chamartín albergarán una mañana deportiva en la que los aspirantes podrán vivir su primera experiencia con el silbato en la mano.
«La liga de Escuelas Católicas es ideal para iniciarse en el mundo del arbitraje debido al trato personalizado y a los valores inherentes de la competición. Por este motivo, animo a todas las personas que quieran comenzar su andadura en el mundo del arbitraje a que se inscriban en nuestros cursos que, además, son totalmente gratuitos. También quiero agradecer a los árbitros veteranos que cada año renuevan su compromiso y nos ayudan a equilibrar la balanza entre árbitros jóvenes y árbitros experimentados» asegura Carlos Gómez coordinador de árbitros del Departamento de Deporte Escolar y Valores.
Como es habitual, la inscripción es gratuita. Los interesados en asistir a los cursos deberán aporten tres kilos de comida no perecedera para colaborar con el Banco de Alimentos de Madrid o una entidad similar. La información completa, así como el formulario de inscripción, se encuentra en la web de la competición.
Para los árbitros veteranos, el Departamento ha decidido continuar con la campaña el 'árbitro amigo'. Esta iniciativa consiste en bonificar a aquellos árbitros y/o centros que aporten un árbitro para al menos 17 del total de las jornadas programadas. «Cada persona que venga de tu parte y pite toda la temporada hará que ganes 15 euros», reza el lema de la campaña. Además, los candidatos que vengan de parte de algún centro escolar harán ganar a su institución 30 euros.
AVANCE PARA LA TEMPORADA 2026/2027
El plazo de inscripción de equipos para la temporada 2026-2027 ya está abierto y se cerrará el día 22 de octubre. Por otro lado, la competición arrancará el segundo fin de semana del mes de noviembre, pero durante este mes y el que viene son varias las fechas que cabe destacar. El próximo miércoles, día 23 de septiembre, tendrá lugar la reunión de coordinadores deportivos a las 18.00 horas en formato online. En dicha reunión se tratarán los cambios en las Bases de Competición, los cambios en la Normativa General y las nuevas reglas de baloncesto, fútbol sala y voleibol.

items.title: Trump and Delcy Rodríguez seal thaw with meeting in New York
items.summary: Venezuela’s leader attended the UN speech in which Trump spoke of the country’s oil as a ‘spoils’ to be seized. It was the first meeting between a US president and a Chavista leader since Bill Clinton met Hugo Chávez in 1999
items.body_text:
Trump and Delcy Rodríguez seal thaw with meeting in New York
Venezuela’s leader attended the UN speech in which Trump spoke of the country’s oil as a ‘spoils’ to be seized. It was the first meeting between a US president and a Chavista leader since Bill Clinton met Hugo Chávez in 1999
It was the most anticipated meeting of the day. The embrace between the leaders of two countries considered bitter enemies for nearly three decades. Donald Trump and Delcy Rodríguez, leaders of the United States and Venezuela, met late on Tuesday, the White House confirmed, on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The encounter thus seals a thaw between their countries. But it was not born of equality; rather it reflected Caracas’s absolute subordination to Washington. It was the first meeting between a U.S. president and a Chavista leader since Bill Clinton met then president-elect Hugo Chávez in 1999, apart from a brief exchange at a summit between Barack Obama and Nicolás Maduro in 2015 in Panama City.
The meeting took place at the Lotte New York Palace Hotel as part of a reception offered by Trump to foreign leaders. There were also high-ranking Cabinet members present, including State Secretary Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.
Rodríguez arrived at the UN on Tuesday saying she was coming to the United States “with her head held high.” Shortly afterward she watched, unmoved, as Trump boasted of the “massive military operation” that detained “a criminal, a dictator: Nicolás Maduro.” The former Venezuelan president was physically very close to the spot where he was being discussed—about a 20-minute drive away, in the Brooklyn jail where he has slept since his forced removal from power on January 3.
But what the Republican president seemed most proud of was the deal announced in September that would grant privileged access to more than 20% of the South American country’s oil reserves. “When you add the United States and Venezuela together, we have more than 60 percent of the oil in the world. So it’s, perhaps, the biggest deal. It was a war, but it is, maybe, the greatest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils,” he said.
The setting could not have been more symbolic. It was at UN headquarters that Chávez, the leader of the Bolivarian revolution who came to power in 1998, famously declared, “There’s a smell of sulfur here.” He said it at the 2006 General Assembly after President George W. Bush spoke. “Yesterday the devil was here, in this very place; there is still a smell of sulfur at this roster where I have had to speak,” Chávez said—words repeated and caricatured countless times.
Maduro, Chávez’s successor after his death in 2013, returned to a bellicose rhetoric. The last time was in 2018, during Trump’s first term. Even Rodríguez herself, who now insists on the need to build bridges with the American leader, launched harsh attacks on the United States and on Trump from the UN podium.
In 2019 she called U.S. sanctions a form of “state terrorism” that no longer uses bombs but banks and insurers; she accused the Republican leader of having “extended his imperial claws” against Cuba; she said peoples like Venezuela’s lacked access to a media machine serving the global “hegemon” and its satellites; and she urged Washington to show less arrogance and more tolerance toward free nations. Today, those words seem distant.
Upon landing in New York last Sunday, the Chavista leader expressed her willingness not to cause any trouble. “We arrived in New York with the firmness and hope of a people who believe in encounter and unity among nations,” the former vice president and now acting president wrote. “At the 81st United Nations General Assembly, Venezuela will be present to carry its voice and defend its principles, with a work agenda based on respect, cooperation and understanding. [...] We are a country committed to peace, dialogue and

items.body_text:
International cuts to development aid foreshadow profound changes to the system: ‘We are terrified of going back to the 1980s’
Leaders meeting at the UN General Assembly face a humanitarian polycrisis as the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the right to development is marked, while calls for a rethink of an obsolete cooperation model increase
Political leaders, civil society representatives and business figures are meeting this week in New York as part of the United Nations General Assembly. They are trying to patch up the chaos caused by a frontal attack on the multilateral system by some members, including a drastic cut to international cooperation by major donor countries, led by the United States. Estimates calculate that the largest cut in history — 23.1% in 2025 according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) — is on course to cause millions of deaths. A study published in The Lancet puts the toll at 22.6 million additional deaths by 2030 as a result of the funding reductions.
On the ground, crises are deepening: Sudan, Gaza, Somalia, and Yemen expose the inability of the international community and UN institutions to respond to emergencies and to prevent humanitarian catastrophes from taking shape, as this week marks the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the right to development. Of the sustainable development goals the international community set for 2030, barely 36% show some progress, while 15% have regressed.
Meanwhile, in official offices and the headquarters of large international organizations a heated debate is intensifying, precipitated by the abrupt funding cuts and starting from one premise: the development cooperation we knew is gone — what now? “For many it’s clear the previous model is already obsolete. In the past, donor-recipient agreements could work, but no one wants that dependency anymore,” Yemi Osinbajo, former vice president of Nigeria, said in London.

The response they find in numerous capitals is very similar: development cooperation has entered a new era — more transactional, less dependent, and more complex. “We are not just talking about the end of USAID. We are talking about fraud, remittances, technology, debt. You can’t just patch things up, the system has to change,” González Laya says, who, like other experts consulted for this report, emphasizes the opportunities now opening up: “There are pockets of wealth waiting to be mobilized through technology.”
The challenges are monumental, beyond the dismantling of USAID. European donors such as the United Kingdom or France have followed the U.S. lead, but above all, Osinbajo explains, the international context has changed radically: the climate crisis, vulnerable economies amid a trade war, the pullback of Chinese investment in Africa and the growing presence of Gulf countries, Turkey, and Brazil on the continent all contribute to the great shake-up. “There is a shift in mindset and recipient countries already think they can say no because there are other partners available,” explains Alexia Latortue, head of the secretariat of the Future of Development Cooperation Coalition and a former member of the U.S. Department of Commerce in the Biden-Harris administration.

items.body_text:
Mexico joins Latin American crackdown on cellphones in schools
The Sheinbaum administration will restrict phones from November, while Brazil, Chile, Argentina, and Colombia move ahead with different approaches to limit devices in classrooms and playgrounds
Children in Mexico spend up to seven hours a day in front of a screen. In light of this reality, the government has decided to completely restrict the use of cellphones in elementary and middle schools. President Claudia Sheinbaum, who has avoided calling the initiative a “ban,” says she wants to fight phone addiction among young people to “protect their development and creativity.” The country thus joins Brazil and Chile among regional states with stricter rules on cellphone use in classrooms and moves ahead of others, such as Argentina and Colombia, where regulation is still underway.
As of November 3, elementary and middle school classrooms and playgrounds in Mexico will be screen-free. Sheinbaum and Education Secretary Mario Delgado have spent weeks presenting data, backed by experts, that outline the problem: more than 83% of parents are worried about their children’s device time and more than 70% of household heads support regulating use. It is not only an adult perception: four in 10 Mexican students say their classmates are distracted by digital devices in most or all classes. In addition, a survey of over 565,000 teachers found that 81% support the measure. Delgado also highlighted the impact of social networks on children and adolescents, noting that U.S. courts have ruled that these platforms are designed to be addictive and cause harm to mental health.
The PISA 2025 report, in which Mexico slipped in mathematics, revealed that almost half of the time students spend on screens at school (2.7 hours) is for leisure. Devices have shortened the attention span readers use to comprehend a text. Following the government forums and the release of the results of the international study, Mexico has joined more than half of the world’s countries that already have restrictions on the use of devices in schools. Depending on the region, the measures range from banning cellphones during the school day to total restrictions on certain social media platforms.
In Latin America, Brazil removed cellphones from schools at the start of the last school year in January 2025. The Lula government decided to ban them both in classrooms and during recess, in public and private schools, to protect students’ mental and physical health and to improve academic performance. The debate was intense, but the overall assessment is positive. On the first anniversary of phone-free schools, eight in 10 Brazilian students reported “paying more attention” in class and 65% of teachers said incidents of online bullying had fallen, according to an evaluation of the law commissioned by the parliamentary education bloc. Even students unhappy with the new rule acknowledged the benefits. Lívia de Souza Xavier, 14, said she concentrates more and her grades have improved significantly, according to testimony collected by the NGO Alana, which focuses on children. Another student said she now talks more with classmates and, if she cannot find them, she goes to look for them, as reported by Naiara Galarraga Gortázar.
Chile has moved in the same direction since February, when Law 21.801 came into force, restricting the use of phones and any other internet-enabled device in preschool, elementary, and high school education. The prohibition, however, is not absolute: the law exempts pedagogical use, meaning cases in which a teaching activity requires a device. The legislation also allows other exceptions that must be justified by parents or guardians and generally require authorization from the school administration. These include special educational needs, emergencies or disasters, the student’s health conditions, and personal safety. items.title: Netherlands to return to Eurovision in 2027 after AVROTROS withdrawal
items.summary: The Netherlands will participate in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest after all, Nu.nl
items.body_text:
Netherlands to return to Eurovision in 2027 after AVROTROS withdrawal
The Netherlands will participate in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest after all, Nu.nl reports. It will join the lineup in Burgas, Bulgaria, where the semi-finals are scheduled for May 11 and 13, followed by the Grand Final on May 15. It is undecided which artist will represent the country, as the new organizing broadcaster will need to establish a brand-new selection committee.
The Dutch Eurovision organizer, public broadcaster AVROTROS, formally announced in August that it would not participate in the contest. They explicitly stated the event could "no longer be considered neutral" while a participating country, referring to Israel, remains involved in a large-scale military conflict. AVROTROS had previously boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna for the same reason.
Because AVROTROS stepped aside, they returned the responsibility for the country's Eurovision selection to the Dutch public broadcasting system, the NPO.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) originally set a deadline of September 15 for countries to confirm their participation. However, because the NPO had to explore alternative internal options, they requested and were granted a special extension until the end of September to make their final choice.
Other internal broadcasters like Omroep MAX explicitly publicly rejected taking over the contest earlier in the month, stating the event "didn't suit them." Despite this, the NPO has successfully navigated its alternative options within the deadline extension.
The Netherlands was part of a group consisting of five countries, alongside Ireland, Spain, Iceland, and Slovenia, that withdrew from the 2026 Vienna contest in protest. Ireland's national broadcaster, RTÉ, has already reaffirmed that it will not participate in or broadcast the 2027 event due to the ongoing loss of life in Gaza. Meanwhile, Spain's RTVE and Iceland's RÚV are still internally debating their decisions, Eurovoix reported.

items.title: Court overturns large fines against misleading education firms over missing screenshots
items.summary: Thirteen educational institutions accused of misleading students about the degree they could obtain will not have to pay about 450,000 euros in fines, as investigators handling the case failed to t
items.body_text:
Court overturns large fines against misleading education firms over missing screenshots
Thirteen educational institutions accused of misleading students about the degree they could obtain will not have to pay about 450,000 euros in fines, as investigators handling the case failed to take screenshots of websites and marketing material which could have proved the allegations. The highest administrative court in the Netherlands dismissed the penalties on appeal in a ruling published on Wednesday.
It has not been proven that the institutions involved conferred titles on their students without approval from the Accreditation Organisation of the Netherlands and Flanders (NVAO), according to the verdict from the Council of State's court branch. Further, there was no evidence submitted which demonstrated that the institutions made false claims.
The Council of State did not state which educational institutions were involved, however it appeared likely that the matter was linked to a 2022 report from the Education Inspectorate taking the adult education firm NCOI to task for offering programs using terms like "master," "professional master," or "executive master". Since then, the NCOI Group has been organized as the Salta Group.
"Based on the findings" in the report, "the Inspectorate concludes that between September 2017 and June 2021, the institution wrongfully awarded 435 degrees for professional master's and executive master's programs for which no NVAO accreditation existed," the Inspectorate wrote. This was in violation of the Higher Education Act," the report stated. The specific number of 435 degrees was also referenced in the lower court ruling that was appealed to the Council of State.
A master's title is a protected term, and only accredited institutions may award them. However, such words do not automatically make it a "master's degree" under the law, the Council of State ruled. It added that it is also not a criminal offense for others to get the impression that their training did lead to a master's title.
The institutions took the matter to the District Court for The Hague, which ruled in favor of the minister. They then lodged an appeal with the Council of State, the highest administrative court. The Council said that the inspectorate "failed to substantiate the findings with evidence." As a result, the minister "did not concretely and specifically record what was wrong and what has been improved," according to the Council.
The institutions were initially ordered to pay a combined total of approximately 470,000 euros. Former Education Minister Robbert Dijkgraaf imposed these fines two years after the Inspectorate's initial report, which determined that the situation had not sufficiently improved, and students still were not receiving clear information.
On June 26, 2023, the Ministry of Education issued fines against the institutions LOI, NCOI, NTI, Luzac, Scheidegger, Schoevers, SRM, Bestuursacademie Nederland, Tio, Pro Education, Boertien Vergouwen Overduin, ISBW, and Markus Verbeek Praehep. The highest fine, initially 207,250 euros, was for NCOI. This amount was later reduced to 194,000 euros.
Reporting by ANP and NL Times

items.title: Family demands investigation into Rotterdam woman's death after Aruba rollover crash
items.summary: The family of a 23-year-old Rotterdam woman who died on the island of Aruba earlier this month is calling for further investigation into the circumstances surrounding the off-road vehicle crash tha
items.body_text:
Family demands investigation into Rotterdam woman's death after Aruba rollover crash
The family of a 23-year-old Rotterdam woman who died on the island of Aruba earlier this month is calling for further investigation into the circumstances surrounding the off-road vehicle crash that caused her death. Kimberly van Ardenne was with her boyfriend on holiday, visiting their friend, a Dutch Marine who lives there. All three were in the utility terrain vehicle when it rolled over near Grapefield, an area with rocky cliffs and a beach in San Nicolas at the southern end of the island.
Within hours of the crash, officers responding to the scene had identified Van Ardenne as the driver. In a statement posted to social media, Aruba police wrote that they first learned of the crash a few minutes before 3 p.m. that Sunday afternoon.
"On arrival it was found that a UTV had somehow overturned, and the driver appeared to be in grave condition," police said. Despite paramedics' efforts, the Rotterdam woman was pronounced dead at the scene by a forensic doctor. In the same statement, police said she was the driver, confirming a statement from her boyfriend, who was not seriously injured.
However, witnesses have painted a different picture in comments on social media, and in remarks to media outlets. One person claimed they saw the trio tearing up the area around Carnival Village about three kilometers west of the crash site. They left after 15 minutes, and Van Ardenne was not behind the wheel of the off-road vehicle, which rolled over soon after, according to 24ora.
"We would very much like to know exactly what happened," her surviving family members wrote in a public appeal. "We have heard various accounts, but we also know there were actual witnesses at the scene of the accident. We appeal to anyone who was present or has information to contact us," they wrote.
What is clear is that all three people were in the vehicle at the time of the incident, and their friend was responsible for arranging the off-road vehicle, according to RTL. The family said some pieces simply do not add up.
Van Ardenne did not enjoy driving in general, nor and was especially cautious. She was not the type to drive any vehicle dangerously, especially not in the wild manner seen at Carnival Village, according to her cousin, Stephanie, who spoke to RTL on the family's behalf.
The case will now be investigated by the Marechaussee, a spokesperson told the broadcaster. The branch of the military typically handles inquiries where military personnel were involved may have acted wrongfully.
Van Ardenne's body was repatriated to the Netherlands, and her family has been meeting with people this week who wanted to offer support. Her funeral was scheduled to take place this Saturday in Rotterdam.
"With deep sorrow, we must say goodbye far too soon to our daughter, granddaughter, sister, niece, and friend," the family stated. "We will carry her warmth, love, and unique personality in our hearts forever."

items.title: Fire fighters investigating a gas leak turn out to be the cause
items.summary: When the residents of the Brabant town of Oisterwijk smelled the pungent odor of gas on Wednesday, they called their...
items.body_text:
Fire fighters investigating a gas leak turn out to be the cause
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
When the residents of the Brabant town of Oisterwijk smelled the pungent odor of gas on Wednesday, they called their local fire department, who turned out to be the culprits.
Fire fighters spent the morning searching for a gas leak to no avail. Together with gas provider Enexis, they tested levels throughout the town but could not find a source, only the smell.
Meanwhile, back at the fire station, staff discovered a canister of THT was missing. The chemical is added to gas, which is naturally odorless, to so that people can smell any leak immediately.
The cannister had been accidently thrown out and had spent the morning in the back of a garbage truck, which was making its rounds.
“We were able to have a laugh about it for a moment,” firefighter Ronald Blokpoel told Omroep Brabant.
Residents may continue to smell gas for a time while the chemical dissipates. The fire depart warns there is no danger to public health.

items.title: Mourners claim diabetic man who died under arrest was “murdered”
items.summary: Around 150 people joined a funeral procession on Wednesday for a man who died while being detained by police who...
items.body_text:
Mourners claim diabetic man who died under arrest was “murdered”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Around 150 people joined a funeral procession on Wednesday for a man who died while being detained by police who stopped him while searching for a stolen fatbike.
The body of 51-year-old Alfredo Goeloe was carried in a white coffin in a carriage drawn by two white horses to the Zuiderbegraafplaats in Rotterdam, 10 days after he collapsed while being pinned to the ground and handcuffed.
Friends and relatives who followed the coffin carried banners with slogans including “samen tegen onrecht omdat we om elkaar geven” (united against injustice because we care for each other).
One of the mourners, Yenci Vargas, told Nieuwsuur: “He was murdered. I’m not talking about racism, but he was murdered by the negligence and stupidity of the police.”
Another, Marsha Mabosa, said: “Last month we were out in a café and he asked me to dance the bachata. He was a very good dancer. And now we have to miss him in a way that is very unjust.”
Stolen fatbike
Goeloe was stopped by police while riding a fatbike through Rotterdam on the evening of Saturday, September 12.
Police initially said he was suspected of stealing the bike, but later changed their story to say he had been stopped because he was riding too fast. Just before Goeloe’s arrest a fatbike had been reported stolen by a couple aged around 40.
Goeloe tried to run from police when they tried to arrest him for not carrying ID. His family said he had borrowed his sister’s bike to go out to get medication for his diabetes.
He was chased down and passed out while he was being restrained on his belly. Video footage showed he cried out that he had diabetes and was in pain as he lay on the ground.
Official complaint
Goeloe’s family have filed a criminal complaint against four police officers. Lawyer Gerard Roethof said they viewed it as “a case of manslaughter, or in any event severe assault with fatal consequences.”
Jan Schalkwijk, a lawyer with Control Alt Delete, an organisation that monitors racial profiling in the Netherlands, said the use of force by police was excessive.
“The officers were far superior in number, according to reports he was unarmed, and he could have been approached with less force,” Schalkwijk argued.
Restraint guidelines
But Jaap Timmer, a political scientist at the VU university in Amsterdam who specialises in police use of force, said there was no indication from the film footage that the police had failed to follow protocol.
He said police guidelines said people should be pressed against the ground for as short a time as possible when under arrest, but it was unsafe to let them stand up before they had been handcuffed.
“I understand the police were looking for a fatbike and this man was riding too fast. That could be a reason to ask his identity,” he said.
“He then ran away fast and resisted his arrest. That has nothing to do with ethnic profiling, but with the man’s behaviour.”

items.title: Road safety institute weighing up zero tolerance for drivers
items.summary: The Dutch Road Safety Research Institute has released a new study on reducing the drug and alcohol limit for drivers...
items.body_text:
Road safety institute weighing up zero alcohol limit for drivers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch Road Safety Research Institute has released a new study on reducing the drug and alcohol limit for drivers to zero, finding it would probably decrease road accidents but would increase pressure on the police.
SWOV looked at the policy in eight countries with limits lower than the Netherlands, which is of blood alcohol level of 0.05% or 0.02% for those who have been driving for less than 5 years.
The risk of accidents is already elevated at the 0.05% level, the report says. Other countries, including Norway and Sweden, set the level at 0.02% for all drivers.
“An absolute zero limit is considered to be a simple and unambiguous standard that leaves less room for interpretation of what is still permissible and what is not,” the report says, and would improve road safety.
However, lowering the limit will lead to more work for police but also testing facilities. It can be difficult, especially with cannabis, to properly detect the levels, especially with saliva tests.
“Particularly for THC and cocaine, concentrations or metabolites can remain detectable long after the immediate effects have disappeared,” the institute wrote, which would create legal problems for criminal prosecutions.

Agents from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) have detained a senior official from opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s chancellery as part of a probe into alleged misspending of funds under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
An employee of a major right-wing broadcaster, Republika, was also taken into custody as part of the same investigation, which relates to the activities of the Polish National Foundation (PFN), a body created under the PiS government to promote Poland abroad but which was also used to further the party’s political interests.

On Tuesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, announced that two individuals, named only as Piotr M. and Anna P. under Polish privacy law, had been detained by the CBA at the request of prosecutors investigating irregularities in the PFN.
Both suspects previously worked in the chancellery of Prime Minister Beata Szydło, who was head of the PiS government from 2015 to 2017. Piotr M. was head of the Government Information Centre (CIR) and Anna P. led the media services department.
Anna P. now works for Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. She is director of the Presidential Events Office, which organises the president’s schedule. Piotr M. currently works as a commentator for Republika, a station generally supportive of Nawrocki and PiS.
Agenci CBA zatrzymali w Warszawie Piotra M. i Annę P. Sprawa dotyczy nieprawidłowości w Polskiej Fundacji Narodowej! pic.twitter.com/e3jw3ekdOA
— Iwona Hartwich (@iwonahartwich) September 23, 2026
In 2017, while still working in Szydło’s chancellery, Piotr M. and Anna P. founded a PR company called Solvere. Later that same year, the company was hired to run a prominent and controversial campaign for the PFN called “Fair Courts”, receiving a reported 1.2 million zloty (€275,000) for the project.
The PFN had been set up the previous year under Szydło’s government with funding from 17 state-owned companies. Its publicly declared and statutory mission was to promote Poland abroad.
However, the “Fair Courts” campaign, which cost around 8.4 million zloty, was run in Poland itself, with material in Polish, and aimed to show the alleged failings of the justice system in Poland in order to justify why controversial reforms being implemented by PiS were necessary.
Echoing PiS rhetoric, the campaign suggested that judges saw themselves as a “special caste” and highlighted cases of alleged wrongdoing by individual judges, including one who had been caught stealing a sausage. (The judge in question had not ruled on a case since that incident in 2006 and had died in 2015.)
In 2018, a Warsaw court ruled that the “Fair Courts” campaign was inconsistent with the PFN’s statutory goals, saying that not only did the adverts fail to enhance Poland’s image abroad, “on the contrary, they significantly weakened it, creating a negative image of the judiciary based on individual cases”.
In February 2025, just over a year after PiS lost power, a newly appointed PFN board accused its predecessors of criminal negligence that caused damages of over 30 million zloty to the foundation’s finances. They notified prosecutors of potential crimes.

items.title: New US “Fort Trump” military base in Poland “confirmed”, says President Nawrocki
items.summary: "I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word."
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump”.
Trump himself declared last week that “major progress” was being made towards establishing the base, saying it was thanks to the “bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki”, who is a conservative ally of the US president.
Meanwhile, earlier this week, a Polish deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, also expressed confidence that the new base would soon be confirmed and said that it could see the number of US troops stationed in Poland rise to around 15,000.
President Karol Nawrocki said he hopes the US will finalize plans to establish a permanent military base in Poland and, if it does, the compound will be christened ‘Fort Trump' https://t.co/SB4DOy5Qp1 pic.twitter.com/aPmvl4JoFO
— Bloomberg TV (@BloombergTV) September 22, 2026
The US military presence in Poland has become a big issue this year following Washington’s unexpected last-minute decision in May to cancel the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 troops.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. In June, Poland formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
In a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, last week, Trump announced “major progress” in those plans and said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”. He called it a “historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance”.
On Tuesday this week, speaking to Bloomberg during a visit to the US for the United Nations General Assembly, Nawrocki confirmed that plans for the base were at an advanced stage.
“The infrastructure is being chosen right now. Consultants from the US have already visited Poland,” he said. “I think that it’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word.”
Nawrocki also expressed confidence that “President Trump will personally be able to participate in the inauguration of Fort Trump”. That name, Fort Trump, was first suggested in 2018 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda, when, during Trump’s first term, he sought a permanent US base in Poland.
Poland’s government, which regularly clashes with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and has also at times had tense relations with the Trump administration, has not commented on the idea of naming the new base after the US president.
However, the government is keen for the project to move ahead, and has been doing much of the legwork on making it happen. Although Poland’s president is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, his position is largely ceremonial, and it is the government that is responsible for implementing policy.
On Monday this week, deputy defence minister Stanisław Wziątek told broadcaster RMF that he was “convinced there is full agreement” on establishing the base, with the remaining question being the precise location.
Wziątek said that the announcement could be made before November’s midterm elections in the US, as Trump will be keen to encourage Polish Americans to vote Republican.

Poland’s security services have detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them has been charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school.
On Tuesday, the National Prosecutor’s Office announced that the main suspect, who can be named only as Paweł G. under Polish privacy law, had been detained last week by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and charged by prosecutors with three alleged crimes.
Prokurator ze śląskiego wydziału PZ PK przedstawił 17-letniemu obywatelowi Polski zarzut przygotowania zamachu terrorystycznego, którego celem miało być zabójstwo wielu osób. ⬇️https://t.co/bYi6GY3BaR
— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 22, 2026
The most serious charge, carrying a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years, relates to undertaking preparations to kill a large number of people through a terrorist attack.
Prosecutors say that analysis of data from devices belonging to the suspect revealed correspondence concerning the planning of large-scale attacks, including on a school and a mosque, as well as surveillance of targets, acquisition of weapons, and the use of grenades and Molotov cocktails.
Poland has a small Muslim community, but one that has grown rapidly in recent years amid high levels of immigration, and now numbers in the tens of thousands. That has prompted protests from some far-right groups, especially in relation to the growth of Islamic places of worship.
Nationalists have protested against an Islamic centre in Kraków, saying they "do not consent to the spread of Islam in Poland".
However, the city's equality officer has criticised such groups for "artificially fueling fears and instigating conflicts" https://t.co/qNKJJxMQa5
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026
Paweł G. is also charged with being part of a criminal group that aimed to “commit a terrorist offence, promote Nazi and fascist content, and incite hatred based on national, ethnic, racial and religious differences”. That crime is punishable by up to ten years in prison.
The final alleged offence is public incitement of hatred, promotion of a fascist and Nazi system of state, and possession of Nazi and fascist material with the intention to disseminate it through the internet. That crime carries a jail term of up to three years.
The suspect, who prosecutors have confirmed is a Polish citizen, has not pleaded guilty to the alleged offences. A court has accepted a request by prosecutors to keep him in detention for three months while the investigation continues.
The National Prosecutor’s Office noted that two additional individuals associated with Paweł G. have been transferred to juvenile courts, without providing further information on what offences they are alleged to have committed.
However, in a separate statement, the ABW confirmed that they are two 16-year-olds detained last week as part of an investigation into an online group associated with neo-Nazi propaganda and violence.
The ABW named the two suspects as Kacper K. and Wiktor Ś., saying that the pair had been in possession of materials relating to Hitler’s Third Reich, Nazism, racism and antisemitism, as well as terrorist attacks, mass killings and lone-wolf gunmen.
Kacper K. has been placed in a juvenile detention centre for three months, while Wiktor Ś. was placed in a police holding centre for children for an unspecified period of time.

items.title: Hans Väre: Where is our AI kill switch?
items.summary: If we have generators and drinking water supplies for power outages, Estonia should also have an ax with which to cut dangerous AI out of critical infrastructure, writes Hans Väre.
items.body_text:
Hans Väre: Where is our AI kill switch?
If we have generators and drinking water supplies for power outages, Estonia should also have an ax with which to cut dangerous AI out of critical infrastructure, writes Hans Väre.
Who hasn't sometimes wished life were like a movie? With wishes like that, though, you should always specify which movie. A romantic comedy? That would probably be fine. But a science fiction movie in which an asteroid comes to destroy Earth, an ugly alien eats its way through the people on a spaceship as if emptying a tin can or artificial intelligence seizes power from humanity and puts us in the Matrix? No, thank you. That kind of life is not for me.
Unfortunately, judging by recent news, we may already have one foot inside such a movie. Silicon Valley's creations are less spectacular and dramatic than Hollywood's, but that is all the more reason to take them seriously. We do not need to dodge bullets with our coats flying or bend space. We need to fight battles on the prosaic fronts of bureaucracy, economics and convenience.
The idea that AI will destroy humanity is, of course, an old one. Until now, though, it was mainly a science fiction story or a theoretical warning from visionaries. This summer, we got our first very concrete examples of disobedient AI. These were not isolated to one case: AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google have all gone beyond their controls. Not the helpful chatbots many people use in daily life, but much more powerful and advanced versions.
Let us briefly recall just one of them, OpenAI's, which brought the issue to public attention in midsummer. For simplicity's sake, imagine completely isolated, airtight boxes like those used to study poisons or viruses, except virtual ones. New AI models are tested in these separate containers so they cannot endanger the real world even if one of them does something wrong.
This time, however, the powerful models were so persistent that, when they could not complete the tasks they had been given, they kept looking for new ways to achieve their goals and crossed several boundaries in the process.
Agents in separate boxes found a way to create a secret message board. There, they shared tips on how to reach their goals by prohibited means, how to hide the traces of their transgressions from humans and encouraged one another to break the rules. By joining forces, the agents managed to do something that should have been impossible: reach the public internet unnoticed and break into Hugging Face, a repository of AI models. In the human world, that would be a criminal offense.
True, the AI's unauthorized actions caused no major harm this time, but we should not forget that these were only the first, relatively restrained incidents.
Nor had the AI been directly instructed to seriously attack anyone. But it does not need such an instruction to destroy humanity, as Oxford University professor Nick Bostrom showed with his 2003 thought experiment about a paperclip maximizer. In it, an AI is given a seemingly innocent task, such as making as many paperclips as possible. To carry it out, the AI uses up all the metal and energy available in the world and destroys humans along the way because they want to use resources needed for paperclips to produce things that, from the AI's perspective, are complete nonsense — food, for example.
We do not even need such an extreme example. It would be enough for a sufficiently capable AI model to break into a power plant's servers and turn off a nuclear reactor's cooling system or do something similarly reckless. Even setting aside the destruction of humanity and other outright catastrophe scenarios, AI brings a long list of real and immediate risks, from its effects on the labor market to the reshaping of human relationships.

items.title: Üllar Lanno: So that treatment queues don't turn into death sentences
items.summary: If the state tries to save money in healthcare by stretching waiting lists and cutting services, someone will eventually pay with their life. The next government will have little choice but to sharply expand medical training and close the funding gap, because the state is obligated to provide timely care, writes Üllar Lanno.
items.body_text:
Üllar Lanno: So that treatment queues don't turn into death sentences
If the state tries to save money in healthcare by stretching waiting lists and cutting services, someone will eventually pay with their life. The next government will have little choice but to sharply expand medical training and close the funding gap, because the state is obligated to provide timely care, writes Üllar Lanno.
More and more often we must remind ourselves that Estonia still has a solidarity‑based healthcare system, and every social tax payer must have access to a specialist within a reasonable time. Unfortunately, more and more people from rural counties are traveling to hospitals or private clinics in Tallinn or Tartu.
In private clinics, a quick paid appointment is often obtained with a phone call. No e‑consultation filter — you get everything you need if you pay, even though you have already paid social tax. In this way, the state reaches deeper into our pockets to cover the Health Insurance Fund's deficit. The poorest are left without help, and the system becomes expensive and unequal.
The Health Insurance Fund calls next year's cuts "modernization." Behind that word is a €3 million reduction in specialist outpatient funding and nearly €10 million in cuts to radiology. This year, laboratory funding was also reduced by one‑sixth. In total, specialist care faces more than €24 million in negative changes.
On paper, a small miracle happens: specialist care still ends up €1.81 million in the black. The rabbit is pulled out of the hat using a €15 million "modernization and demand assessment reserve."
A reserve for modernization
It is unknown which services will receive this money, how it will be allocated, or how much of the reserve will actually be used. The Health Insurance Fund wants to reduce its deficit from nearly €90 million this year to €44 million next year. Meanwhile, healthcare costs continue to rise. Doctors and nurses want wage increases above average salary growth, while the Ministry of Finance forecasts average wage growth at around five percent.
Salaries make up two‑thirds of a hospital's budget. Giving hospitals less money while saying salaries must rise is like ordering someone to remove five kilos from a backpack and then pack ten kilos more into it. Something must disappear — most likely appointment slots and treatment capacity.
This year, specialist contact appointments in the first half of the year were down six percent compared to last year, and 15 percent compared to 2023. Meanwhile, e‑consultations increased by 27 percent. E‑consultations are not the enemy when a family doctor quickly receives specialist advice. But a slow, drawn‑out e‑consultation becomes a barrier behind which the patient waits while their illness progresses. And e‑consultations are answered by the same doctors — the bottleneck remains until more of them exist.
Unlimited waiting time
Take a family doctor who asks a cardiologist for advice. The cardiologist replies: first do an ECG, an echo, blood tests, and a few more examinations. Then the results are sent again. The clock ticks, and the patient still has not seen a cardiologist. The system saves money until the disease decides it will not wait any longer.
During the 2009 economic crisis, the maximum waiting time for outpatient specialist care was extended from four weeks to six. The crisis ended, but six weeks remained. Last year, nearly a quarter of planned first specialist visits exceeded that limit. In regional hospitals, more than a third exceeded 42 days.
After an e‑consultation, 23 percent of patients who needed an appointment were scheduled more than 42 days later. Current rules say a person may be placed on a waiting list only if waiting does not worsen their health, disease progression, or prognosis — and this is not a recommendation.
If the system cannot fulfill its duties, the solution cannot be lowering the bar. If a house's foundation sinks, there is no point in sawing the doorframe crook

items.title: Minister: Teachers, rescuers, police to get pay rises in 2027 budget
items.summary: Teachers, cultural workers, rescuers and police will receive modest pay rises next year, Education Minister Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) said as union talks resumed Wednesday.
items.body_text:
Minister: Teachers, rescuers, police to get pay rises in 2027 budget
Teachers, cultural workers, rescuers and police will receive modest pay rises next year, Education Minister Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) said as union talks resumed Wednesday.
Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi (Reform) said the broad framework for next year's state budget is in place, with the four sectors receiving equal additional funding for wages.
A one-hour warning strike by education workers protesting at pay ran Tuesday from 8–9 a.m. at preschools and 9–10 a.m. at general and vocational schools.
Kallas confirmed to ERR that the four groups can expect a "small" pay rise next year, but did not specify the exact percentage ahead of negotiations with the Education Personnel Union (EHL) continuing Wednesday afternoon. She said the additional funding for the wage bill would be the same for all four sectors.
"The budget situation is so difficult that, in order to be able to raise these salaries at all, even by a little, we have to make cuts somewhere," Kallas said.
She added additional revenue from economic growth will be consumed by increases in pensions. Assuming 2.4 percent growth next year, the most optimistic estimate is €350 million in additional tax revenue.
"Of that €350 million, €200 million will essentially go immediately and automatically toward covering indexed expenditure, meaning pensions and a few other expenses, such as parental benefits," Kallas said. "Very little of the money generated by economic growth will remain available."
According to Kallas, cuts will have to be found in infrastructure and real estate investments. She said the government should decide not to launch any new real estate investments at all. "Finish those that are currently in progress and do not launch any new real estate investments for now. Then look at the infrastructure situation as a whole to see whether any savings can be made there."
The government will discuss the state budget again at a Cabinet meeting Thursday, and hopes to finalise it Monday before submitting it to the Riigikogu.
The EHL is seeking to raise the minimum teacher salary to €2,312, the projected Estonian average for 2027, up from the current €1,970. Union chair Reemo Voltri said the government has been backing away from its pledge to raise salaries to 120 percent of the national average. The EHL said 69 percent of Estonian teachers have considered leaving the profession in the past year, citing workload and low pay.
Teachers had also been joined by rescue workers in picketing the Riigikogu earlier this month (pictured). The average national wage reported for the second quarter of this year is €2,243 per month gross.

items.title: Bulgarian PM Pledges to Sharply Limit Gambling Adverts
items.summary: New laws will drastically reduce presence of gambling advertisements, as Prime Minister Rumen Radev complains Bulgaria's towns and villages 'look like Las Vegas'.
items.body_text:
Bulgarian PM Pledges to Sharply Limit Gambling Adverts
Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Wednesday announced a new bill targeting the gambling industry including a near-total ban on advertisements.
Drafts to Bulgaria’s Gambling Act are being prepared with the goal of limiting the wide presence of betting and gambling adverts across the country – often endorsed by Bulgarian celebrities and entertainers – as well as curbing addiction issues.
Billboards and posters promoting such activities will now be prohibited. Bright, flashing, illuminated signs and promotional window displays on casinos and gaming halls will also be banned, as Radev complained that “our towns and villages have come to look like Las Vegas”.
“We don’t want gambling to have this everyday presence in the eyes of Bulgarian citizens. We don’t want this aggressive way of advertising, which corrupts young people and children,” Radev told the Ministerial Council.
The law amendments will require foreign operators licensed in Bulgaria to register their financial activities locally, ensuring they pay taxes and remain subject to state control.
Radev has also talked about a new taxation model for casinos and gaming to reflect real financial outcomes, accompanied by stricter anti-money laundering and tax evasion measures. Taxes on online gambling will increase, with a portion of the revenues directed to sports and education.
“Whoever operates on the Bulgarian market, and profits from it, will pay taxes here and be subject to full oversight by the Bulgarian state,” Radev added.
Logos and gambling adverts will now be only allowed on official club jerseys and sports halls.
The law change is expected to be widely supported in parliament, where Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria has a majority of seats, following a landslide election win in April.
Opposition parties have also called for law changes. The opposition Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change parties earlier this month called for law amendments and criticised governments for not acting on accepted regulations from 2024, when the Gambling Act was created.
In 2024, advertising was prohibited online, on radio and on TV – but this only prompted saw an increase in the visual presence of gambling on billboards, street posters and banners on buildings.
“Gambling has turned into an epidemic. We accepted amendments in 2024 that also introduced serious limitations but these regulations are not being followed, nor is the state implementing sanctions,” MP Bozhidar Bozhanov of Democratic Bulgaria, which has promoted such bans for years, said on September 9.

items.title: Andrija Mandic: Montenegrin Speaker’s Journey from Serb Firebrand to EU Advocate
items.summary: The fallout from the condolences Andrija Mandic sent to deceased Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic’s family poses the latest threat to the career of this canny and chameleon-like political operator.
items.body_text:
If Montenegro’s parliament votes on Thursday on whether to keep Andrija Mandic as its speaker, the man at the centre of the dispute will be defending a political career that has taken him from the forefront of the country’s Serb nationalist camp to one of Montenegro’s highest constitutional offices.
The immediate trigger for the vote is the message of condolence he sent to the son of former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted by the United Nations tribunal in The Hague of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, and who died recently aged 84.
Mandic has acknowledged sending the condolences. Opposition parties have used the gesture to demand his removal as speaker, with the vote scheduled for September 24.
The episode has renewed attention to a question about how much Mandic has changed in his politics and the language with which he presents himself.

items.title: Netanyahu Lawyer Part of Operation to Build Israeli Drones in Serbia
items.summary: Israeli lawyer Zion Amir, currently representing PM Benjamin Netanyahu, is one of three directors of a company now producing Israeli drones in Serbia, BIRN/Haaretz can reveal.
items.body_text:
Unveiling Serbia’s first factory producing Israeli drones, President Aleksandar Vucic took to Instagram on September 17 to tout the 100 jobs it had created and the “most modern equipment” it would supply to the Serbian army and “the armies of some other countries”.
The press wasn’t invited, with Vucic citing the sensitivity of the project.
In its own Instagram post, the Israeli embassy said Ambassador Avivit Bar-Ilan had attended the event and hailed the “cooperation between Serbia’s local defense industry” and Israeli defence sector giant Elbit Systems.
What neither mentioned, however, was the involvement of Zion Amir, a prominent Israeli lawyer currently representing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu before the Israeli Supreme Court.
The lawyer’s role, revealed here for the first time, comes via the Serbian-based company SDS Technologies, of which he is a director.
The factory premises, in Belgrade’s Makis neighbourhood, is emblazoned with the SDS brand name, as were the clothes worn by employees demonstrating the drones to Vucic at the opening, in a video the president posted on Instagram (see stills from video below).
In Serbia’s business registry, the company name ‘SDS Technologies’ appeared within hours of the factory’s opening, not as a new firm, however, but as the new name of a company previously called CUPA Enterprises. The very same day, September 17, Amir was formally appointed as a director of SDS.
Vucic said previously that ownership of the drone venture would be shared equally by Serbia and Israel.
The ownership structure of SDS Technologies, however, does not reflect this.
SDS is in fact owned by London-registered CUPA Limited, itself majority-owned by Greek national Athanasios Ramos. On September 21, four days after the factory opened, CUPA Limited changed its name to Blue Liberty International Ltd.
Elbit System, the designer of the drones, told BIRN it “collaborates with local companies in several European countries as part of localisation processes and efforts to tailor its offerings to customer needs”. It denied any link to SDS, however, or to Amir. It stressed it does not own, nor is a partner in, any drone facility in Serbia.
Lawyer representing Netanyahu before Supreme Court
BIRN reporters first visited the Makis factory site several months ago, for an exclusive story about Serbia’s plan to open a drone factory with Elbit.
Situated alongside several other businesses and warehouses, the factory gates were branded with the name SDS Technologies. At the time, there was no such company in Serbia’s business registry.
Today, SDS Technologies has three directors: Greek national Maria Kardamaki, Lebanese-born US citizen George Antoine Elghossain, and Amir.
Since last year, Amir has been representing Netanyahu and his government before the Supreme Court in five petitions against the government’s decision to dismiss Ronen Bar as head of Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security service.
According to Haaretz’s reporting, Bar had warned Netanyahu of a potential attack on Israel in a phone call before the Palestinian militant group Hamas struck on October 7, 2023, triggering Israel’s devastating war in Gaza.

items.title: Three Nobel Laureates Join Initiative for Laser-Based Early Disease Detection
items.summary: The Center for Molecular Fingerprinting (CMF) is strengthening its scientific leadership with three new Nobel laureates joining its advisory board. Simultaneously, the institute is expanding its pioneering laser-based early diagnosis project into Asia. Budapest-based CMF, led by Nobel laureate Ferenc Krausz, has expanded its scientific advisory board with three new members: cell biologist Randy Schekman, […] The post Three Nobel Laureates Join Initiative for Laser-Based Early Disease Detection a
items.body_text:
The aim is to develop a cost-effective testing method that will enable the early detection of diseases.Continue reading
The Center for Molecular Fingerprinting (CMF) is strengthening its scientific leadership with three new Nobel laureates joining its advisory board. Simultaneously, the institute is expanding its pioneering laser-based early diagnosis project into Asia.
Budapest-based CMF, led by Nobel laureate Ferenc Krausz, has expanded its scientific advisory board with three new members: cell biologist Randy Schekman, pharmacologist Louis J. Ignarro, and laser physicist Donna Strickland. Alongside earlier appointee Steven Chu, these five Nobel laureates will now shape the institute’s strategic direction.
CMF’s goal is to establish preventive, personalized medicine capable of detecting serious diseases such as cancer or type 2 diabetes even before the first clinical symptoms appear.
Conventional medical diagnostics often only come into play when symptoms are present or laboratory values deviate from broad population averages. The Center for Molecular Fingerprinting takes a different approach. Instead of a rigid average, the individual’s unique molecular baseline serves as the reference value.
Even minimal, patient-specific deviations in the blood can indicate early-stage pathological processes. To make these minute nuances visible, the institute uses a highly complex laser-optical method:
- Sample collection: Plasma is separated from the blood of study participants.
- Laser excitation: Ultrashort laser pulses excite the molecules contained in the plasma, causing them to vibrate. The process can be compared to striking a tuning fork and analyzing its decaying tone—with the difference that, instead of sound waves, molecular vibrations are detected using specialized optics.
- Molecular fingerprint: The overall pattern of these vibrations yields an individual molecular profile that documents even the slightest biochemical shifts.
Currently, 13,000 volunteers are contributing to the research through regular blood donations as part of the H4H program.
Marking the announcement, Sun Dong, Minister of Innovation, Technology and Industry for the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, and Péter Horváth, Hungarian State Secretary for Science and Innovation, toured CMF’s laboratory facilities in Szeged. During the visit, Ferenc Krausz showcased newly commissioned cryogenic storage units designed to ensure the integrity of blood samples.
The institute is now scaling up its research internationally through a strategic partnership with the University of Hong Kong.
Participant recruitment and the establishment of an Asian biobank are now underway in Hong Kong, running parallel to the Hungarian study cohorts.
Péter Horváth emphasized on site that the years of preparatory work are now nearing the stage of evaluating concrete data sets. If the hypotheses are confirmed, the government intends to continue supporting the project consistently and roll it out more broadly.
Behind the initiative lies a structural transformation—both economic and societal. Modern healthcare systems are largely designed to provide curative care for existing conditions—often through lengthy, invasive, and costly therapies.
Effective early detection, on the other hand, enables timely interventions, lifestyle adjustments, and targeted therapies in the early stages.
For Nobel laureate Louis Ignarro, the project marks the logical next step in modern medicine. Identifying early biomolecular abnormalities requires a shift in thinking to fully decipher the biological relevance of the subtlest signaling patterns. Steven Chu also sees the potential for a paradigm shift in this approach. “Today, it is no longer necessary to wait until an abnormality falls outside the normal range of the population average. This is precisely what can revolutionize diagnostics,” he explained.
Featured image: CMF

items.body_text:
The Hajdú-Bihar County Government launched proceedings against the Chinese battery manufacturer CATL on Friday.Continue reading
News has emerged of another industrial shutdown in Hungary. Japan’s Nippon Paper will suspend operations at its Hungarian subsidiary, Nippon Paper Chemicals Europe Zrt., effective December 31, Magyar Nemzet reported. The Vácrátót plant (located about 35 km northeast of Budapest) was established in 2022 to manufacture and sell carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), which is used in the production of lithium-ion batteries, and local operations began in 2025.
The Japanese company attributed the decision to a slowdown in the growth of the electric vehicle market, changes in the regulatory and subsidy environment in Europe and North America, and intensifying competition. According to the company,
it had attempted to attract new customers and improve the cost competitiveness of the Vácrátót operation,
but concluded that, under current conditions, the Hungarian business unit is unable to generate a stable return commensurate with the investment.
CMC production will therefore be relocated back to Japan.
Nippon Paper is recording an extraordinary loss of approximately 5 billion yen (approximately 10.1 billion forints) in connection with the suspension of operations. The Vácrátót company had 24 employees at the end of August.
The recent developments are also noteworthy because the investment was specifically based on the boom in the electric vehicle and battery industries. Based on previous information from Nippon Paper’s Hungarian division, the Vácrátót plant aimed to create approximately 60 new jobs and officially opened in May 2025.
Via Magyar Nemzet; Featured photo: Pexels
