The new organization is already working to build its own funding base and network of partners, and is preparing a large-scale initiative in response to the EU’s attempts to monitor and influence the upcoming elections in France, Germany, Poland, Spain, and other countries.

to oppose the centralization of political power in Europe, to defend the sovereignty of nations and democratic accountability, and to provide a platform for the arguments and perspectives that are all too often excluded from mainstream European debates.
To this end, the European Freedom and Sovereignty Initiative publishes comprehensive research and launches campaigns on the most important issues facing the continent, including democracy, election interference and national sovereignty; freedom of speech and censorship; migration and social fragmentation; culture, gender and family; energy, agriculture and environmental protection; the economy, regulation and innovation; and defense, competitiveness and strategic autonomy.
In addition to its research activities, the organization has launched an ambitious digital media program:
through bold videos, investigative reports, podcasts, and social media campaigns, it aims to offer a strong, intellectually grounded alternative to the European public.

However, despite their significant successes, the political forces of change have so far failed to develop a comprehensive intellectual and political alternative. As patriotic forces gain increasing momentum, Europe’s traditional, establishment parties feel more threatened than ever before.
They will attempt to cling to power through ever-increasing control over democratic processes and political narratives. We will consistently expose these attempts, which aim to prevent political change brought about through democratic means.”

items.title: Tisza's support drops 3 points among total population, while Fidesz's support grows by same amount, survey finds
items.summary: This leaves the Tisza Party with 54 percent of the total population supporting it, while Fidesz stands at 22 percent.
items.body_text:
Tisza's support drops 3 points among total population, while Fidesz's support grows by same amount, survey finds
The Tisza Party stands at 54 percent among the entire Hungarian population, and at 64 percent both among those eligible to vote and certain voters, according to the latest Medián poll published by HVG. Fidesz’s support is at 22 percent among the entire population, at 26 percent among those eligible to vote, and at 27 percent among certain voters. Medián measured support for the far-right Mi Hazánk at 7 percent among the entire population and at 8 percent in each of the other two voter categories.
Compared to Medián’s July poll, support for the Tisza Party has fallen by 3 percentage points—within the margin of error—while Fidesz’s support has risen by the same amount among the total population. The Tisza Party’s voter base did not shift in favor of smaller parties, nor did the proportion of unaffiliated voters increase; instead, Fidesz was able to capitalize on the ruling party’s loss of a few percentage points.
Compared to the July survey, the public mood has slightly deteriorated, but 60 percent of the Hungarian population still said that things are heading in the right direction. In July, this figure was 63 percent. 32 percent of the population currently believes that things in Hungary are heading in the wrong direction, compared to 29 percent in July.
Methodology
The Medián Public Opinion and Market Research Institute conducted the survey between September 14 and 18, 2026 via telephone interviews with a nationally representative sample of 1,000 people. Minor distortions in the sample were corrected using a mathematical method—known as weighting—based on data from the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), ensuring that the sample accurately reflects the composition of the country’s voting-age population by settlement type, gender, age, and educational attainment. The margin of error for the reported data is at the most ±3.1 percent of the total sample, depending on the distribution of responses.

Egy hete jelentette be a Partizán, hogy szakmai vitanapot szerveznek, amire elhívják azokat a pályázókat, akik a Madách Színház, az Újszínház és a Trafó igazgatói székére beadtak pályázati anyagot. Az esemény előtt két nappal viszont a Partizán lemondta az eseményt, mivel azt írták: a kedd esti határidőig csak a pályázók töredéke jelezte, hogy elfogadja a meghívásukat, és többen érdektelenséggel reagáltak, vagy kifejezetten ellenséges gesztusként élték meg a meghívásukat. 
De mint kiderült, nemcsak a pályázók, a Fővárosi Önkormányzat sem szeretett volna senkit delegálni a rendezvényre, a kulturális minisztérium részéről pedig Nagy Ervin államtitkár és Sipos Imre helyettes államtitkár is azt jelezte, hogy nem vesznek részt a fórumon. 
És elzárkózott a színházi szakszervezet (SzíDoSz) is, valamint a két legfontosabb érdekvédelmi szervezet, a Magyar Színházi Társaság és a Független Előadó-művészeti Szövetség is, akiket a szervezők szerint éppen a szakma kihívásairól és a pályázati kiírások ellentmondásairól kérdeztek volna.
„Ha mindenki szembejön veled az autópályán, akkor te haladsz rossz irányba: ez akkor is igaz, ha meggyőződésünk, hogy a rendezvény a demokratikus szakmai nyilvánosságot, és ezzel a terület iránti közbizalmat erősítette volna” – olvasható a Partizán bejegyzésében, aminek a megtartását így indokolatlannak tartják.
Az eset viszonylag jól mutatja, milyen feszültségek uralkodnak jelenleg a színházi szcénában.
A pályázati határidő lejárta után három nappal a Társadalmi Kapcsolatokért és Kultúráért Felelős Minisztérium arról tájékoztatta a közvéleményt, hogy a Madách Színház igazgatói posztjára 7, az Újszínház igazgatói posztjára 16 pályázat érkezett, a pályázók nevét viszont a sajtó érdeklődésére sem hozták nyilvánosságra. A tárca annyit írt, hogy a kiválasztási folyamat a vonatkozó kormányrendeletben meghatározott keretek és határidők szerint zajlik. Néhány név azért már ekkorra tudható volt (róluk ebben a cikkünkben írtunk), és azóta további nevek lettek nyilvánosak. Egy korábbi posztban a Partizán is közzétette, addig kik jelezték a biztos részvételüket az (azóta tehát törölt) eseményen:
Újszínház:
- Berettyán Nándor
- Pozsgai Zsolt
- Schilling Árpád
Madách Színház:
- Lőrinczy György
- Gémes Antos
Trafó:
- Boronkay Soma
Nagy Ervin kultúráért felelős államtitkár később az elmaradt transzparenciát azzal magyarázta, hogy „a pályázat tisztaságának megőrzése érdekében és a befolyásolás lehetőségének kizárása miatt kiemelten fontos a pályázók személyes adatainak védelme”.
Közben a Trafó négy pályázója a Fővároshoz fordult a Partizán és az Örkény színházi fóruma miatt. Stern Lili, Gulyás Hermann Sándor, Gulyás Gábor és Bagossy László pályázók szerint a nyilvános jelölti szereplés „informális elvárássá válhat”, és hátrányba hozhatja azokat, akik nem vesznek részt benne.
A Partizán a szerdai posztjában azt írta, hogy a szakmai vitán nem a pályázatokról akarták volna dönteni, inkább a nyilvánosságot és a párbeszédet erősíteni, ehhez képest olyan ellenkezést tapasztaltak, amelyek „már-már paranoid feltételezéseken” alapultak. „Ami kirajzolódott ebből a folyamatból, az azt erősíti, hogy nemhogy rendszerváltás nem történt a szcénában, hanem az erre való igénye sincs meg a döntő többségnek: tulajdonos/fenntartónak, a pályázók túlnyomó részének és az érdekvédelmi szervezeteknek sem.”

items.body_text:
Czech Man Jailed 13 Days After Protest on Moscow's Red Square
Prague Morning
A judge at Moscow’s Tverskoy District Court sentenced a Czech man to 13 days in jail on Tuesday for staging a protest on Red Square.
Identified as Michal Plamenek, the man was arrested for holding up a sign in English next to Lenin’s Mausoleum on Sunday afternoon, the court’s press service said in a statement.
No details were provided as to what was written on Plamenek’s sign, but the court press service said a judge ruled that the inscription was “aimed at discrediting the Russian Armed Forces.”
Police officers arrested Plamenek because Red Square directly adjoins the Kremlin, where protests are banned. He allegedly refused to listen to a request by officers to accompany them to a police station and resisted arrest.
A judge found Plamenek guilty on three separate administrative counts of discrediting the Russian military, violating protest rules and disobeying a police officer.
He was also fined a total of 60,000 roubles, around CZK 15,000.
The Czech Foreign Ministry said its embassy in Moscow has been providing the detained man with consular assistance from the outset. It declined to comment further because of the sensitivity of the case.

items.body_text:
Heating Season Starts Across Czechia as Temperatures Fall
Prague Morning
District heating plants across the Czech Republic are beginning to supply heat as temperatures drop, with conditions for the start of the heating season now being met in much of the country.
Some plants have already begun providing additional heat during the colder morning and evening hours. The first systems to respond were mainly in mountainous parts of northern and western Czechia and in the Vysočina region.
Other heating plants are expected to gradually start operating in the coming days, depending on local temperatures and weather forecasts.
Since 2010, district heating systems have generally started supplying heat after September 20, although the exact timing varies considerably from year to year.
If temperatures rise again in late September or early October, heating can be suspended. Under the standard rules, heating is normally interrupted when the average outdoor temperature exceeds 13°C for two consecutive days and the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue to rise.
Last winter was colder than average
The previous heating season placed greater demands on heating systems than the years immediately before it.
According to figures from the Czech District Heating Association, the season was 4.9 percent colder than the previous year. It was also 3.2 percent colder than the average of the preceding 15 years.
The colder conditions translated into higher demand for heat, particularly during periods of sustained low temperatures.
Heating costs could increase next year
Households are not currently expected to face a direct increase resulting from a recent change in the interpretation of a fuel tax exemption, but some other users of district heating could see higher costs.
The issue concerns combined heat and power (CHP) generation. This year, the state changed how an existing fuel tax exemption is interpreted, limiting its application to the amount of heat supplied to households.
Heating companies say the change could increase annual heating bills for institutions such as hospitals and schools by tens or even hundreds of thousands of Czech crowns.

items.body_text:
Crowdfunding Campaign Launches for Book Tracing the History of Prague's Roxy Club
Prague Morning
A new book documenting the history of Prague’s Roxy club and the alternative cultural scene that grew around it is seeking public support ahead of its planned publication this autumn.
Titled Kopneš do plechovky a dva dny se tančí (“Kick a Can and Dance for Two Days”), the book looks at Roxy’s development from its beginnings in the early 1990s to its current role in Prague’s music scene.
A crowdfunding campaign to finance the publication has been launched on Donio.cz.
Rather than focusing solely on the history of one nightclub, the project examines the people, artists and cultural movements connected with the venue.
More than 40 musicians, promoters, artists and other figures associated with Roxy contribute their memories and perspectives.
Roxy opened in 1992 and quickly became an important venue for alternative music in Prague. Over the years, its programme has covered genres including hardcore, house, trip-hop, hip-hop and drum’n’bass.
The book is the result of almost five years of research by cultural journalist Ondřej Horák. He examined thousands of archival documents, located previously unpublished photographs and interviewed nearly 50 people connected with Roxy and its history.
The campaign will also feature newly created artwork. Graphic designer and typographer Jozef Ondrík has produced a series of three screen-printed posters based on visual elements from Roxy’s history.
The design draws on three pages from the original handover document for the non-residential premises at Dlouhá 33, which were transferred to the Linhart Foundation.
Large-format photographs and works by artists connected with Roxy and the NoD Gallery are also expected to be among the campaign rewards.

items.body_text:
Two New Constitutional Court Judges Appointed As Critics Fear ‘No More Dissenting Opinions’
Two new judges, Goga Kikilashvili and Sergo Metopishvili, were appointed to fill the two vacant seats at Georgia’s Constitutional Court, with the appointments feared to leave the key judicial body, long accused of pro-government leanings, now almost fully dominated by loyalists of the ruling Georgian Dream party.
Kikilashvili was appointed by Georgian Dream-elected President Mikheil Kavelashvili, while Metopishvili was selected by the Supreme Court’s Plenum. Three of the nine judges of the Georgian Constitutional Court are appointed by the President, three are elected by Parliament by a majority of at least three-fifths of its full membership, and the remaining three are appointed by the Supreme Court. Judges are appointed to serve 10-year terms.
The appointments come as the Constitutional Court is set to consider a Georgian Dream-filed constitutional lawsuit seeking to ban several key opposition parties, including the United National Movement, Ahali/Coalition for Change, Lelo/Strong Georgia, Federalists and, most recently, Gakharia For Georgia.
Kikilashvili, 37, will replace Constitutional Court Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze, whose 10-year term expires on October 2. Kverenchkhiladze was among the few judges known for issuing dissenting opinions in rulings perceived to favor the ruling party’s positions. The term of another judge known for similar dissenting opinions, Teimuraz Tughushi, is also set to expire in the coming months, while another, Irine Imerlishvili, prematurely quit the Court last year.
Recently appointed Kikilashvili is the son of former Constitutional Court Judge Khvicha Kikilashvili, who was appointed to the Court by the Supreme Court’s Plenum in April 2020 but resigned in 2025. Khvicha Kikilashvili was among the six judges who ruled in favor of finding that then-President Zurabishvili had violated the Constitution in the impeachment case.
Goga Kikilashvili has been an invited lecturer at several Georgian universities and, since October 2023, has served as a non-judge member of the High Council of Justice of Georgia, a supervisory body for the Georgian judiciary.
The second appointed judge is 65-year-old Sergo Metopishvili, who has served as a judge of Tbilisi City Court since 2016 and, since July 2025, as a judge of the Tbilisi Court of Appeals. He previously chaired Tbilisi City Court’s Civil Cases Panel and later headed its Investigation, Pre-Trial, and Substantive Hearing Panel.
Metopishvili has long been considered by critics to be part of Georgia’s “judicial clan” — a group of powerful judges accused of wielding significant influence over the country’s courts. He has been among judges who opposed the introduction of a judicial “vetting” mechanism, which envisaged external integrity checks of judges as part of Georgia’s judicial reform in 2024, arguing that it could potentially undermine judicial independence and Georgia’s sovereignty.
‘No More Dissenting Opinions’
The latest appointments have drawn criticism from opposition figures and civil society representatives.
Nika Gvaramia, leader of the opposition Ahali party, linked Kikilashvili’s appointment directly to the Constitutional Court case seeking to ban opposition parties.
“Soon he [Goga Kikilashvili] will be reviewing the case on the abolition of all of Georgia’s major opposition parties, and, of course, he won’t embarrass his father,” Gvaramia wrote on Facebook.
Gvaramia also sharply criticized Metopishvili’s appointment, writing that “the occupation of the Constitutional Court is complete: today the Supreme Court filled the last vacancy and appointed Sergo Metopishvili, one of the clan’s most odious sonder [referring to “sondercommando” Nazi SS death squads, used in Georgian as a denigrating term for militant partisan supporters], as judge.”
Gvaramia further linked the appointments to Georgian Dream’s repeated addition of parties to the opposition-ban laws

items.body_text:
Jailed UNM-Era Official Megis Kardava Gets Another Multi-Year Sentence in Embezzlement Case
Tbilisi City Court sentenced Megis Kardava, a jailed former senior Defense Ministry official and one of the most controversial figures under the United National Movement government already been convicted in several high-profile criminal cases, to 11 years in prison over alleged misappropriation and embezzlement of GEL 768,107 in state funds. The sentence was subsequently reduced to five years and six months under the 2012 Georgian Amnesty Law, the Prosecutor’s Office said on September 22.
Kardava had been wanted by the Georgian authorities since 2013 on multiple charges in eleven criminal cases. He was detained in Ukraine in 2017 and extradited from Kyiv in 2021. He has previously been found guilty in cases concerning the Navtlugi special operation, the 2006 prison riot, the torture and sexual abuse videos case, as well as organizing the torture and sexual abuse of retired colonel Sergo Tetradze, for which Kardava was sentenced to nine years in prison in absentia.
According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the latest case concerns the alleged misappropriation and embezzlement of GEL 768,107 between November 16, 2011, and August 2012, with the funds allegedly taken under the guise of operational expenses with the assistance of other senior Defense Ministry officials.
The agency said that on May 22, 2012, Kardava, then head of the Military Police Department, submitted a written request to then-Defense Minister Bacho Akhalaia “under the article on covert expenses,” requesting GEL 330,000 for the department.
“With the minister’s consent, the funds transferred to the Military Police Department’s account were withdrawn from one of the banks on Megis Kardava’s instructions and converted, after which Megis Kardava illegally appropriated 200,000 US dollars,” the prosecutor’s office said.
According to the agency, fictitious documents were subsequently prepared on Kardava’s orders to conceal the misappropriation and embezzlement, “purporting to show that funds had been spent by a unit of the Military Police Department deployed to the Republic of Afghanistan for operational-search activities.” This allowed the funds in question “to be written off and the accounting records to be reconciled accordingly.”
The latest case is not Kardava’s first conviction for embezzlement. In September 2023, he was found guilty of embezzling GEL 60,000 belonging to the Defense Ministry and sentenced to eight years in prison. The sentence was subsequently reduced to four years under the Georgian Amnesty Law, along with a six-month ban on holding public office or employment.

Grape Purchasing Prices Adjusted Amid Kakheti Protests As Officials Expect ‘Unprecedented Harvest’
Georgian authorities adjusted grape purchasing prices following two days of protests by grape growers in the country’s eastern wine-making region of Kakheti, where locals demanded higher prices for their harvest, including by blocking roads and paralyzing local traffic.
The protests, which ended following the government’s September 22 decision to revise the prices, come amid what officials have described as an “unprecedented” harvest in the history of the country’s independence, but also climate-related challenges reportedly affecting the sugar content of grapes.
The demonstrations began in Shilda, a village in Kvareli Municipality, before spreading to Akhalsopeli and Velistsikhe villages. Some growers refused to deliver their harvested grapes, with grape-laden vehicles remaining lined up near purchasing facilities, and resumed deliveries only after authorities adjusted the prices.
Much of the discontent focused on the more recent pricing scheme that differentiates between grapes by sugar content and grape condition.
Under the pricing scheme announced in August for this year’s harvest, in the event of a surplus harvest, the state-run Harvest Management Company would purchase grapes at a pre-defined differentiated scheme, first introduced during last year’s harvest and meant to promote the production of “competitive and high-value products.”
For most grape varieties, grapes with sugar content below 17% would be purchased by the state for GEL 0.3 (USD 0.12) per kilogram, while those with sugar content between 17% and 20% receive GEL 0.8 (USD 0.31). Undamaged grapes exceeding 20% sugar content were priced at GEL 1.3 (USD 0.5) per kilogram.
Different thresholds applied to Saperavi grapes, with the state paying GEL 1.5 (USD 0.58) per kilogram for undamaged grapes with a sugar content of at least 21%, GEL 0.9 (USD 0.35) for grapes with a sugar content of 17% to 21% and/or those that are partially damaged, and GEL 0.3 (USD 0.12) for grapes with a sugar content below 17% and/or those that are damaged.
The winegrowers said the prices offered for their harvest were insufficient to cover production expenses, including vineyard maintenance, agricultural chemicals, labor, and transportation.
“Kakheti needs attention. We are asking for an appropriate price,” one protester told the media.
‘Unprecedented Harvest’
The protests came amid what officials have described as an “unprecedented harvest” in Georgia but also challenges caused by “climate conditions” for grape sugar content.
“This year will be an unprecedented harvest in terms of quantity,” Davit Songhulashvili, Georgian Dream minister of agriculture, was quoted by the ministry on September 21. Songhulashvili predicted the harvest to exceed 320 tons, “which, perhaps, will be the first case of such a big harvest in the history of independent Georgia.”
The minister, however, warned that this year’s “climate conditions created certain challenges,” including some grapes struggling to develop proper sugar levels, which he said may delay the harvest.
The growers have also disputed measurements of the sugar content of their grapes at the purchasing facilities. Some protesters say measurements taken before delivery have differed from those recorded at the facilities, resulting in their grapes being downpriced. They have particularly objected to the GEL 0.3 state purchasing price applicable to the lowest category of grapes, saying they are unwilling to sell their harvest at that rate.
Protest Ends After Government Revises Prices
The growers ended their protest and resumed deliveries after Levan Mekhuzla, chair of the National Wine Agency, announced the changes on September 22, saying the decision was made following consultations with the government and the Minister of Environmental Protection and Agriculture.

Georgian authorities target Council of Europe and Tbilisi school over ‘unauthorised grant funding’
Georgia’s pro-government media and ruling party have targeted a Council of Europe-backed seminar held in the western Georgian resort of Bakhmaro, raising questions whether the Council issued an unauthorised grant for the event. The State Audit Office said it had begun ‘monitoring’ the matter.
The seminar, titled ‘Choosing Democratic Culture’, was held on 18-19 September. According to the Council of Europe, it was a joint initiative of its ‘Supporting Civil Dialogue in Georgia’ project and the Tbilisi School of Political Studies (TSPS).
The TSPS was founded in 1999 by Georgian academic and politician Armaz Akhvlediani, a prominent critic of the ruling Georgian Dream party. Throughout the years, it was supported by a number of Western institutions and international organisations.
Pro-government media focused on the event from its first day, with a journalist from state-affiliated TV Imedi approaching participants, including members of the diplomatic corps, to ask who was funding the project.
In its coverage, Imedi referred to restrictive amendments to Georgia’s grant legislation adopted by Georgian Dream and its parliamentary allies, and questioned whether the event had violated regulations, which make issuing foreign grants — with few exceptions — subject to government approval.
The TV channel contacted the Government Administration about the matter, which responded by saying that the council had not applied to it for permission to issue the grant to the TSPS.
The council answered Imedi’s questions on the first day of the seminar, stating that it was directly implementing and supporting the event, while the school was its partner and host, and that the event did not involve providing a grant to any recipient Georgian actor.
Meanwhile, high-ranking representatives of the ruling party began commenting on the issue one after another. On 18 September, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said that ‘if it is established that the transparency legislation has been violated, there will, of course, be an appropriate legal response’. He added that ‘it is clearly apparent that this is what we are dealing with’.
On Monday, Parliamentary Speaker Shalva Papuashvili further expressed suspicion that ‘this may be a case of circumventing Georgian legislation’.
Responding to the council’s explanation, Papuashvili noted that it might indeed not have been a grant, but rather expenses directly incurred by the organisation to hold the event, including for the hotel, transport, food, and speakers.
‘If that is the case, then it is clear that we are dealing with an attempt to circumvent the law’, he added.
The verbal comments were soon followed by legal proceedings, with the State Audit Office saying on Monday that its Department for Financial Transparency had launched ‘monitoring’ into the TSPS’s ‘alleged receipt of a grant without the consent of the Georgian government’.
‘The State Audit Office, as part of the monitoring, will systematically and progressively carry out all necessary actions. This will include interviewing all persons who may have information relevant to the matter and examining all relevant documentation’, the agency told OC Media in a written comment.
The following day, Tuesday, the council provided a more detailed explanation, saying in a comment sent to the local press that the project was implemented within the framework of its 2024–2027 Action Plan for Georgia, which was prepared in close consultation with the Georgian authorities.
The council reiterated that it directly implemented and supported the seminar and had paid no fee to Akhvlediani or any other representative of the TSPS, which was a partner.
The ruling party and its allies began actively introducing laws restricting international funding in spring 2024.

items.title: Abkhazia says Education Department violations cost $180,000 from budget
items.summary: An investigation found multiple violations within the government department.
items.body_text:
Abkhazia says Education Department violations cost $180,000 from budget
An investigation found multiple violations within the government department.
The Prosecutor General’s Office of Abkhazia announced on 16 September that over ₽15 million ($180,000) in funds were misused by the Education Department from 2022 to the middle of 2026.
An audit also found the department regularly signed contracts with people who worked at branches of the Education Department, entailing a conflict of interest under Abkhaz law. The investigation also noted that the department did not form a commission for the receipt and disposal of assets, as well as reporting ‘financial violations in the area of tax and budget legislation’, amounting to more than $180,000. While the Prosecutor General’s Office said that most of the money has already been repaid, the sum has caused upset on Abkhaz social media.
Following an audit, a proposal to rectify the violations was submitted to the administration of Sukhumi (Sukhum). Out of this, ₽12 million ($150,000) has already been reimbursed by the department. The process of recovering the remaining amount is ongoing. The Education Department is creating a phased repayment plan, according to the Telegram channel Apsny Iakha’.
Corruption offences have historically been treated leniently in Abkhazia. From 2020–2024, no violations led to a criminal case. Accordingly, Abkhazian social media users have been pessimistic about the chances of the money being returned and have expressed anger over the perceived leniency of the punishments given, with one user asking, ‘Why fire them?’ They should be jailed for this!’
One Facebook user asked: ‘And is it too much to ask the General Prosecutor's Office to fire the corrupt official?’
Another claimed, ‘Everyone should be prosecuted according to the law, but unfortunately, the law doesn’t work for everyone here, only for ordinary people. Has anyone held officials accountable? No! “Everything will be decided, everyone will be able to drive in but not out”’.
Another decried what they perceived as lack of transparency in the case. ‘They stole 15 million, and they don’t even want to show these “heroes’” faces? Why should we believe this information? Maybe it’s not true at all? Who are these people, and where do they work?’
The issue of corruption has historically been highly contentious — in 2020, legislation requiring civil servants to declare their interests as well as that of their relatives was finally passed following 10 days of hunger strikes.
The amended law meant civil servants would lose their jobs and be banned from employment in the public sector if they fail to declare all the required information or provide false information.
Before the vote, several MPs, criticised the proposed draft. MP Givi Kvarchiya went as far to call the protests an ‘application of Orange [Revolution] methods of pressuring the power’. Ukraine’s 2004 Orange Revolution has been widely portrayed in Russia being sponsored by Western intelligence agencies.
For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

items.title: Kela researcher on mental health gender gap: "the system reaches young women better"
items.summary: Nearly 16 percent of women born in 1997 have received rehabilitative psychotherapy in their lives, compared to just 3.6 percent of men.
items.body_text:
On Tuesday Yle News reported that women born in 1997 have received significantly more rehabilitative psychotherapy and sickness allowance than their male counterparts.
By their 28th birthday, 33.9 percent of women and 15.3 percent of men had received at least one of these benefits or rehabilitative psychotherapy, according to data compiled by Kela, the country's social insurance agency.
The gender gap was particularly striking in terms of rehabilitation psychotherapy: 15.9 percent of women had received it, compared to only 3.6 percent of men.
The country's mental health services system may not be adequately reaching young men, according to Kela's research chief Miika Vuori.
Vuori said the data shows that boys are referred to rehabilitation services earlier in life — in particular between ages 6-10. According to Kela's data, primary school-age boys are prescribed ADHD medication considerably more than girls.
"Research shows that psychological symptoms in girls and young women become more common during adolescence. Rehabilitation psychotherapy is only available from age 16, so the system reaches young women better," Vuori said.
He further noted that health service use is also linked to people's socioeconomic status — those in more difficult financial situations may have fewer opportunities to access rehabilitation psychotherapy.
Unknown factors
Diagnoses and treatment for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) have also increased among young girls over the past five years.
Earlier this year, it was reported that the number of children and young people in Finland being diagnosed with ADHD has continued to increase. Young boys tend to be more likely to receive an ADHD diagnosis, but the rate among girls aged 13-17 years old has also risen significantly in recent years.
"If we go back ten years, ADHD was hardly recognised in girls born in 1997. This shows that practices for seeking treatment and identifying service needs are changing," Vuori said.
Public health care has seen a significant increase in young people seeking mental health care. Vuori confirmed that mental health problems and neurodevelopmental syndromes are especially common in childhood and adolescence, and that the conditions affect their studying and work ability.
Kela's revelation about the data showed for the first time what percentage of an age group born in Finland accessed mental health benefits or rehabilitation psychotherapy between adolescence and early adulthood.
However, precise information about factors causing gender differences is not yet available.
"Such large differences between genders undeniably raise the question of whether something in our system or healthcare is partly producing these differences. This will be investigated in Kela's future research," Vuori said.

items.title: Supreme Court: Finnish police's forcible removals of hijabs from women was lawful
items.summary: The long-running legal case dates back to an incident at a police station in Hämeenlinna in May 2017, and the verdict has been seen as potentially setting a precedent for future cases.
items.body_text:
Finland's Supreme Court has upheld a ruling by the Court of Appeal, which found that police officers were justified in their actions when they forcibly removed hijab headscarves from two female asylum seekers.
The Supreme Court's ruling is especially relevant because it has been viewed as potentially setting a precedent for any similar cases in the future.
The long-running case relates to an incident at a police station in Hämeenlinna in May 2017.
Police officers were required to take registration photos of the two women in order to process their asylum applications, and instructed them to remove their head coverings. Both women however refused, citing their religious beliefs.
According to the Finnish Police Board's guidelines for the taking of such photos, if a person is wearing a "headscarf or veil" which is related to their religious beliefs, the photos must be taken both with and without the covering.
Because of this guideline, an inspector at the station ordered his officers to remove the women's scarves, by force if necessary.
As a result of the incident, the police officers and security guards — comprising seven defendants in total — were later charged with assault, incitement to assault and breach of duty.
Kanta-Häme District Court dismissed the charges in September 2022, and that verdict was upheld by the court of appeal in 2024.
In its decision, the appeals court ruled that the officers had no reason not to comply with the Finnish Police Board's policy that existed at the time, and they therefore were ruled to have not committed any offence.
The Supreme Court's latest ruling confirms this interpretation of the law.
The court noted that the police's necessity to photograph the women without headscarves was based on an acceptable societal objective — the proper processing of an asylum application and verification of an applicant's identity.
The court however also emphasised that force should only be used as a "last resort measure" in such situations and only if "advice, requests, and orders" have not been sufficient.

items.title: Government promised 500 positions for young people in public sector, only 29 filled so far
items.summary: Despite the slow progress, there is confidence that the quota will be filled by the end of this year, a finance ministry spokesperson told Yle.
items.body_text:
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's (NCP) government revealed in April how it plans to tackle the problem of youth unemployment — with one method being the recruitment of young people for fixed-term positions in government agencies.
The initiative aimed to recruit a total of 500 young people aged 18–25 who were applying for their first job or traineeship. The positions would be for a maximum of three months, and the government earmarked four million euros in its supplementary budget to fund the programme.
Its purpose is to offer young people their first steps into working life at a time when the employment situation for young people has been especially challenging.
However, despite the ambitious projections, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Finance told Yle that by the end of August, only 29 young people had been recruited by 16 government agencies as part of the scheme.
"During September, the number will increase considerably, so you can't draw any conclusions from these figures yet. We believe that most of these internship positions will be filled during early autumn," Janne Öberg, a Senior Financial Officer at the ministry, told Yle.
He added that the ministry is confident the quota of 500 positions will be filled by the end of the year.
Interest among agencies
Although progress has been slow, Öberg noted that government agencies are keen to take in new recruits under the programme.
"We received over 700 positions from agencies which wanted new young workers within the framework of this initiative. We limited the positions by agency so that the total number came to 500," Öberg said, adding that summer is "not the best time for internships".
"We believe that many prefer to take interns for the autumn season," he said.
Government agencies contacted by Yle noted that the additional funding came too late to have an impact on the summer season, as recruitment processes take time and some positions require security clearances.
For example, the Finnish Tax Administration said it could not take in new recruits under the scheme until senior staff had returned from summer holidays, while public health authority THL wanted to open applications in August.
Under the terms of the initiative, agencies can continue to recruit and hire young people into the first six months of next year. If agencies fail to meet their assigned quota, Öberg noted, the positions will be reallocated.

items.title: INTERVIEW: 'The last word has not yet been said on Swedish citizenship'
items.summary: In an interview with The Local, Fredrik Löndahl, chief judge at the Malmö migration court, explains why his court gave special attention to a single citizenship rejection appeal, and why he believes the ruling will be tested again at the highest court.
items.body_text:
When Sweden's new citizenship law came into force on June 6th, appeals against rejected applications soon began piling up in the post box at the Migration Court in Malmö.
Rather than process them individually, however, the court chose one as a test case, with its chief judge Fredrik Löndahl sitting on the panel alongside a senior judge and three lay judges.
In an interview with The Local, Löndahl explained why the court gave this case unusual attention – and why he believes its ruling could ultimately be tested by Sweden's highest migration court.
"This is something we can do in the Swedish legal system, when, for example, there are issues involving new legislation," Löndahl told The Local in an interview. "This case raised issues related to the EU law, and also, of course, the big issue of whether the now available law or the old law should be applied. So there were some big issues that needed great attention."
READ ALSO: Chief judge expects Swedish citizenship case to head to highest migration court
On September 10th, three months after the appeal had been lodged with the support of Fair Transition, a citizenship campaign group, the court ruled that the appeal should be rejected, taking the unusual decision of publishing the ruling in a press release along with a redacted copy of the decision.
"The administrative court does not issue press releases very often, but it occasionally happens, and the reason why we did it in this case was because we were aware of the big general interest. Many people are affected by this, there are many appeals regarding this issue, and it has also been discussed a lot within the court."
The Fair Transition legal team based its appeal on three arguments, one based on national law, one on EU law, and another arguing that there were shortcomings in the way the Migration Agency handled the case.
READ ALSO: How to appeal if your application for Swedish citizenship is rejected
Could the new law apply to old applications?
The first and most important question under Swedish law was whether the stricter citizenship requirements could be applied to applications submitted before the law changed.
The lawyers supporting the appeal argued that doing so breached the principles of "legitimate expectations" and "equality before the law".
This argument was partly based on previous Swedish cases in which courts had overruled legislation where the parliament had failed to introduce adequate transitional arrangements. In this case, they argued, long waiting times at the Migration Agency meant many applicants could have had no way of knowing when they applied that their application might end up being judged according to different rules.
This, they argued, was "contrary to the principles of legitimate expectations", and also contrary to "equality before the law", because another person with identical circumstances to the applicant could have applied at exactly the same time and been accepted simply because they had an efficient case officer.
Löndahl, however, said the cases cited as precedents were different because in each of them the courts had concluded that parliament had not intended the unfair consequences.
In this case, parliament had deliberately decided not to introduce transitional rules, despite being aware of the likely consequences.
"For us as a court to not apply the Swedish law, there have to be very big errors," he said. "Could the parliament have made a mistake by not including transitional rules? Obviously, in this case it could not have done so because this question was very much debated. So it was the intention of the majority not to have such rules."
"In the other cases, they have always looked for the intention of the lawmaking body, which sometimes is not very clear. However, in this case there was a very clear intention."

items.title: Swedish Migration Agency rejects police request to deport EU researcher
items.summary: The Migration Agency has rejected a police request to deport a researcher and climate activist over civil disobedience
items.body_text:
David Alcer, a German-Hungarian citizen who works at Lund University, has taken part in a series of climate protests in Sweden since moving here in 2019, including storming the Melodifestivalen stage with a poster reading "restore the wetlands", demonstrating at parliament, blocked an obstacle course race and tried to stop peat extraction, reports Aftonbladet.
Swedish border police have twice stopped him – once on his way to work and once on his way home after a visit to the doctor – and taken to a police station to discuss his right to be in Sweden, despite not being suspected of a crime.
Last year the Police Authority wrote to the Migration Agency and argued that he constituted a threat to the democratic order in Sweden and requested that he be deported, despite being an EU citizen.
But in its decision the Migration Agency writes that there is nothing to suggest that Alcer has caused damage to people or property, or exposed the general public to serious danger, reports Aftonbladet.
"Against this background, the Migration Agency considers that it is not currently shown that your deportation is particularly warranted on grounds of public policy and public security," the decision states.

items.title: Newly elected MP steps aside amid Swedish electoral fraud probe
items.summary: Newly elected Left Party MP Mohamed Abdukardir Ali is taking a leave of absence, following allegations of election fraud.
items.body_text:
"We have agreed that Mohamed Abdukardir Ali will take a timeout and will not serve as an MP from the start of the parliamentary term due to the ongoing investigation into voter fraud," wrote the Left Party's party secretary, Maria Forsberg, in a statement to news agency TT.
"These are exceptionally serious allegations against everyone involved. If we can assist the investigation in any way, we will do so. I cannot stress enough that we take this with the utmost seriousness, and we welcome the fact that this is now being investigated."
Abdukardir Ali denies any involvement and it has not been confirmed whether he actually appears in the investigation. No one has been formally notified of criminal suspicion.
According to reports in several media outlets, the investigation concerns pre-marked ballot papers in the general election. An anonymous police report claims that individuals drove voters to polling stations and supplied them with pre-marked ballots. A person was also allegedly seen handing out ballots and money to people.
Abdukardir Ali received 648 personal preference votes, securing Dalarna's single parliamentary seat for the party. Speaking to public broadcaster SVT, he expressed shock over the allegations of electoral misconduct.
"It's completely, completely wrong. I haven't done this," he said. "I know the law. I received support across every district in Dalarna."
The Left Party's press office declined to answer questions regarding Mohamed Abdukardir Ali's timeout, referring instead to the party secretary's official statement.
It remains unclear whether he intends to attend when the new parliament convenes for roll call on Monday. As of Tuesday afternoon, the Riksdag Administration had received no notification of absence, nor any application for leave or sick leave.
Another Left Party member who appears poised to take a seat on the municipal council in Borlänge via personal preference votes is also taking a pause from politics until everything is cleared up, local newspaper Borlänge Tidning reports.

items.title: What Germany's rising mortgage rates mean for home owners and buyers
items.summary: Mortgage rates on 10-year fixed-rate loans are now above four percent in Germany. What does this mean for homeowners and buyers?
items.body_text:
Many people in Germany dream of owning their own home, whether it's an apartment in the city or a cottage in the suburbs.
But there is not so great news: purchasing property is becoming more expensive.
According to the financial services provider Interhyp, mortgage interest rates for 10-year fixed-rate loans currently stand at just under 4.2 percent.
Another German mortgage provider, Dr Klein, estimates average annual interest rates at 4.1 percent. By way of comparison: a year ago, the corresponding rate at Dr Klein stood at 3.4 percent. That means within 12 months, mortgage rates have risen by around 0.7 percentage points.
What higher mortgage rates mean for buyers
Anyone thinking of buying a home has to factor in the latest numbers into their calculations.
"People are doing their sums very carefully," Thomas Kreil of Interhyp told German broadcaster ARD.
"Prospective buyers are scrutinising things more closely: Which property should they go for? What monthly repayment makes financial sense in the long term?"
The financial advice service Finanztip illustrates just how significant the recent rise in interest rates is. Property expert Dirk Eilinghoff said that for a loan of €300,000, the new rates could see customers paying an extra €250 a month.
READ ALSO: Will baby boomer homes soon flood the German property market?
Why mortgage rates are rising now
The long-term interest rate level on the capital market is the key factor determining mortgage rates.
Yields there have recently risen sharply. In mid-September, 10-year German government bonds temporarily yielded more than they had for over 17 years.
Rising long-term yields make it more expensive for banks to refinance – and this in turn feeds through to higher mortgage rates.
High energy prices resulting from the war in Iran recently heightened concerns on the financial markets about prolonged inflation.
Interhyp CEO Jörg Utecht therefore does not expect the situation to ease any time soon. "Buyers should prepare themselves for rates to remain above the four percent mark for the time being," he said.
Demand for mortgage loans falls
Figures from the German central bank, the Bundesbank, show that many potential buyers have already become more cautious.
In the second quarter of this year, demand for housing loans fell by the largest amount in three years.
At the same time, banks tightened their lending criteria. The net share of banks imposing stricter requirements rose to seven percent, up from four percent in the previous quarter.
Banks cited higher credit risks, increased refinancing costs and lower risk tolerance as reasons for toughening their lending rules.
This means that it's not only the cost of a mortgage that is increasing – in some cases, it's also becoming harder for potential house buyers to access the financing they want.
READ ALSO: The German words you need to know when buying property
The energy efficiency of a property is also playing a more important role than ever. Banks are generally providing less financing for properties with poor energy efficiency than for well-renovated ones.
Finanztip expert Eilinghoff said: "The worse the energy efficiency, the lower the value of the property tends to be."
Refinancing getting more expensive
The rise in interest rates is not only affecting people buying property. Homeowners with a fixed-rate period that's coming to an end are also facing more expensive refinancing.
However, after years of mortgage repayments, their remaining debt is often significantly lower than it was at the start.
As a result, Interhyp's Kreil says the actual increase in monthly payments will in many cases be considerably smaller than a simple comparison of interest rates might suggest.
One option available to homeowners is a forward mortgage (Forward-Darlehen). This allows borrowers to lock in current interest rates for a future refinancing deal. Banks charge an additional premium for this.

items.title: How EasyJet passengers travelling from Germany could be affected by strikes this autumn
items.summary: EasyJet passengers travelling between Germany, Portugal and France could face disruption during the autumn holidays and Christmas period as cabin crew and pilots threaten strike action.
items.body_text:
Travellers flying with EasyJet from Germany in the coming weeks may want to keep a close eye on their bookings, as separate labour disputes in Portugal and France threaten to disrupt flights during some of the busiest travel periods of the year.
It remains unclear exactly how many flights will be affected, but strike notices announced by Portuguese cabin crew and French pilots have raised the prospect of cancellations, delays and rebookings for passengers heading abroad during the autumn school holidays and the Christmas travel season.
Portugal strikes could hit holiday travel
The biggest immediate disruption could come from Portugal, where EasyJet cabin crew have announced two strike periods: October 2nd-6th and December 19th-23rd.
The first strike coincides with the start of the autumn school holidays in the German states of Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland, while the second falls just days before Christmas.
According to Portuguese union SNPVAC, around 500 EasyJet flights could be affected during the October walkout alone. The exact number of cancellations remains unclear because Portuguese law requires a minimum level of service during strikes.
READ ALSO: LISTED - The new direct flights from Germany in Autumn 2026
For travellers departing from Germany, the impact is likely to be most noticeable on routes linking Berlin Brandenburg Airport with Porto and Funchal on the Portuguese island of Madeira.
An EasyJet spokesperson told BILD newspaper that the airline could not yet provide reliable information on the impact on individual flights but said affected passengers would be contacted directly if their travel plans changed.
French pilot strike postponed twice
A separate dispute involving EasyJet pilots in France has created additional uncertainty for travellers.
Pilots represented by the SNPL union are currently scheduled to strike on October 1st and 2nd. But these dates have already been postponed twice as negotiations continue between the union and airline management.
The action was initially planned for September 13th and 14th before being pushed back to September 24th and 25th. The union later postponed the walkout again to give talks more time to succeed.
If the strike goes ahead, flights to and from EasyJet's French bases, including Paris Charles de Gaulle, Paris Orly, Lyon, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux and Toulouse, could face disruption.
Several of those airports have direct EasyJet connections with Berlin, meaning passengers travelling between Germany and France could be affected if services are cancelled or crews withdraw their labour.
READ ALSO: What are your rights in Germany if your flight is delayed or cancelled?
What should passengers do?
For now, passengers do not need to take any action unless they are contacted by the airline.
EasyJet generally informs affected customers directly by email, text message or through its mobile app, often a few days before departure once flight schedules have been finalised.
Travellers flying during the affected periods should regularly check their booking status and monitor any messages from the airline.
Why are workers striking?
In Portugal, cabin crew representatives have accused EasyJet of failing to honour collective agreements, making frequent schedule changes and relying too heavily on overtime due to staffing shortages.
The airline disputes some of those claims and says talks are continuing through Portugal's labour mediation process.
In France, pilots say flight rosters are changed too often and with too little notice. The union argues that pilots should receive the same scheduling protections recently secured by French-based cabin crew after a separate strike earlier this year.
READ ALSO: Ryanair to cut winter flights in Europe to save on fuel costs

items.title: Can Germany save its car industry as job cuts intensify?
items.summary: The move to electric vehicles is accelerating, yet Germany's biggest manufacturers are cutting jobs and losing ground to competitors. Here's why workers are worried and where new opportunities may emerge.
items.body_text:
Tens of thousands of automotive workers across Germany demonstrated on Monday in one of the largest nationwide labour mobilisations the industry has seen in years.
According to the union IG Metall, around 175,000 workers took part in roughly 280 events under the slogan "A Future Instead of Mass Layoffs".
Employees from Volkswagen, Audi, BMW, Mercedes, Bosch and dozens of suppliers joined rallies, workplace meetings and demonstrations.
The protests may look like a familiar conflict between unions and company management, but the dispute also provides an insight into an industry battling to reinvent itself at the same time as profits are falling, factories are under pressure and global competition is intensifying.
The key question is not whether the industry is in trouble – it clearly is – but whether it can successfully turn the shift to electric vehicles (EVs) into a new source of growth and jobs.
Why workers are worried
The immediate backdrop to Monday's day of action is a growing list of job cuts and restructuring plans.
Earlier this month, Volkswagen approved plans to cut a further 50,000 jobs globally, bringing the group's planned workforce reductions to around 100,000 positions over the coming years. The future of several German plants also remains uncertain.
Porsche and BMW are pursuing their own cost-cutting programmes, while workers at suppliers across the country are facing layoffs, short-time work or insolvency risks.
At Audi's Neckarsulm plant, thousands of employees protested against uncertainty surrounding the site's future after 2034. Workers and union representatives argue that the factory's long-term survival depends on securing a high-volume electric vehicle model.
Mercedes is currently negotiating changes aimed at improving competitiveness, including a proposal for employees to work an additional three hours per week without extra pay.
READ ALSO: Tesla announces plan to add 1,000 jobs in Germany
The electric vehicle transition is real
Germany is increasingly moving towards electric and hybrid vehicles. Fully electric vehicles accounted for 32.4 percent of all new car registrations in August 2026 and hybrids for a further 39.8 percent, according to figures from Germany's Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA).
Petrol vehicles accounted for just 16.7 percent of registrations, while diesel cars represented 10.6 percent. That means more than seven out of every 10 newly registered cars were either electric or hybrid.
And the trend is visible beyond registration statistics. Car giant Volkswagen now has more electric vehicle orders than combustion-engine orders in its home market, according to Motor1.com.
But while German consumers are increasingly buying electric vehicles, there are fears the car industry may be missing out on the rewards.
A recent study by consulting firm EY suggests Germany's biggest carmakers are falling behind international competitors. According to the study, revenues at Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes fell by 2.9 percent in the first half of 2026.
By contrast, revenues across the world's 19 largest automakers increased by 3.6 percent over the same period.
The problem for Volkswagen is that even though demand is moving in the right direction, it’s not necessarily translating into greater security for some of its traditional factories. Sites such as Wolfsburg were built around the combustion engine, while much of the new EV demand is being met by vehicles produced elsewhere in the company's manufacturing network.

At the same time, foreign competitors are gaining ground in Germany. For example, Chinese brands increased their market share from 4.4 to 8 percent in just a year, partly by exploiting gaps in the entry-level electric vehicle segment, according to EY.

items.title: Nine bodies recovered from Virgo 8 wreckage: Basarnas
items.summary: Divers joint team from Basarnas Special Group (BSG) and Indonesian Navy was able to locate and recover nine ...
items.body_text:
Head of National Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas), Mohammad Syafii, said the nine bodies were recovered from the wreckage of the vessel on the 11th day of the search and rescue (SAR) operation.
"Despite challenging underwater currents and visibility conditions, the joint team of divers persisted in searching the ship's interior until they successfully located the victims," Syafii said in Banjarmasin.
The victims were subsequently transferred to the rescue vessel KN SAR Pacitan and airlifted by a Basarnas HR 3601 helicopter to the Sjamsudin Noor Air Force Base in Banjarbaru.
Afterwards, they were transported to Bhayangkara Hospital in Banjarmasin for identification and further processing.
Related news: Indonesia to launch probe into deadly Virgo Transport 8 sinking
Syafii noted the successful recovery of the nine victims was the result of the hard work and courage of the entire SAR team, who continued the search amidst difficult underwater conditions.
"The joint team's efforts continued. Nine victims were found. Thanks to the courage of BSG and Navy divers who continued searching inside the vessel. We will keep working to provide answers to the families who are still waiting," Syafii said.
Of the nine fatalities, the dive team initially recovered one body at around 11:20 Central Indonesian Time (WITA). The diving operations then continued, leading to the recovery of eight more bodies. A total of nine bodies were recovered between the morning and afternoon.
Related news: Basarnas finds bodies trapped in sunken Virgo 8 passenger cabins
With the recovery of the nine bodies, Basarnas confirmed that as of 17:00 on Wednesday, 135 people had been accounted for, comprising 108 survivors and 27 fatalities.
Meanwhile, 108 people remained missing and were still being searched for, out of the 243 people listed on the ferry manifest.
The figure does not include a body found by fishermen in the waters of Central Kalimantan on Tuesday (Sept 22).
The body is undergoing identification at Bhayangkara Hospital in Banjarmasin to determine whether the person was a victim of Virgo Transport 8 accident or from another cause.
Related news: Authority urges coastal communities to report missing Virgo 8 victims

items.title: DNA of body in Enggano Bengkulu matches Arupadatu crew member: Police
items.summary: The Banten Regional Police confirmed that DNA test results have identified a body found on Enggano Island, Bengkulu, as ...
items.body_text:
The boat was carrying a group of journalists when it lost contact in the waters of the Sunda Strait off Pandeglang, Banten, on September 7.
Banten Regional Police Chief Inspector General Hengki said the identification was confirmed after the Disaster Victim Identification (DVI) team conducted a thorough examination and matched DNA data.
“DNA examination of the body found on Enggano Island identified the individual as Sukarman, a crew member and the biological father of Yayan,” he said at a press conference on Wednesday.
Hengki explained that the identification was part of the SAR operation for eight people — five journalists and three crew members of the speedboat — who lost contact after departing from Pagedongan Carita Pier in Pandeglang at 2 p.m. local time to cover the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau.
After 10 days of intensive searches by a joint team, a breakthrough came on September 12 when Bengkulu police officers discovered an unidentified male body in the waters of Sawang Bengkok, Kahyapu Village, Enggano Subdistrict.
Following the discovery, the Banten Regional Police's Medical and Health Division coordinated with the local police to secure the body and transport it by Cessna aircraft to Bhayangkara Hospital in Bengkulu for further identification.
“The authorities then submitted antemortem and postmortem data on the eight missing victims. The team conducted data matching by analyzing fingerprints, dental records, and DNA samples,” Hengki said.
Following the identification, Sukarman’s body is scheduled to be flown from Bengkulu to Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Tangerang before being transported to his home in Pandeglang.
“The body will be transported tomorrow from Bengkulu to Soekarno-Hatta Airport, after which it will be handed over to the family,” Hengki said.

items.title: Business players urge EU-ASEAN partnership on ASEAN Power Grid
items.summary: The European Union-ASEAN Business Council (EU-ABC) has called on leaders from both regions to establish a flagship ...
items.body_text:
The proposed partnership would entail technical and financial support from the European Union to implement the grid, leveraging the EU’s extensive experience in developing interconnected electricity systems and European funding projects.
"To date, 105 million euros (US$117 million) in grant funding has been allocated to various Team Europe initiatives on sustainable connectivity and the green transition," Executive Director of EU-ABC Chris Humphrey said in a statement released here on Wednesday.
The business council envisions the power grid partnership as one of three headline outcomes to mark the 50th anniversary of ASEAN-EU relations in 2027. The other two goals include building a region-to-region economic architecture and strengthening resilient trusted regional systems.
Humphrey expressed hope that the upcoming milestone will yield not only commercial rewards but also broad economic benefits to uplift communities across Southeast Asia.
"The 50th anniversary of ASEAN-EU relations should not be merely symbolic. It must focus on delivering tangible outcomes in order to build a trusted, long-lasting partnership that is rooted in practical cooperation," he noted.
Beyond the three headline outcomes, the council stressed the need for greater high-level political engagement between the two blocs. Humphrey pointed out that while there has been a slight uptick in recent years, leader-level engagement with ASEAN counterparts remains limited.
"We urge the EU to considerably increase its high-level presence at ASEAN forums and extend political engagement to a wider range of sectors, including digital, finance, energy, and health, among others," he said.
Chairman of EU-ABC Jens Ruebbert added that the council is also advocating for the establishment of a region-to-region free trade agreement (FTA).
According to the EU-ABC’s latest Business Sentiment Survey, nearly three-quarters (74 percent) of European business respondents believe an ASEAN-wide FTA would deliver greater benefits than bilateral agreements with individual Southeast Asian countries.
Furthermore, almost half (49 percent) would like to see negotiations for a regional FTA launched next year to coincide with the 50th anniversary of bilateral relations.
Currently, the EU only has FTAs in place with Singapore and Vietnam. Agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines have concluded and are pending ratification, while talks with Thailand and Malaysia remain ongoing.
"We strongly believe a regional deal would provide a competitive edge for European and Southeast Asian companies alike, bringing trade and investment to a level that reflects the scale and strategic importance of the ASEAN-EU relationship," Ruebbert concluded.

items.title: PH leads ASEAN, partner navies in West Philippine Sea drills
items.summary: A Chinese Navy vessel is seen close to where eight countries are sailing for the drills, but it does not respond to challenges from the Philippine Navy
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- The Philippines hosted a joint maritime security exercise involving eleven ships from eight countries as part of the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) EWG-MS.
- The exercises focused on interoperability among regional navies and included drills for medical evacuation, search and rescue, and aiding grounded vessels, while China did not participate in the sea phase despite being present at the opening.
- Maritime security in the South China Sea remains a critical concern for ASEAN nations, with ongoing tensions between the Philippines and China over territorial claims, particularly in the West Philippine Sea.
ABOARD THE BRP JOSE RIZAL – In waters off the coast of Zambales on the morning of Wednesday, September 23, the domineering figure of the helicopter destroyer JS Ise inched closer and closer to the Navy’s flagship, the BRP Jose Rizal.
It was a welcome sight — a signal that a joint activity under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) would soon commence.
Dotting the waters around Rizal was an impressive array of gray ships — the Philippine Navy’s own BRP Tarlac, two from India, two from New Zealand, and one each from Singapore, Brunei, Australia, the United States, and Japan. All eleven ships from eight countries were in these waters for the sea phase of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) Experts’ Working Group on Maritime Security (EWG-MS).
ADMM-Plus is the premier platform for the region’s defense ministers to take up a long list of issues. For the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS, the focus was on maritime security and environmental resilience in the face of climate change.
On Wednesday, the Rizal was the lead ship for formation drills and a medical evacuation, while the Japanese forces led search and rescue efforts. The BRP Tarlac, meanwhile, practiced aiding a grounded oil tanker and cross-deck landing drills.
China did not participate in the sea phase of the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS, although they could have. Representatives from China were present at the opening of the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS in Zambales on Monday, September 21.
Reporters embarked on the Rizal, including a team from Rappler, saw at least one People’s Liberation Army Navy or Chinese military warship close to the area where the vessels were sailing together. The Rizal issued radio challenges to the Chinese vessel but did not get a response.
Regional cooperation
The sea phase and even the meetings on land aren’t just for showing off new and old assets.
They’re meant to test and practice interoperability, or the ability of different navies and units to work with each other. On a more human level, it’s about establishing familiarity and trust between the armed forces of the bloc and its partners.
Aside from chairing ASEAN, Manila is also chair of the ADMM. The Philippines, with Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. as host, is expected to host ministers of the ADMM-Plus before 2026 ends.
“Our collaboration and cooperation not merely in response but in early prepositioning, working together, and in detection becomes more critical,” said Teodoro on Monday, at the opening of the ADMM-Plus EGW-MS.
Alongside the joint cooperative activity is a Future Leaders Program or FLP, which brings junior officers of different navies together to “engage their counterparts on climate change, maritime security, and key topics, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and Critical Underwater Infrastructure security.”
In the region — and in ASEAN especially — maritime security is a major concern. The South China Sea, where up to a third of global trade passes through, encompasses several ASEAN countries. It is also the flashpoint for regional tensions, mostly between Southeast Asian claimant nations and superpower China, which is part of the ADMM-Plus and is an ASEAN dialogue partner.
Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, and the Philippines are all claimants to various areas and features of the South China Sea.

items.title: Carlos, Eldrew Yulo anchor PH to sixth in Asian Games team event
items.summary: Set to compete in the floor exercise, vault, and parallel bars finals, Carlos Yulo flashes medal-winning potential, with an Asian Games gold also well within reach
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- Carlos Yulo led the Philippine gymnastics team to a sixth-place finish in the men's artistic gymnastics team all-around event at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.
- The team scored a total of 227.359 points, with China winning gold, Japan taking silver, and Chinese Taipei securing bronze.
- Carlos Yulo showed strong individual performances, posting the highest score in floor exercise and competing for medals in upcoming finals for floor exercise, vault, and parallel bars.
MANILA, Philippines – Carlos Yulo anchored the Philippines to a sixth-place finish in the team all-around event of the men’s artistic gymnastics in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, as he and his teammates got some practice in before the apparatus finals in the coming days.
The team, composed of Carlos, his younger brother Eldrew, Juancho Miguel Besana, Justine Ace de Leon, and Zachary Nunez, totaled 227.359 points across the six apparatuses in the eight-team final.
China topped the event for the third consecutive edition, registering 255.095 points to edge reigning Olympic champion Japan for the gold.
Despite being led by Olympic individual all-around gold medalists Daiki Hashimoto and Shinnosuke Oka, Japan settled for silver with 253.826 points.
Chinese Taipei finished a distant third with 239.896 points for the bronze, while Kazakhstan (237.596) and South Korea (236.359) placed fourth and fifth, respectively, ahead of the Philippines.
Set to compete in the floor exercise, vault, and parallel bars finals, Carlos showed medal-winning potential, with a gold also well within reach.
Carlos posted the highest mark in floor exercise with 14.266 points, netted the fourth-best score in vault with 14.566, and tied for the fifth-highest mark in parallel bars with 14.166.
Meanwhile, Eldrew recorded 13.966 points in vault, 13.166 in horizontal bar, 13.0 in floor exercise, 12.233 in rings, 11.933 in parallel bars, and 11.366 in pommel horse — the only one in the team to see action in all apparatuses.
In the team event, only three of the five gymnasts compete in each apparatus, with their scores combined to determine the total.
De Leon contributed 13.833 points in vault, 12.533 in rings, and 10.933 in floor exercise, Nunez added 12.333 in pommel horse and 12.066 in horizontal bar, while Besana chipped in 11.933 points in pommel horse, 11.733 in horizontal bar, and 10.0 in parallel bars as the Philippines came in ahead of Vietnam (214.428) and Singapore (200.928).
Aside from Carlos, Eldrew vies for a medal in floor exercise and horizontal bar, while Besana shoots for a podium finish in vault.
The floor exercise final is scheduled on Thursday, September 24, while the vault, parallel bars, and horizontal bars finals are set on Friday, September 25. – Rappler.com

items.title: DOF backs excise tax relief on LPG, kerosene, but not diesel or gasoline
items.summary: Finance Secretary Frederick Go says broader relief could cost P12 billion a month in lost revenue.
items.body_text:
DOF backs excise tax relief on LPG, kerosene, but not diesel or gasoline
MANILA, Philippines — Finance Secretary Frederick Go has signed a resolution seeking the suspension of excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene, while holding off on similar relief for diesel and gasoline over concerns about who would benefit and the potential P12-billion monthly revenue loss.
Go announced the move during the Department of Finance's Senate budget hearing on Tuesday, September 22, after Sen. Bong Go asked what the government was doing to cushion consumers from rising oil prices.
"Actually kanina mga 15 minutes ago, pumipirma ako dito. Pinirmahan ko iyong resolution to remove excise taxes on LPG and kerosene, which is very similar to what we did in the first round of the Middle East War," the finance chief said.
(Actually, about 15 minutes ago, I was signing it here. I signed the resolution to remove excise taxes on LPG and kerosene, which is very similar to what we did in the first round of the Middle East War.)
The resolution still requires the approval of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. before the tax suspension can take effect.
Under Republic Act 12316, the president may suspend or reduce excise taxes on specific petroleum products upon the recommendation of the Development Budget Coordination Committee and in coordination with the energy secretary once the average Dubai crude price reaches or exceeds $80 per barrel for a month.
The Department of Energy certified on September 15 that the benchmark had been breached, with Dubai crude averaging $99.41 per barrel from August 13 to September 11.
The law allows excise tax relief to last for up to three months.
Earlier Tuesday, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said the government's recommendation on fuel excise tax relief was expected to reach Marcos within the week.
The move would effectively revive relief granted earlier this year, when Marcos suspended excise taxes on LPG and kerosene for three months beginning in April.
Not for diesel, gasoline
The economic team, however, is not recommending the suspension of excise taxes on diesel and gasoline for now.
"Ang conclusion po ng DBCC nung una namin itong pinag-usapan ay, number one, if you remove taxes on diesel and gasoline, it will not be progressive," Go said.
(The DBCC's conclusion when we first discussed this was, number one, that removing taxes on diesel and gasoline would not be progressive.)
Go said the DBCC's assessment was that higher-income consumers would receive a larger share of the benefit because they consume more gasoline and diesel.
"So we thought for that point is to keep the taxes and instead do a targeted subsidy to the vulnerable sectors," Go said.
The finance chief also said suspending excise taxes on gasoline and diesel would cost the government around P12 billion in revenue each month.
"In the absence of any revenue enhancing measure to replace the P12 billion a month that we will lose, in the meantime the DBCC is not endorsing that to the president," Go said.
The government has instead favored targeted assistance for sectors most affected by rising fuel costs, including fuel subsidies for public transport drivers.

items.title: Leni Robredo endorses Leonen as chief justice
items.summary: In Robredo’s letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. dated September 11, Robredo urged Marcos to appoint the senior magistrate to head the judiciary, citing his experience and efficiency.
items.body_text:
Leni Robredo endorses Leonen as chief justice
MANILA, Philippines — Former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo has endorsed Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen as the next chief justice of the Supreme Court.
In Robredo’s letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. dated September 11, Robredo urged Marcos to appoint the senior magistrate to head the judiciary, citing his experience and efficiency.
“Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen is the most senior among all the justices of the Court. He has proven to be way beyond the constitutional requirements of competence, independence, probity, and integrity,” Robredo’s letter read.
Robredo highlighted Leonen’s nearly 14-year tenure in the High Tribunal since 2012, pointing out that he has authored thousands of ponencias and separate opinions characterized by legal depth, clarity, and an awareness of the nation's "postcolonial and multi-ethnic reality."
Robredo also added that despite his heavy workload, Leonen maintains one of the lowest case dockets in the Supreme Court.
The Naga City mayor also cited Leonen’s background prior to joining the bench, including his service as a public interest lawyer representing indigenous groups and marginalized sectors, his tenure as dean of the University of the Philippines College of Law, and his role in brokering the landmark peace framework agreement with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
"At this juncture in our political economy, we need his leadership to inspire credibility and genuine social justice—measures which we all share," Robredo added. "I have no doubt that his appointment will be acceptable to all sectors, including big business, small and medium-scale entrepreneurs, local and national government officials, and those who suffer from poverty, inequality, and disempowerment,” Robredo said.
Leonen is set to serve as an acting chief justice of the Supreme Court while the position of chief magistrate is still vacant after the retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo on November 6.
He is also included among the five Supreme Court justices invited by the Judicial and Bar Council to apply for the position of chief magistrate.
