items.title: Trump and Xi: Strongmen at the Temple of Thymos
items.summary: The ego-driven fragility of a world run by Xi Jinping and Donald Trump.
items.body_text:
When U.S. President Donald Trump made his second state visit to China in May 2026, Xi Jinping escorted him through Beijing’s magisterial Temple of Heaven, where the Ming and Qing emperors performed rites that mediated between heaven and the earthly order. But when these two men with autocratic impulses and outsized egos strolled through the complex, it became not a Temple of Heaven but a Temple of Thymos – a stage for distributing recognition rather than cosmic concerns. Now, the neoclassical architecture of the White House provides the set for their September 23–25 encounter.
Readers of The Diplomat can find in it many articles on the “Thucydides Trap” popularized by the political scientist Graham Allison. The Thucydides Trap suggests that China and the United States are headed for inevitable conflict. Several scholars dispute Allison’s reading, and yet the ancient historian’s ghost still hovered as Xi and Trump moved through the temple, with the Chinese Communist Party’s general secretary, who has a pattern of citing Allison, even referencing the phrase.
I want to propose a lens for power rivalry that’s equally ancient but different and complementary: a Thymos Trap.
Thymos – also rendered thumos – is an ancient Greek word (θυμός) that expresses the desire for recognition. Both Xi and Trump display an unquenchable thymos and take pains to appear outwardly strong. But in fact, countries led by strongmen who build regimes around their personalities are only outwardly magnificent. Internally, they tend to be precarious. Anyone who assumes that the superficial strength of such regimes and leaders makes them permanently durable may be falling into a Thymos Trap.
As popularized by the political philosopher Francis Fukuyama, thymos is “the part of the soul that craves recognition of dignity.” It’s innate to all of us and not a marker of damaged, narcissistic men. But Fukuyama makes distinctions between isothymia (recognition as equal) and megalothymia (recognition as superior). The genius of liberal democracy is that it satisfies the human need for isothymia. But megalothymia can never be extinguished, because its fossil fuel is the trauma of prior humiliation, now powering a yearning for reversal. Nationalism can transfer that dynamic from individual to nation: Xi wears it on his sleeve as China’s “century of humiliation,” ensuing “hurt feelings of the Chinese people,” and his Chinese Dream of rejuvenation. Trump emblazons it on his “Make America Great Again” baseball caps.
This desire for status, as the journalist Will Storr explained in “The Status Game,” is pursued through dominance, virtue, or success. These differing tactics can depend on the cultures in which status-seeking individuals operate.
According to political philosopher Ye Xue, in the United States, where status is relative and must be defended, the cultural tendency is to pursue self-esteem through demands for honor. China, by contrast, is rooted in a stable hierarchy in which status is relational and harmony is sought. Trump and Xi represent these different cultural approaches to recognition perfectly; Trump’s is deeply individualistic and even antagonistic, while Xi’s is more concerned with a collective megalothymia that demands deference to China as a whole.
For all their differences, Xi and Trump share a common insistence on staking their own legitimacy on the nation’s self-esteem, updating French King Louis XIV’s apocryphal line, l’État, c’est moi (“I am the State”). But they do differ in noteworthy ways. Per Ye Xue’s research, Trump demands conspicuous displays of deference to him as an individual, while Xi is more concerned with displays of “face” – something he has fused with gestures toward China as a whole. In that way, Xi is a quintessentially Chinese statesman, in being tactful, understated, and formal.

items.title: 3 Ts Will Dominate the Trump-Xi Summit
items.summary: Expect little movement on trade, less on Taiwan, and who knows on tech.
items.body_text:
When Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping last sat down in May 2026, talk was centered on three Ts: trade, technology and Taiwan. Their next summit, due to begin in the United States on September 24, looks set to focus on the same set of issues again. The main difference will be that the technology element has been given added urgency by the sudden and rapid shift in developments in artificial intelligence.
What’s less clear is whether the two sides will be able to come to any sort of transformative agreement on that, or any other issue.
The most urgent issue, but also the simplest to solve, will be on trade. Nearly a year ago at Busan in South Korea, Trump and Xi hammered out an agreement whereby the United States agreed to lift some export controls on high-end technology and to reduce the then three-figure tariffs on Chinese goods. For its part, China agreed not to restrict the flow of critical minerals and rare earths to U.S. users.
That pact – only good for one year – is now up for renewal. Both sides are likely to want a continuation of the current arrangement, and while there may be some tweaking on the side, the new deal will probably be similar to the old one.
Each side has proposed in previous meetings that there should be a new instrument, a Board of Trade, that will assess non-sensitive China-U.S. business interests. However, details about the institution remains vague. Some announcements are likely during the summit, but business leaders will want to know how comprehensive and lasting the arrangements for the board will be.
There is still less information on a proposed Board of Investment, which remains on the drawing board. The Chinese side has proposed bringing major Chinese CEOs to the summit to match the likes of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk – both of whom accompanied Trump on the Beijing trip. But the choice of business leaders is likely to turn on which aspects of trade China thinks are likely to develop most effectively in the short term.
Taiwan is a much harder issue to solve, but it’s unlikely that much that is discussed on Xi’s visit will determine its outcome.
Trump has been less willing than his predecessor to commit the United States to defending the island should Beijing invade, instead reasserting Washington’s long-held position of strategic ambiguity.
And although the U.S. is currently distracted from East Asia by the Iran conflict, China still prefers to find methods short of war to bring the island under Beijing’s control.
The island’s January 2028 presidential election is likely to be a more crucial moment for Taiwan’s future, particularly if the opposition – and more China-friendly – Kuomintang (KMT) wins the presidency, or indeed if an isolationist candidate becomes U.S. president later that year. If the next U.S. president opted to change course by taking a less active involvement in overseas issues – as has been floated by early contenders on both the left and right – that would change things all the more.
For now, Beijing will continue to build the People’s Liberation Army’s naval capacity to have the option of military action against the island. But its preference will be to take advantage of changes within Taiwan’s internal politics while combining economic incentives and coercion, squeezing Taipei’s international footprint and hoping for a slackening of U.S. interest in the western Pacific.
Other international issues are likely to gain less attention. China is expected to make clear its unhappiness about the war on Iran, and the U.S. may remind China that it has passed new legislation allowing sanctions on countries that buy Russian oil – of which, China is the largest purchaser. However, neither issue is likely to lead to any major change in practice.

items.title: A Debate Is Raging in China Over English Education
items.summary: Rising youth unemployment, the advent of AI translation, and growing anger against everything foreign are fueling public anger against English education in China.
items.body_text:
In the heated public discussions in China over English education, those calling to downgrade or abandon English in Chinese schools and colleges are using an ancient saying: 刻舟求剑 (ke zhou qiu jian), literally “notching the boat to find a sword.” Less literally, the phrase describes a foolish approach to solving problems that fails to account for changing circumstances.
The phrase refers to an ancient fable from the Warring States period (475 BC to 221 BC). In the story, a traveler from the State of Chu was crossing a river in a boat when his precious sword accidentally slipped from his hand and fell into the water. Instead of diving into the water to retrieve it, he calmly took out a small knife and carved a notch on the side of the boat right where the sword fell.
On being asked why he didn’t immediately jump into the river to retrieve his sword, he replied: “There is no need to worry. My sword fell into the river at this marked place. As soon as the boat reaches the dock and pulls into shore, I will jump down from here to retrieve my sword.”
That’s the context needed to understand those using this idiom in order to ridicule the continuation of English being taught in primary, secondary and high schools. Critics point out that the decision to incorporate the English language as a mandatory part of the school curriculum was made 50 years ago. “At the time, the aim was to quickly strengthen education, learn science and technology from abroad, and improve the overall quality of the population. Forcing everyone to learn English, while perhaps a bit of an overreaction, was understandable given the specific circumstances,” Chinese scholar Xiang Ligang commented on WeChat. But, like the position of the boat in the fable, China’s circumstances have changed.
It’s a widely held figure that English learning for a Chinese student – from early schooling to entering a university, in total 12 years of education – requires 3,000 to 5,000 hours of study and at least 100,000 yuan. Many in China are raising the question: is it worth it?
Arguments against the continuation of English as a compulsory subject in schools and colleges were recently further strengthened by a call to “end English’s core status” issued by Tang Jiafeng. Tang is a mathematics professor and online celebrity who has long taught mathematics to candidates taking postgraduate entrance examinations. The latest controversy stemmed from his comments on reforms to the locally administered zhongkao (senior high school entrance examination). Saying that “the history of Chinese people worshiping foreign things and fawning on foreign countries should end,” he advocated for reducing the weight given to English proficiency on the exam.
Currently, English is a required subject starting in third grade. It is weighted on par with Chinese language and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after ninth grade, and the high school graduation exam. Chinese, English, and mathematics (collectively known as CEM) are the three most important subjects on the gaokao, China’s college and university entrance examination. Each subject counts for 150 points out of a total of 750.
Tang Jiafeng called for downgrading the status of English as part of an angry reaction to Chinese history being removed as a scoring subject in exams in several provinces. A large section of China’s nationalist intellectuals – who are also generally labeled as “conservatives” – have come out in support of Tang. Also on their side are parents and students who oppose making English a compulsory subject. English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. Learning English thus increases the students’ burden and parents’ or guardian’s financial pressure.

items.body_text:
September 22, 2026
Letter to the Editor: Cambodia’s campaign against online scams
Mu Sochua’s September 22 op-ed, “Cambodia’s anti-scam summit can’t whitewash its own record,” does not reflect Cambodia’s current efforts to combat online scams.
Cambodia does not claim to have eliminated all scam operations. Some smaller, less visible scam activity remains. However, authorities have dismantled the large scam compounds that once operated openly. We are now targeting the criminal networks behind them.
Since July 2025, Cambodian authorities have investigated 832 locations suspected of housing online scam operations and carried out operations at 663 of them. Eighty-six scam compounds have been dismantled. We have sent 446 cases involving 3,927 people from 29 nationalities to the courts, including alleged ringleaders.
The Anti-Corruption Unit has acted in four cases involving 15 senior officials and law enforcement officers. Authorities have frozen more than US$300 million in scam-linked bank accounts.
It is inaccurate to suggest that Cambodia’s response is limited to closing compounds and deportations, or that influential individuals are shielded from accountability. Cambodia’s Law on Combating Online Scams, enacted in April, gives authorities stronger powers to pursue those who organize or support these crimes. No one is above the law.
The International Conference on Combating Online Scams (ICCOS 2026) in Phnom Penh this week is not an exercise in image management. Representatives from the FBI, INTERPOL, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, ASEAN and the UK Home Office, along with ministers and law enforcement officials from Asia and other regions, are gathering to strengthen international cooperation.
The goal is to help affected countries pursue the criminals behind these networks and follow illicit money across borders, reducing the risk that operations shut down in Cambodia simply re-emerge elsewhere.
Cambodia has also invited international journalists to visit former scam compounds, question officials, and assess our progress. We are not seeking uncritical endorsement. We ask that Cambodia’s current record be judged fairly on the evidence.
Sincerely,
Neth Pheaktra
Minister of Information
Royal Government of Cambodia

items.title: Why China’s Silicon Valley won’t need American degrees
items.summary: For nearly a century, American global power has rested on a three-legged tripod: unmatched military firepower, the ubiquitous sovereignty of the US dollar and the intellectual dominance of its higher-education system. While aircraft carriers project hard power and Wall Street manages global capital, the American university system has quietly manufactured the “soft power,” technological breakthroughs […] The post Why China’s Silicon Valley won’t need American degrees appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
For nearly a century, American global power has rested on a three-legged tripod: unmatched military firepower, the ubiquitous sovereignty of the US dollar and the intellectual dominance of its higher-education system.
While aircraft carriers project hard power and Wall Street manages global capital, the American university system has quietly manufactured the “soft power,” technological breakthroughs and elite talent required to keep the empire running.
Yet, tectonic shifts rarely announce themselves with a trumpet blast; they begin as subtle disruptions in the data. In the 2026 Nature Index, Harvard University — which had comfortably held the global top spot in scientific output since the index was created in 2014 — fell to third place. More striking still was the scenery surrounding it: nine of the top ten research institutions in the world are now Chinese.
For prominent public intellectuals like Fareed Zakaria, who has spent decades on his CNN GPS show, in columns in The Washington Post and in his landmark book “In Defense of a Liberal Education” arguing that American academic preeminence is essentially unrivaled, this shift should serve as an alarm bell.
Zakaria is quick to credit the perpetual dominance of American education with a well-worn list of structural merits such as top rankings internationally, an inherent capacity for recruiting talent from around the world, plentiful government and private research funds, an integrated approach to liberal and applied science subjects and an environment which encourages innovation and discovery rather than mere memorization.
In recent years, he has added a cautionary coda to his thesis, warning that hyper-politicization, culture-war battles, budget cuts and restrictive visa policies could cripple this delicate ecosystem.
While Zakaria’s diagnosis of current American strengths is accurate, his prognosis for the future reads more like wishful thinking than cold-eyed realism. His fatal oversight lies not in what he observes inside the campus gates, but in what he ignores outside of them to the factory gate.
Zakaria correctly maps the dimensions of American hard and soft power, yet fails to grasp the seismic economic transformations reorganizing the wider world. Academic dominance is not something the US easily achieves through the liberal way of life; it is simply a consequence of its industrial domination in the past.
As manufacturing moves from west to east, academic dominance will follow. Over the next decade, American higher education risks losing its historic leadership in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, management and financial technology.
Unless dramatic changes occur, American universities may find their global domain restricted largely to the humanities and social sciences — fields like English literature, Western philosophy, mass media, film studies and sociology.
Universities do not operate in a vacuum of pure intellectuality. Universities have been engineered to produce specific types of knowledge, and their worth has been measured by how efficiently they run the machinery of industry.
To understand why China is mounting such a formidable challenge, one must look at the historical nexus between the factory floor and the lecture hall. The world-class stature of American universities in the mid-20th century did not happen by accident; it was bankrolled and sustained by the massive industrial output of post-World War II America.
When a nation controls the world’s primary production lines, its universities naturally become the nerve centers for applied science, industrial engineering, operational management, and commercial finance.
Today, that industrial center of gravity has moved. China now accounts for roughly 37% of global manufacturing output and controls nearly 40% of advanced technology production and trade.

items.title: Pakistan’s new Chengdu trade route shows CPEC can work
items.summary: Earlier this month, more than 80 metric tons of dried chilies from Pakistan arrived at the Chengdu International Railway Port. Packed into eight containers, the cargo entered China through Qinzhou Port in Guangxi, then moved inland to Chengdu via a sea-rail intermodal service operating under the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor. items.body_text:
Earlier this month, more than 80 metric tons of dried chilies from Pakistan arrived at the Chengdu International Railway Port. Packed into eight containers, the cargo entered China through Qinzhou Port in Guangxi, then moved inland to Chengdu via a sea-rail intermodal service operating under the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor.
On the surface, this is an unremarkable agricultural transaction — one spice crossing a border. Yet the shipment carries significance well beyond its weight in chilies.
It was the first consignment to arrive in China under an agricultural cooperation project tied to the Belt and Road Initiative-financed China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, or CPEC, and it offers a rare, concrete glimpse of what the next phase of Pakistan-China connectivity might look like.
Chilies destined for southwestern China have traditionally traveled through northern Chinese ports before being redistributed inland — a route that adds handling, storage and time costs.
The Qinzhou-Chengdu link changes that sequence: Cargo now moves more directly from the coast to Sichuan’s provincial capital, cutting delivery time by an estimated seven to 10 days and reducing logistics costs by roughly 1,000 yuan (about US$140) per ton, according to figures cited by the Chengdu port authority.
More than 900 additional tons are reportedly already in transit, with the operator hoping to move the service toward regular, scheduled operation. None of this amounts to a new corridor built from scratch.
It is, more precisely, a new logistics channel threaded through existing infrastructure: Qinzhou’s port facilities, the land-sea trade corridor, and Chengdu’s rail and bonded-warehousing network.
That distinction is noteworthy because it points to where CPEC’s value is likely to be tested going forward. The corridor’s first phase was measured in kilometers of highway, megawatts of power and tons of cargo moving through Gwadar. Those remain necessary foundations, but infrastructure alone does not sell a farmer’s crop in a foreign market.
What the chili shipment demonstrates — modestly, and for a single commodity — is the harder, less visible work of connecting Pakistani producers to Chinese processors, distributors and retail chains. This is the terrain that discussions of “CPEC 2.0” increasingly point toward: not a rebranding of the corridor, but a shift in emphasis from building connectivity to using it.
Chengdu’s role here is not incidental. Sichuan and Chongqing are among China’s most significant chili-consuming markets, driven by hotpot culture, a large condiment industry and a dense concentration of restaurants and food processors. China imported roughly 400,000 metric tons of dried chilies in 2025, with Pakistan, India and Myanmar among the leading suppliers.
Chengdu’s railway port is also positioned as a logistics hub linking the land-sea corridor with China-Europe freight services, combining transport, bonded warehousing, trading and distribution functions in one location.
For Pakistani exporters, the opportunity is not simply a shorter shipping route, but potential proximity to an integrated supply chain — the kind of arrangement that can turn a one-off sale into a recurring commercial relationship.
It would be a mistake, however, to treat the arrival of eight containers as proof that Pakistan’s agricultural export problem is solved. Pakistan produces chilies, rice, mangoes and a range of other agricultural goods in substantial volume; the constraint has rarely been production capacity alone.
The real constraint has been everything that happens after harvest: logistics costs, transit time, inconsistent supply, packaging standards, compliance with sanitary and phytosanitary requirements, and the absence of durable links with Chinese buyers and processors. A faster, cheaper route addresses one piece of that chain.
It does not, by itself, guarantee reliable quality control, consistent volumes across seasons, or the trading relationships needed t

items.title: Africa must get permanent seats on Security Council – UN chief
items.summary: Africa’s lack of permanent representation on the UN Security Council is unjust, Antonio Guterres has said Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Africa must get permanent seats on Security Council – UN chief
Africa’s continued lack of permanent representation on the United Nations Security Council is unjust and must be addressed, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has said.
Speaking at the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly debate in New York on Tuesday, Guterres called for reform of the 15-member body to better reflect the modern global order. Africa remains the only continent without a permanent seat on the council despite accounting for more than a quarter of UN member states and every third child born.
“We must reform the security council ... A 21st UN security council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible. This must change,” the UN chief said.
UN Security Council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible — Antonio Guterres
‘Security Council was designed in the aftermath of WWII, but the world has fundamentally changed since then’ https://t.co/L8S7U38rY5pic.twitter.com/wlNk3cB5sw
The Security Council has five permanent members – Russia, China, the US, the UK and France – which hold veto powers, as well as ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. African countries – the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia – currently only participate through the latter category.
Earlier this month, Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama renewed calls for permanent African representation on the Security Council, arguing that the continent’s continued exclusion undermines the legitimacy of the UN’s most powerful body.
“It is no longer acceptable for Africa to be excluded from permanent seats on the United Nations Security Council,” the leader said.
Other African leaders have made similar demands. In July, representatives of several countries renewed calls for the continent to be granted permanent representation on the Security Council, arguing that its current structure no longer reflects global realities. The African Union’s shared position calls for at least two permanent seats with the same privileges as existing members, including veto powers.
Calls for reform have also received support from Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously backed expanding the Security Council to include greater African representation.
In August, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov noted that greater representation for the continent would help correct a historical injustice, arguing that any future expansion should primarily benefit African countries rather than Western states, which he said are already overrepresented.

items.title: UK charges doctor over Rwandan genocide
items.summary: Rwandan doctor Vincent Brown has become the first person charged in the UK over the East African nation’s 1994 genocide Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
UK charges doctor over Rwandan genocide
A former Rwandan health official has been charged by British prosecutors over his alleged role in the 1994 genocide in his home country, bringing the first UK charges linked to the massacre.
Vincent Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, appeared in a London court on Tuesday. He faces one charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. Prosecutors allege Brown, 65, led a group to a house in Kigali’s Rugenge district on April 8 and ordered three people shot. They say he subsequently ordered the killing of a woman and her infant son, and directed a group that stoned a taxi driver to death. Brown denies involvement.
“Dr. Brown… is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others,” chief crown prosecutor Frank Ferguson said.
More than 800,000 people, predominantly Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were killed in roughly 100 days after the genocide began on April 7, 1994. The UN tribunal established afterward indicted 93 people.
Brown, a physician, headed the family health department at Rwanda’s National Office of Population when the genocide began. He later moved to Britain as an asylum seeker and took the name Vincent Brown after gaining British citizenship in 2004. Rwanda sought his extradition, but UK courts refused over concerns that he would not receive a fair trial there. The British investigation began in 2019 following a request from Kigali. Brown, who denies involvement, is due back in court on October 9 after being released on £25,000 ($33,400) bail. His lawyer, Sam Blom-Cooper, described the killings as “appalling crimes” and said Brown welcomed the charges as an opportunity to clear his name, according to Reuters.
Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo welcomed the UK charges as a “long overdue” step toward accountability and urged Britain to speed up its remaining cases, local daily New Times reported. President Paul Kagame has previously accused the international community of failing to stop the killings, saying it failed Rwanda “whether from contempt or cowardice.”
The UK case follows prosecutions of suspects in other countries. In 2024, a French court upheld former Rwandan gendarme Philippe Hategekimana’s life sentence for organizing roadblocks and taking part in massacres around Nyanza. A Belgian court sentenced former militia leader Seraphin Twahirwa to life in 2023 for directing killings in Kigali and raping Tutsi women. Germany arrested another suspect, identified as Innocent S., in July on suspicion of complicity in genocide and involvement in 25 murders.
Rwandan businessman Felicien Kabuga, accused of financing militias and using his radio station to incite attacks on Tutsis, died in UN tribunal custody in May before his trial reached a verdict.

items.title: South Africa won’t ‘bow its head’ in US talks – president
items.summary: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has said Pretoria will negotiate with the US without bowing its head Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
South Africa won’t ‘bow its head’ in US talks – president
South Africa will continue engaging with the US despite new visa restrictions imposed by Washington, President Cyril Ramaphosa has said, insisting Pretoria will defend its sovereignty and dignity in negotiations.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the targeted restrictions last week against foreign nationals whom Washington says are responsible for, or complicit in, policies involving uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination and the incitement of violence against minority groups in South Africa. No individuals were named when the policy was announced.
Ramaphosa was speaking to journalists on the sidelines of the ANC Veterans League fundraising golf day at the Johannesburg Country Club in Woodmead on Monday. He said the government had taken note of the restrictions but remained prepared to engage with Washington. ”We are quite willing and prepared to continue engaging with the United States as we engage with all other countries in the world,” the president noted.
”Where there are challenges, we will go in with our dignity, with our sovereignty to engage with those countries without bowing our heads and treating those nations respectfully and expecting them to treat us also respectfully,” Ramaphosa added.
The president said the US remained an important market for South Africa and that both countries had products they needed from each other. He also said discussions between South Africa and the US had been under way for some time, including on trade and tariff issues. The US had also raised ”the so-called five issues”, and South Africa had responded to a number of them, he stressed.
Asked what had happened to the discussions, given the latest announcement, Ramaphosa answered he could not explain what had prompted the move. ”So I just don’t know what happened. Only they can answer and say what exactly happened,” he said.
Ramaphosa noted South Africa remained willing to negotiate with the US to resolve the challenges in the relationship. ”We also trade with them and there are certain things or products that they need from us that we also need from them,” he said. ”So that in itself should bring about the state of equilibrium. So as we deal with each other, as states that respect each other, we will find solutions.”

items.title: Pope appeals for care and protection of migrant children
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV appeals for the protection of migrant and refugee children, and for everyone to take responsibility for minors on the move. His appeal comes ahead of the World Day of Migrants and Refugees. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope appeals for care and protection of migrant children
Vatican News
Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday issued an urgent appeal to everyone to take responsibility for young migrants and refugees exposed to violence, exploitation and traumatic conditions along migration routes.
His appeal comes four days before the 112th World Day of Migrants and Refugees, to which the Pope has issued a message on the theme âEven just one of these children.â
âSunday, September 27, marks the World Day of Migrants and Refugees,â he said at the conclusion of his General Audience in St Peterâs Square, noting that his âthoughts go out to migrants and refugees, especially minors forced to leave their homelands.â
âChildren and adolescents are the most vulnerable,â he continued, noting that they âoften endure unspeakable sufferingâviolence, torture, exploitation, and traumatic conditionsâand not infrequently lose their lives along migration routes.â
The Pope then made a direct appeal: âI appeal to everyoneâs sense of responsibility. Let everyone feel personally involved in the lives of these young people, who must always be protected and cared for.â
Pope Leoâs appeal came as the Church prepares to celebrate the World Day of Migrants and Refugees on 27 September.
âEven just one of these childrenâ
In his message for the World Day, published in August, the Pope recalls that minors are among the most vulnerable people involved in migration and forced displacement.
In it he notes that millions of children and adolescents âare forced to leave their homeland because of war, poverty, violence, environmental disasters and other tragedies. Sadly, their number continues to grow.â
Pope Leo also points to âdeaths along migration routes, trafficking and exploitation, the recruitment of minors for use in armed conflicts, sexual violence, forced marriages, and the atrocities they have suffered or witnessed during their travels. Their dignity is trampled upon in countless ways.â
Yet the Pope insists that the response cannot be reduced to statistics.
âBefore this tragic reality,â he writes, âmy thoughts turn to the words of Jesus that profoundly challenge our consciences: âWhoever receives one such child in my name receives meââ.
Human faces behind the numbers
According to UNHCRâs Global Trends 2025, published in June 2026, 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced at the end of 2025 as a result of persecution, conflict, violence, human rights violations and the climate crisis.
The figure included 41.6 million refugees, 9 million asylum-seekers and 68.7 million people displaced within their own countries by conflict or violence.
Children make up a particularly large share of displaced populations. UNHCR estimates that 45 million children under the age of 18 were among the 117.8 million forcibly displaced people at the end of 2025. Among refugees, people in refugee-like situations and other people in need of international protection, 39 per cent were children.

items.title: Pope: Progress is truly human if it makes the world better for everyone
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV continues his catechesis on ‘Gaudium et spes,’ focusing on the chapter dedicated to the meaning of human activity in the universe. ‘Gaudium et spes,” he says, invites us to share “the bread of knowledge and know-how,” so that humanity can develop its potential and, with the help of God, work together to build “a better future.” Read all
items.body_text:
Pope: Progress is truly human if it makes the world better for everyone
By Christopher Wells
Vatican IIâs Pastoral Constitution on the Church, Gaudium et spesâthe subject of Pope Leo XIVâs current cycle of catecheses at the General Audiencesâaddresses the âfundamentalâ question, âWhat is the value of human activity in the world, and therefore of technical, social, and scientific progress?â
In his remarks on Wednesday, the Holy Father clearly affirms, âthe human being is the agent of progressâ advancing society through freedom and intelligence.
Pope Leo lamented the modern prejudice that sees scientific and technical progress as weakening the relationship with God. âIn post-Christian humanist thought,â he explained, âhuman beings and God are erroneously presented as rivals: in order to assert his knowledge, his freedom, and his progress, man is thought to have to emancipate himself from God.â
Such a denial, however, results in losing âthe possibility of affirming the transcendent value of the human person.â
Human beings cooperate in God's plan
Instead, Gaudium et spes states clearly that Christians âcan justly consider that by their labour they are unfolding the Creatorâs work, consulting the advantages of their brother men, and contributing by their personal industry to the realization in history of the divine plan.â
In essence, Pope Leo said, âGod has placed in the hands of men and women a creation that is still in statu viaeâthat is, on a journey, in the process of growthâso that they may bring it to fulfilment through their wise activity.â
Tying this idea to âthe mystery of the Incarnation,â the Pope said, âhumanityâ¦ is not absorbed or nullified by the encounter with God, but rather taken up in its entirety, continuing to be, in Christ, free and active.â
âFrom this perspective,â he continued, âan important truth emerges: to encounter God, the human being must not abandon his earthly vocations, but can live his vocation fully carrying out his daily work and sanctifying it.â
Like all human beings, Christians work to build up âthe city of man,â which must be distinguished from the development of âthe Kingdom of God.â However, the Pope noted the Councilâs affirmation that progress in building up human society âis of vital concern to the kingdom of God.â
Progress must be inspired by charity
Finally, Pope Leo insisted that âin order to be authentic human progressâ¦ technical and scientific progress must be inspired by charity. Only in this way can it always be placed in the service of human dignity and promote the living conditions of all, especially the most disadvantaged.â
The Second Vatican Council, he concluded, âinvites us to share the bread of knowledge and know-how, so that every person and every people may develop their potential, and together, with Godâs help, we may build a better future.â

items.body_text:
Archbishop Gallagher: Reconciliation is born of accepting truth about past
By Dorota Abdelmoula-Viet
Reconciliation is born not from forgetting the past, but from the ability to face it truthfully, with courage and trust, while opening ourselves to sincere dialogue.
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, Secretary for Relations with States and International Organizations, said at the Polish Embassy to the Holy See during the presentation of a publication on Polish-German reconciliation after the Second World War.
Entitled âWe Forgive and Ask for Forgiveness,â the publication takes its title from the historic message addressed by the Polish Bishops to the German Bishops in 1965.
It is the fruit of an academic conference held last year at the Pontifical Gregorian University to mark the 60th anniversary of that unprecedented event.
Forgiveness is born of accepting the truth about the past
Archbishop Gallagher attended the presentation and highlighted the contemporary significance of the gesture made by the two episcopates decades ago.
âThe words âWe forgive and ask for forgivenessâ, spoken in a Europe still deeply scarred by the wounds of war, retain a particular power and relevance today,â he said. âThey remind us that reconciliation is born not from forgetting the past, but from the ability to face it truthfully, with courage and trust, while opening ourselves to sincere dialogue, remembering also that, for a Christian, it is above all a gift from the Lord, as Saint Paul says: âIn Christ, God reconciled us to himself.ââ
The Archbishop stressed that the publication also invites reflection on the value of this witness âfor the present and the future, at a time when new divisions and conflicts abound. It reminds us how precious it is to safeguard what has been patiently built over decades.â
He also expressed gratitude to the Polish and German Embassies to the Holy See for their commitment to preserving the memory of an event that made an unprecedented contribution to reconciliation in post-war Europe.
World needs courageous gestures of reconciliation
The host of the gathering, Ambassador Adam Kwiatkowski, thanked Archbishop Gallagher for repeatedly recalling the example of the Polish Bishopsâ message to their German counterparts in his addresses.
âFor us, for Poland and for Germany, this is enormously significant,â he said, highlighting the significance of devoting the final event he is organizing before returning to Poland to the subject of reconciliation.
âThe world needs something more. It needs more courageous gestures and decisions capable of being ahead of their time. It needs a willingness to reach out to another person. It needs expressions of respect and gratitude towards others, despite existing differences,â he said.
German Ambassador Bruno Kahl likewise spoke of the urgent need to draw inspiration from the gesture of reconciliation made years ago by the Bishops of both countries.
âReconciliation is difficult, but it is possible. Someone, however, must take the first step,â he said. âMay this publication help awaken the relevant institutions and make the right people more aware of these values and this fundamental understanding, so that similar initiatives to overcome hatred, violence and war may also emerge today.â
Memory that heals relationships
âThis book brings together all our activities connected with the 60th anniversary of the Polish bishopsâ letter to the German bishops,â Dr Andrzej Jerie, director of the âRemembrance and Futureâ Centre in WrocÅaw and the initiator of the anniversary commemorations, told Vatican News.
âWhen we read its contents carefully, we can see the concrete fruits of our joint efforts to build good Polish-German relations,â he said. âAmong them are the moving words of Knut Abraham, who said during the conference that the WrocÅaw commemorations of the 60th anniversary of the Polish bishopsâ letter to the German bishops had contributed to the Bundestagâs almost unanimous vote to fund the Polish

items.title: Texans have real reasons to be worried. Indian Americans enjoying football isn’t one of them.
items.summary: (RNS) — All of us fans cheering on our team didn't know much about each other, but we wanted the same thing. Then, the reaction to a photo shared online told a different story.
items.body_text:
Texans have real reasons to be worried. Indian Americans enjoying football isn't one of them.
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!
(RNS) — This past weekend, I found myself at The University of Texas’ football stadium to cheer on the Longhorns as they took on the UTSA Roadrunners. Memories quickly flooded back about the heat my friends and I endured as students at the games, the frustration of entering campus right after the glorious title win in 2005, and the fun nights after big wins.
But walking onto campus and striding up to the stadium 15 years after I graduated felt different. And it was abundantly clear why: I now had my kids with me. My 6-year-old son and 4-year-old daughter were decked out in Longhorn gear, absolutely buzzing with excitement, and it felt like everyone noticed.
I’ve always felt a sense of belonging and comfort in Austin, but seeing the warm smiles and encouragement for bringing my kids into the Longhorn family was palpable. Whether it was the high fives offered to the kids, or the knowing grins from fellow parents rushing their children to the bathroom, the shared feeling of being a Longhorn parent passing down this cherished experience to a new generation was incredible.
So, I shared a photo of myself and my friends at the game with the Hindu American Foundation, where I serve as a board member. Feeling so secure on the ground was something I wanted to share with my fellow brown-skinned Longhorns, knowing we’ve all felt confused, hurt and angry at the sentiment we’ve all seen online about whether we belong in the stands. Just a week earlier, a candidate for state railroad commissioner, Bo French, shared a racist post on X about the diversity in the stands at the Longhorns’ stadium.
After, we enjoyed the game and put away our phones. The man behind me accidentally poured beer on my shoulder, and we both laughed. Another fan teased us for the number of pretzels we’d bought for our group of 19. We cheered our boys on and booed the refs into reviewing a call. We celebrated the 30 points and griped with each other about whether quarterback Arch Manning looked hesitant and why we weren’t scoring more.
All of us fans cheering on the team in our section didn’t know much about each other, but we knew what mattered. We were wearing burnt orange, and we wanted the same thing. Walking out, my kids were still talking about the fireworks, still holding onto the day.
Then, I glanced at my phone and saw that the photo I shared was attracting vitriol on the HAF account. Commenters posted memes about Indians eating cow dung. People said they could imagine how bad the picture smelled. My face was marked with demonic symbols. They attacked every facet of us that was visible.
My friends and I asked for the post to be deleted — and it was — hoping for some safety from this swarm of people who didn’t pause and ask themselves what they were actually upset about before turning it on us.
As a psychologist, I think I’m profoundly tuned into what’s happening in America right now. This wave of hate has the same root as so many that have rocked the world: fear and apprehension.
I feel scared, too. I don’t know if my own work providing psychotherapy is safe from being lost to AI. I don’t know how I’ll cover the tuition my kids will need as the cost of living climbs. I don’t know what it will take to protect kids from the depression and anxiety already rocking their generation. I don’t know how we will elect a Congress that actually represents me. It’s real fear, and it isn’t irrational.
And here’s the uncomfortable part: I don’t think the people who wrote those replies are wrong to be afraid. I think they’re afraid of many of the same things I am — a shrinking middle class and futures that feel less secure by the year. Many of us feel a sense that the systems meant to protect us are instead protecting somebody else.
That fear is legitimate. What isn’t legitimate is who they’ve been told

items.title: Under congressional pressure, a major Muslim charity cuts ties and changes its name
items.summary: (RNS) — Islamic Relief USA, a humanitarian organization with a $150 million annual budget, rebranded itself as the Islamic Development and Empowerment in America after members of Congress threatened to have its tax-exempt status revoked.
items.body_text:
Under congressional pressure, a major Muslim charity cuts ties and changes its name
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!
(RNS) — One of the nation’s largest Muslim charities has changed its name and cut ties with a network of international partners after calls from members of Congress to revoke its tax-exempt status.
In early September, Islamic Relief USA, a humanitarian organization with a $150 million annual budget, rebranded itself as the Islamic Development and Empowerment in America.
An official from IDEA told RNS the name change reflects a commitment to addressing charitable needs in the United States, in addition to the 60 countries where it operates.
The change follows a messy break with Islamic Relief Worldwide involving a lawsuit filed by Islamic Relief USA and countercharges by IRW. It culminated this month with IRW announcing it had expelled its former American partner, claiming that the affiliate “damaged the work of the entire federation.”
The dispute between these major Islamic charities — both of which had been independent partners under the Islamic Relief umbrella — came after members of the House Ways and Means Committee called on the IRS to revoke the tax-exempt status of Islamic Relief USA, Jewish Voice for Peace, American Muslims for Palestine and the Tides Foundation. They alleged that the groups have links to designated foreign terrorist groups and were “sowing chaos” in their support for pro-Palestinian protests.
Committee Chairman Jason Smith, a Missouri Republican, alleged in a September 2025 letter that because of its ties to IRW, Islamic Relief USA had “engaged in conduct that appears to provide support for a designated terrorist organization and other conduct designed to incite chaos in a way that is contrary to the public good.”
IRW denied wrongdoing. But in October 2025, IRUSA suspended its association with IRW, and the group also met with the congressional committee multiple times to provide information that would clear its reputation, said Mohamed Elibiary, chief external affairs officer of IDEA, formerly IRUSA.
Then, in March 2026, IRUSA filed a federal lawsuit against IRW, seeking a court order to formally sever ties, citing the Ways and Means letter and saying the international group’s “conduct has harmed IRUSA.”
IRUSA also made several allegations in the lawsuit against the UK-based charity, including that IRW illegally targeted American donors for fundraising. In July, a federal judge ordered the two groups to resolve their dispute through mediation.
Smith, the committee’s chairman, took credit for the IRUSA lawsuit against IRW, saying in March that it was a “significant response that would never come about but for our Committee’s oversight.” Smith did not respond to requests for comment about IRUSA’s rebranding.
Muslim charities in the U.S. have long faced federal scrutiny, especially in the years following the Sept. 11 attacks, said Sumayyah Waheed, senior policy counsel at Muslim Advocates, a D.C-based national civil rights group that uses litigation and policy to counter anti-Muslim discrimination. In 2001, the federal government seized the assets of the Holy Land Foundation, then one of the nation’s largest Muslim charities, alleging that funds from the group had been channeled to Hamas. Several leaders were convicted in 2008.
“That was devastating for the Muslim charitable community, which is pretty much our whole community, because charity is part of our faith,” she said. Because of the crackdown on other groups, Muslim Advocates partnered with the Better Business Bureau in 2008 to train Muslim nonprofits on federal compliance and overcoming perceptions of wrongdoing.
Waheed said there are renewed fears that nonprofits, including Muslim ones, are being unfairly targeted.

items.summary: (RNS) — Latter-day Saints have grown more diverse and a bit less religious, and more of them are leaving the church, says a new report from Pew Research Center.
items.body_text:
9 ways US Mormons are changing, according to Pew data
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!
(RNS) — Christmas has come three months early, at least for me and other religion data nerds. Pew Research Center has just released a detailed 65-page report specifically about Latter-day Saints in America.
Called “Tradition and Change Among Latter-day Saints in the U.S.,” the report primarily utilizes Pew’s 2023 – 24 Religious Landscape Study, which had 515 current and 316 former members, and compares it to Pew’s data on Mormons from 2007, 2011 and 2014. This may sound like a small sample size, but it’s actually a great sample size for Mormons, who are only about 1 – 1.5% of the U.S. population. The most recent sample size for current LDS members is a little smaller than previous RLS reports, and, for former LDS members, it’s a bit bigger, likely reflecting the changes in more people leaving the church.
The margin of error for Latter-day Saints is plus or minus 6.2%, and for former Saints it’s 8.1%.
There’s a reason my headline is not of the “we’re more religious than everybody else!” variety. Folks, throughout survey history, Mormons have always been more religious than nearly everybody else. That is still the case, many of my readers will be happy to know. But RNS is a news outlet, so we focus on what is new or has changed. For that I want to compare us to our own past selves, as measured by Pew through nearly two decades.
Here are five changes happening with current members, and four among those who’ve left the church.
Current Members
1. Diversity is increasing.
Pew found that “the portion of Latter-day Saints who are White has fallen from 85% in 2007 to 72% in 2023 – 24.” What’s more, the proportion of Hispanic members has doubled (from 6% to 12%), and Black members has tripled (from 2% to 6%).
A higher percentage of current members are immigrants than in the past, or at least had parents who were immigrants. In 2007, 13% of US Latter-day Saints said either they or their parents were not born in the US. Today, that has grown to 21%.
2. Fewer LDS families have kids or teenagers.
In 2007, almost half of LDS families in the U.S. were parents of children under 18. Today, that has dropped to 37%. That’s still high for religious groups in America (and especially for Christian groups), but it’s a decline from the LDS past.
This change can’t be explained by a markedly older population. Mormons’ median age was only three years higher than it was in 2007, rising from 41 to 44. (The median age for U.S. Christian adults in general was, gulp, 54 years old.)
3. LDS women have reversed the college graduation gap.
LDS women now outstrip LDS men in earning a bachelor’s degree (40% to 34%), whereas in 2007 women lagged 8 points behind men in college graduation rates.
Women’s growing educational achievement is driving the overall increase in Latter-day Saints with a four-year degree, which is now 36%.
4. Religiosity has slightly decreased (but is still high).
Latter-day Saints have become less religious on several measures over time, and most of that decline has happened only since the 2014 survey, as the table shows.
These are not dramatic drops, and compared to everyone else, Mormons are still acing religiosity. In fact, when Pew’s RLS was first published last year, it singled them out for excelling at daily prayer. However, LDS daily prayer has declined by nine points since 2007.
5. Political orientation is liberalizing somewhat.
Latter-day Saints are still profoundly Republican (73%), and that GOP identity is consistent across ages, education levels and gender.
However, Pew says Latter-day Saints have liberalized on some issues. Nearly half now say homosexuality should be accepted by society, which is almost double what it was in 2007 (24% to 46%).
